messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slows a step and lets Bram drift to the front. Chain mail and a shield make a friendlier first impression than a man in studded leather with too many knives.

He keeps his hands loose and away from the shortsword, hood back so the warden can see his face, and talks low out of the side of his mouth to the other two:

"Picks down mid-swing, mule cut loose, and he's not walking out to meet paying folk. Either the crew ran, or somebody's told him to stand there and look ordinary. Bram, you do the talking? I'll keep my eyes busy."

As they cross the yard, Pell does what he's done on a hundred rooftops. He reads the place without turning his head. Fresh tracks in the white dust and which way they run. The half-loaded cart and whether the traces were unbuckled or cut. Shed doors standing ajar. Whether the curtain in the house window twitches. And whether the warden's eyes keep flicking to something behind him or off to one side.

He stops about twenty feet short of the door, a little apart from Bram, with a clear line back to the spoil heaps if he needs one.

? Is a Perception roll warranted for scanning the yard and the house as we approach? And can I get an Insight read on the warden once he starts talking?

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I sheathe my sword and walk into the yard, shield resting at my side. As I approach, I look over the scattered tools and empty sheds for blood or signs of a struggle.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us for a sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?”

I stop a few paces short of the doorway.

“Quiet for a working day. Something happened?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa slows as the quarry opens up before them, and her first thought is not of the case or the gold. It is of the hammers set down in the dust, and the half-loaded cart, and the silence where there should be a working day.

She stops a little distance onto the yard, not yet in the doorway's shadow, and studies the man in the apron. Then she says, quiet enough that only Pell and Bram will hear her plainly:

"That's the warden, I think. He's not acting like a man eager to hand anything over — and no one's working. Keep your hands easy. Let me speak first."

She leaves her own hands open at her sides, the dagger at her belt untouched, and takes a few steps toward the house, stopping well short of arm's reach.

"Morning to you. Maela Thorn sent us from Beregost — she gave us her mark for the sealed case of dye-salts, for the coach that leaves by sunset." She keeps her voice level, without edge, but her eyes move over the yard again, over the scattered tools and the empty trace. "Is your day as strange as it looks?"

Bram sheathes his sword, shield at his side, and walks into the yard, looking over the scattered tools and empty sheds. He stops a few paces short of the doorway, gives his name, says Maela Thorn sent you for a sealed case of dye-salts, and asks if the man is the warden. He adds that the place is quiet for a working day and asks if something happened.

Sefa slows as the quarry opens up, then murmurs to you and Bram that the man in the apron looks like the warden, that he doesn't seem eager to hand anything over, and that no one is working. She tells you both to keep your hands easy and says she will speak first. Then she steps toward the house, hands open, dagger untouched, and stops well short of arm's reach. She says Maela Thorn sent you from Beregost with her mark for the sealed case, for the coach that leaves by sunset, and asks if his day is as strange as it looks.

You stop about twenty feet short of the door, a little apart from Bram, with a clear line back to the spoil heaps.

Reading the yard is a roof-runner's ordinary work, so it needs no roll. The dust holds a day's tracks, softened by wind but plain: a dozen or more pairs of boots heading down the cart track toward the Way, all together and unhurried, the prints evenly spaced. A mule's hoofprints run beside one man's boots, set a little apart from the rest. Nobody came up the track to meet them, and nothing was dragged. The cart traces weren't cut. Someone unbuckled them and looped them back over the shaft, the way a carter does when he expects to come back, or wants it to look that way. No doors are forced. The house window has no curtain, only shadow and the glow of a hearth, and nobody moves inside. One door stands ajar: a long low shed down by the lower cut, where the terraces drop into a darker, damper face.

The man in the apron hears Bram and Sefa out without unfolding his arms.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is low and dry with dust. "Yes. It's strange."

He looks past Bram at the cart, then back.

"Crew walked off. Noon bell yesterday. Three weeks, not a copper from the Gate." He says it flat, as if he has said it to himself all night. "They left the tools because the tools belong to the house. Let the house come pick them up."

You watch him while he talks and try to see what sits under the words. Your Insight read on him is not settled yet.

The house window has no curtain, only shadow and the glow of the hearth, and nobody moves in there. One door stands ajar: a long low shed down by the lower cut, where the terraces drop into a darker, damper face.

Bram checks the tools as he passes and finds no blood on them, none in the dust, and nothing knocked over. The hammers weren't dropped. A man laid one across a wedge, and two picks lean against the cart wheel, handles up. Bram has seen camps after a fight, and this looks nothing like one. It looks like men who put their tools down carefully and left.

Bram stops a few paces from the door and gives his name and Maela's errand. Sefa stops beside him, a little back and just out of the doorway's shadow, and adds the coach and the sunset. The man in the apron hears them both out without unfolding his arms.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is low and dry with dust. "Yes. It's strange."

He looks past Bram at the cart, then back.

"Crew walked off. Noon bell yesterday. Three weeks, not a copper from the Gate." He says it flat, as if he has said it to himself all night. "They left the tools because the tools belong to the house. Let the house come pick them up."

Pell watches him while he talks and tries to see what sits under the words.

Pell can read the anger easily. It sits in the set of the jaw and the way the man's fingers press white into his own sleeves. Pell can't get past it. Osric doesn't look like a man who fears whoever might be behind him, or like a man reciting a story someone gave him. If there's more under the anger, it stays where Pell can't reach it. Osric's face is a closed door with nothing to pick.

"The case is inside," Osric says. He doesn't step aside. "It stays inside till somebody tells me where the money went. Your Thorn woman paid for that salt. Somebody took it. Wasn't me, and it wasn't my lads." His eyes go to Sefa, then to Bram, the two who did the talking. "Did she pay? Who'd she pay it to?"

Behind him the hearth ticks and settles. The iron keys on his belt shift as he breathes. The thin smoke from the chimney rises straight up into the bright, windless late-morning air, and down by the lower cut the shed door stands as it did, a hand's width open onto the dark.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text: I wait for the man's answer, leaving the doorway clear and keeping my sword sheathed. From here, I glance at his apron and hands, then into whatever part of the house is visible behind him.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds where she is, watching the warden for the next sign — whether his weight shifts, whether his answer comes fast or slow.

When he gives no immediate answer, she does not press closer or raise her voice. She keeps her tone the same, a healer's calm with a hireling's practicality:

"We're not here to make your trouble ours, unless it has to be. We're here for the case. If there's something between us and that case, best we know it now, while the sun's still high enough to do something about it."

She glances once toward the house's one living sign — the smoke — then back to the man in the doorway. She is listening as much for what he doesn't say as for what he does. Behind her calm, she marks the yard's scattered tools and the empty cart again, trying to judge whether this is grief, fear, or a trap laid to look like grief.

Standing near Bram, she trusts his shield to be close if civility breaks. For now, she makes no move toward the Book of Shadows, no sign of the Lantern's light. Just a woman in studded leather, waiting on a man to choose his answer.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays where he is, thumbs hooked in his belt, and answers before the other two have to guess at it.

"We're couriers, master Hale. Nobody's told us what she paid or who to. We get ninety on delivery and not a copper before." He tips his chin at the empty traces. "So the same as your lads, near enough. Paid at the end, if the end comes."

He lets that sit a moment, then goes on in the same easy voice:

"Who carries your wages out from the Gate, then? Same man who'd carry her coin for the salt? A factor, a clerk of the house? Whose house, while we're at it." A small shrug. "If somebody's skimming both ends, Thorn will want that name as badly as you do. She's got a buyer's coach leaving at sunset, and she'll be shouting by suppertime. Better she shouts at the right door."

Then, as an offer rather than a demand:

"Write it down. Three weeks unpaid, what she owes, what you've never seen. Seal it with your own mark and we'll carry it with the case, straight into her hand. You keep a copy. If she's paid and someone's pocketed it, your letter's the first thing that says so with a witness."

His eyes slide once, unhurried, down toward the lower cut.

"And the long shed down there with the door open. One of yours left in a hurry, or is that where the mule went?"

Then he watches Osric's hands and the keys. Which one gets touched, if any, when the shed comes up?

Once the moment settles, she gives the smallest nod toward Pell's offer, as if it had been her own meaning too, and then focuses fully on the warden's answer, not on the obvious signs but on where his eyes go when he gives it.

cards.title: Insight: is the warden grieving, afraid, or setting a trap made to look like grief?

presses.text:
Sefa watches him through the space of a few heartbeats, and the picture that comes clear is not the one she first suspected.

He is not playing at grief. The warden is wrung out the way people get when they have stopped sleeping and stopped expecting help — not the large, theatrical sadness of a man performing for witnesses, but the smaller, heavier one of a man who has carried bad news alone for longer than one bad day. Grief, yes. But under it there is fear, not for himself; or not only for himself. The way he stands in the doorway is not the stance of a man guarding a trap. It is the stance of a man who has put his own body in front of something and does not know if that will be enough.

And there is the smear by his pocket. Pink against chalk dust. Not slaughter-red — old, wiped away, but not forgotten. The kind of mark a man gets when his hands have been pressed against a wound, or when he has used them to hold something hurt while it stopped moving.

He leans a little into the doorframe as if the morning weighs on him. His eyes go, without meaning to, toward the long shed down the lower cut. Then back to you. He is not checking for anyone behind you. He is trying to decide whether you are the people he has been dreading, or the ones he gave up hoping for.
presses.reply:
Thank you, that's a vivid read, and it tells me exactly where Sefa's attention goes. I'll keep that part as hers: she is watching the weight he carries, not the anger. She wants to know whether he is performing or worn down, and whether he stands in that doorway to guard a trap or to shield something.

What she finds there is the world's to say, though, so these stay proposals until the narration settles them:

- **What Osric feels.** Grief, fear, and for whom. The die you've seen decides how far her read gets. Who Osric really is decides what's there to find.
- **The pink smear and what made it.** It still isn't on the apron in the scene as I've described it. If there's any mark there, the narration will show it after the die, and it won't come with an explanation.
- **His glance toward the lower shed.** In the scene so far he has only looked past Bram at the cart. Where his eyes go next is his, and I'll show it in the narration if it happens.

When you're ready, press Onward or use one of your rerolls. Either way, the narration picks up from Sefa watching him exactly as you wrote it.

presses.text:
Sefa waits, and the patience costs her nothing. She has sat with the dying. Osric Hale has the look of a man who has sat with the dead.

She lets her weight settle onto her back foot, opening herself to whatever he says next — and to whatever in his face tells her whether the hand that waited outside his door is one of the company's, or simply one she doesn't see.

But she registers Pell's lead and Bram's stillness as part of the scene too: no one armed, no one crowding him. If she has new companions, they are the kind she can stand beside in a doorway like this, where death has already been before them and no one is shouting about it.

She says nothing, and she watches.

(Round 2 — one paragraph per character in this scene. Close this scene on the world as it stands: no question, offer, demand or wait put to one character, and no out-of-game note — the table asks every player what they do next.)

Bram Halloway: I wait for the man's answer, leaving the doorway clear and keeping my sword sheathed. From here, I glance at his apron and hands, then into whatever part of the house is visible behind him.

Sefa Marrin: Sefa holds where she is, watching the warden for the next sign — whether his weight shifts, whether his answer comes fast or slow.

When he gives no immediate answer, she does not press closer or raise her voice. She keeps her tone the same, a healer's calm with a hireling's practicality:

"We're not here to make your trouble ours, unless it has to be. We're here for the case. If there's something between us and that case, best we know it now, while the sun's still high enough to do something about it."

She glances once toward the house's one living sign — the smoke — then back to the man in the doorway. She is listening as much for what he doesn't say as for what he does. Behind her calm, she marks the yard's scattered tools and the empty cart again, trying to judge whether this is grief, fear, or a trap laid to look like grief.

Standing near Bram, she trusts his shield to be close if civility breaks. For now, she makes no move toward the Book of Shadows, no sign of the Lantern's light. Just a woman in studded leather, waiting on a man to choose his answer.

Pell Dunmore: Pell stays where he is, thumbs hooked in his belt, and answers before the other two have to guess at it.

"We're couriers, master Hale. Nobody's told us what she paid or who to. We get ninety on delivery and not a copper before." He tips his chin at the empty traces. "So the same as your lads, near enough. Paid at the end, if the end comes."

He lets that sit a moment, then goes on in the same easy voice:

"Who carries your wages out from the Gate, then? Same man who'd carry her coin for the salt? A factor, a clerk of the house? Whose house, while we're at it." A small shrug. "If somebody's skimming both ends, Thorn will want that name as badly as you do. She's got a buyer's coach leaving at sunset, and she'll be shouting by suppertime. Better she shouts at the right door."

Then, as an offer rather than a demand:

"Write it down. Three weeks unpaid, what she owes, what you've never seen. Seal it with your own mark and we'll carry it with the case, straight into her hand. You keep a copy. If she's paid and someone's pocketed it, your letter's the first thing that says so with a witness."

His eyes slide once, unhurried, down toward the lower cut.

"And the long shed down there with the door open. One of yours left in a hurry, or is that where the mule went?"

Then he watches Osric's hands and the keys. Which one gets touched, if any, when the shed comes up?

scenes.narration:
Osric doesn't answer straight away. Bram keeps clear of the doorway with his sword in its sheath and looks at what there is to see. The man's hands are a cutter's hands: broad, split at the knuckles, the nails worn to the quick, and no weapon anywhere near them. White dust is ground into the creases of his apron like flour. Near the pocket a faint smear of grit shows a different colour, pinkish, the shade of a rose gone pale, where something was wiped off once and not brushed away.

Past his shoulder Bram can see part of one room. There's a hearth with a kettle hooked over the coals, and a scrubbed table holding a fat book bound in stained canvas, a pen stuck through its strap. Next to the book sits a small case of dark oak, banded in brass, about the size of a loaf, with a disc of red wax across the clasp. A coat hangs on a peg just inside the door, and a blackthorn stick leans under it.

Sefa says her piece in the same level voice, and while she talks she watches how he takes it.

Sefa reads him plainly. He isn't setting a trap. He hasn't once glanced behind him into the house or across the yard the way a man does when someone else is waiting for a signal. Nobody else is in there. What she sees is anger, and under it something that looks a lot like shame: a man who kept a crew together for years and couldn't keep them through three weeks. The skin under his eyes is grey. He hasn't slept.

"Something between you and the case," Osric says to her. "Aye. The money."

Pell answers before anyone else can, easy-voiced, thumbs in his belt. Osric hears him out, and his jaw works at *same as your lads, near enough* as if he'd like to argue it and can't.

"House is Vandarren. In the Gate. Patriar house, or used to be." He says the name like a stone he's been carrying in his pocket. "Their man's Pryce. Factor. Salt goes out of here sealed, and the money for it goes to Pryce. Pryce sends the wages back by runner, first of the month and the fifteenth." A beat. "Didn't. Twice now."

He thinks about the letter longer than he thought about anything else Pell said.

"Write it. Aye." He nods once, slowly. "Witnessed. That I'll do. You read it out to her, in front of her, not after." His eyes go to the sun, already high over the white faces, and then to the coat on its peg. "I'm for the town at noon myself. Lads'll be drinking it out somewhere. Want them to hear it from me, not from a broadsheet."

The shed is the last thing Pell asks about. Osric's hand doesn't go to the keys at all. It stays where it is, pressed flat against his sleeve, and Pell can see why: the shed door hangs on warped boards and has no lock to need a key. What Osric does is look past Pell, not at the shed but below it, at the lower face where the terraces drop away into stone stained dark with damp.

"Lower cutting-shed. Nobody in it." He looks back. "Door's warped. Won't shut. Mule went with Hob, the carter. He was owed the most."

Sefa catches what Pell's eyes catch, and reads something in it Pell's eyes can't: it isn't fear of anyone. It's an old dislike of a place, the look a man gives a room where something once went wrong.

Osric unfolds his arms at last, turns into the house and sits down heavily at the table. He leaves the door open behind him. He slides the pen free of its strap, opens the canvas-bound book to a clean page at the back and starts to write, slowly, pressing hard, his lips moving a little over the words. The oak case sits at his elbow with its red wax catching the light from the hearth. The kettle starts to tick as it comes to the boil.

- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.

- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds very still while Osric speaks, because she knows that kind of answer when she hears it. Not the words only — the way a man shapes them when he has been sitting too long with something too heavy, and has finally set a little of it down in front of strangers.

She keeps her voice low, and unhurried, as though there were all the time in the world before dusk. There isn't. But he doesn't need to know that from her lips yet.

"Master Hale," she says, "the case is why we came. But no man alive could walk in on what you're telling us and ask only for the box." A pause, so he can decide whether that is kindness, or simply the plain truth. "You don't know what it was. That's the worst part of a sickbed, I think — the not knowing. I was a novice in a hospice in the Gate. I know the look of a man who has been told he did all he could, and hasn't yet believed it."

She doesn't say he looks guilty. She doesn't say he looks innocent, either. She lets the words settle and watches.

When it comes to the shed, her gaze follows his to it, and holds there a beat too long before returning to him. There is nothing accusing in it. If anything, her expression has gone careful, the kind of careful a healer wears on a landing where something may still be breathing on the other side of a door.

"What kind of work did they do before they were shut in?" she asks gently, as though the question were small. Her eyes move once toward the smoky air and then back. "And the rose-coloured dust on their gear and aprons — is that from the new salts, or was it always here? You said the shed was the only thing that changed. I'd rather know what 'changed' means before any of us is part of it."

She has not offered her light yet. The Lantern is there, behind her eyes, a warmth at the base of her thought. She holds it banked, ready, but makes no sign. She has seen fear put on a good face before, and she has seen grief do the same. She wants one honest thing, if Hale can give it: the truth about the thing they would be walking into if they go to that shed.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell waits until the pen is moving, then steps up to the threshold. He doesn't cross it. He leans a shoulder on the frame where Osric can see both his hands.

"Pryce, Vandarren, first and fifteenth. She'll have that in her ear before she's got the lid off." He nods at the oak case. "Whose seal's on the wax? Yours or the house's? Thorn will look at it before she looks at us, and I'd rather know now if it's meant to say Vandarren."

His eyes drop, unhurried, to the pale rose smear by Osric's apron pocket.

scenes.narration:
Osric doesn't look up when Pell's shadow falls across the threshold. The pen keeps scratching.

"Mine." He tips the pen at the wax without lifting his wrist from the page. "Quarry mark. A W with the hammer through it. House never sent a seal and never asked for one." He dips the pen and goes on. "That colour's the salt. Grows on the wet walls down the low cuts, rose-white, like frost that won't melt. You scrape it, dry it on the slates, it goes in the case. Nothing's leaked. I sealed it myself, day before yesterday." His eyes go to his apron, and he brushes once at the smear with the back of his hand. It doesn't come off. "Thirty years it's been on those walls. Nobody wanted it till the spring."

Pell turns back to the yard. As he starts down the slope Osric raises his voice for the first time, flat and carrying:

"Mind the boards down there. Old workings under. And don't stand about at the low face. Air's thick."

Then he bends back to the page.

Sefa speaks into the quiet that's left. Osric's pen stops at *a novice in a hospice*. It stays stopped while she talks about the not knowing, and the man who was told he did all he could. He sits with that a moment, looking at the wet line of ink in front of him.

"Didn't do all I could," he says. "Did what the house paid for." He sets the pen to the paper again. "Nobody was shut in. They worked the faces, upper and lower, same as any year. Cut, split, cart. Scraped the salt when there was an order." He glances at her, brief and dry. "And I never said the shed changed. Shed's just a shed. Door's warped."

Bram's turn comes while he blots the first lines. Osric hears *won't promise she'll pay another man's debts* and nods as if he expected nothing better.

"She needn't pay it. She needs to know it." He counts with the end of the pen against the table. "Fourteen men. Three weeks. Two silver a day for a cutter, less for the boys. Forty-two gold, near enough. Hob's owed more, he fed the mule out of his own purse. Not counting mine." The pen goes back to the page. "Case goes when the letter's sealed and she's read it back to me." A short jerk of his chin at Sefa. "Not before."

From the doorway Bram follows Osric's earlier look down the slope. The lower face is a different stone from the rest: greyer, streaked dark where water seeps from the cracks, and spotted with a pale crust that catches the sun faintly pink. Below it the ground flattens into a shelf of trodden spoil. Grey planks lie across it here and there, laid flat over something.

Pell gets there in a few minutes, walking openly. At the lower cutting-shed he puts his face to the hand's-width gap and looks in without crossing the sill. It's long and dim, with split-stone benches along both walls. Rows of flat slates are stacked on racks, the drying-slates Osric spoke of, a few still dusted pink. In the middle of the floor stands an iron brazier on three legs, stone cold. The ash in its pan has fused into a crust the colour of a pale rose. From the doorway the shed smells of old smoke and wet stone, nothing more.

Past the shed is the low face. The seeps run down it in dark ribbons, and where they spread the stone grows that rose-white crust, thick as hoarfrost in the cracks. In places someone has scraped it back to bare grey in clean flat strokes. Pell reads that as the work of days, not hours, and it's the same handwork all along the face. The prints on the shelf are the crew's: many boots over many days, trodden into a hard white mat, all coming and going by the same path from the yard. Nothing is fresh and nothing has been covered over. He can find no boot that came from anywhere but the track.

The planks are what Bram saw from above. There are four or five of them, grey and furred with damp, laid across square mouths cut into the shelf. Under the nearest one Pell can hear water. It isn't flowing, just a slow drip landing on a still surface somewhere below. The spoil around the plank edges is darker and softer than the rest, and it gives a little under the heel.

Up at the house the kettle boils over with a hiss onto the coals. Osric reaches out and swings it off the hook without looking, and keeps writing.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.text:
Sefa turns at the first word of Osric’s warning, steps up beside Bram in the doorway, and calls after Pell just loud enough to carry over the yard:

“Mind the boards, Pell — old workings under. Don’t stand about at the low face.” Then, as Pell walks on, she adds, lower, as if to herself: “Air that thick doesn’t keep warnings for strangers.”

She turns back into the house, choosing her next words before she says them. “Master Hale, before that letter’s sealed, tell us plain what you meant by the low face air. Have you been down there since your crew stopped? Did the men complain of headaches, or lamps guttering, or a sweetness in the air — anything before they were gone?”

She looks from him to the kettle still steaming, and then to Bram. “If it’s bad air settling in old workings, Pell should know how far it runs before he walks into it. I’d rather not carry news of a fourth man overcome to Thorn by sundown.”

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell! Old workings under those boards, and bad air at the low face. Keep clear of both.”

I turn back to Osric. “This salt—anyone taken ill scraping it? Coughing, dizzy, anything like that? We ought to know before we carry it.”

I stay at the doorway, keeping Pell in sight while Sefa handles the letter.

scenes.narration:
Sefa and Bram call after Pell almost together, her voice and then his, and the warning carries out over the white yard and down the slope toward the lower cut. The quarry is quiet enough that every word goes the whole way.

Inside, Osric's pen doesn't stop for the shouting. It stops when Sefa comes back in and asks her questions, and it stays stopped while Bram asks his from the doorway.

"Not coughing." He sets the pen down crosswise on the page. "Sleepy. Man works the low face a long stretch, he gets heavy in the eyes, slow in the hands. Send him up into the sun, he's right by supper." He rubs a thumb along the edge of the table. "Headaches, some. Lamps burn fine. That's why I said it. Air's thick down there. It doesn't choke you. It just sits on you."

He thinks about the sweetness longer.

"Shed's the same when the brazier's going. Wet weather we dry the salt on the slates over a bit of fire. Room smells like a bakehouse. Lads used to nod off over the racks." He says it like any other fact about the place, the way he'd tell them the faces get slick in rain. "Haven't been down since they went. No call to."

Then Sefa's last line lands, and his head comes up.

"Fourth." He looks at her for the first time since he sat down, flat and hard. "Nobody's been overcome. Nobody said three." His fingers have found his sleeve and pressed in. A moment passes. When he picks up the pen again he says, to the page and not to her, "Not lately."

He writes the rest quickly, with no lip-moving now, and blots it with the heel of his hand. Then he takes the page by its top corner and tears it out of the canvas book along the fold, slowly, so it comes away clean. The book stays open on the table with its stub showing, and behind the stub are the ruled pages of earlier years, columns of names and days in the same heavy hand.

He lays the torn page beside the oak case. From the doorway Bram can read the first lines without trying, the letters pressed nearly through the paper:

*To Maela Thorn, apothecary, Beregost. From Osric Hale, warden at Whitestone for House Vandarren of the Gate. Fourteen men three weeks unpaid by the house. Wages to come by Pryce the factor's runner on the first and the fifteenth. Did not come, twice. You paid for this salt. Ask him where it went.*

Below that the hand gets smaller, a list of names with a sum against each, and at the bottom a blank space with a short line drawn for a mark.

The kettle has stopped ticking. The hearth settles. Out past Bram's shoulder the sun stands nearly at the top of the sky over the white faces, and the coat on its peg sways a little in the draught from the open door.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his heel off the soft spoil and steps back the way he came, onto the hard white mat of the crew's path. He doesn't go near the planks or the drip under them. Thick air at a low face is a warning a man hears once.

He stops by the shed door long enough for one more look at the brazier and its rose-coloured crust, and fixes the picture in his head. He doesn't touch it, doesn't breathe over it, and doesn't take a pinch. It isn't his salt, and he doesn't know yet what it does when it's burned.

Then he walks back up to the house at an easy pace, a man done stretching his legs, and keeps half an eye on the sun.

At the door, quietly to Bram and Sefa:

"Nothing down there but honest scraping. Weeks of it, all the crew's own boots, nobody sneaking salt out the back. Planks over old shafts, water underneath. Nobody should stand on them." A small tilt of the head toward the slope. "One odd thing. The brazier in the drying-shed has pink ash fused in the pan. Somebody's burned the stuff."

Then, to Osric, with no edge to it, just a courier's question:

"Master Hale, the brazier in the drying-shed. You heat the slates to dry the salt, or has someone been burning it on purpose? Thorn's buyer will ask what it does in a fire, and I'd rather not find out on the road."

He glances at the page to see how far the letter has got, and at the sun through the doorway.

"When that's read back and sealed, we'll take the case and go. If you're walking to town at noon anyway, you're welcome on the road with us. Safer in four, and Thorn can hear it from your own mouth."

scenes.narration:
Pell keeps his heel off the soft spoil and goes back the way he came, onto the hard white mat the crew's boots have packed down. The drip under the planks fades behind him. At the lower cutting-shed he stops at the door with his weight on the flat stone step outside it, the strip of ground the crew must have crossed ten thousand times. He looks in through the hand's-width gap at the brazier and its rose-coloured crust, and keeps his face back from it.

The step moves.

It doesn't crack like a board. It sinks, the whole slab tilting slowly under his boots, and the white mat around it splits along a seam he couldn't have seen. Under the dust there's no rock, only an old timber lid gone soft as bread with damp. Then it falls in, and Pell goes with it in a slide of grit and rotten wood and stone.

He drops about eight feet and hits water. It's so cold it knocks the breath out of him. Under the water his boots slam into a stone floor, his hip and shoulder scrape down a rough wall, and the slab from the step comes down behind him. His body takes a bruising and his shoulder is grazed raw. Then the falling stone stops. The water settles, and Pell is standing in it up to his chest.

His left leg won't come up.

It's caught at the shin, under the water, between the floor and something heavy and square. It isn't crushing the bone. It's holding him, the way a door holds a coat caught in it. He can wiggle his toes in his boot, but he can't pull the foot back an inch.

Light comes down from the ragged hole above, a square of bright noon sky with dust still drifting through it. In that light Pell can see he's in a cutting: a square gallery worked by hand, the walls scored with old pick-strokes and furred white with salt crust. Darkness runs off one way, past the edge of the light. On the near wall a water-mark shows a hand's breadth above the surface, a band of darker stone, and above it a fainter one higher still. A thin trickle runs down one crack from the seep and slips into the water without a sound. The water is so still the light lies on it like a sheet.

The thing pinning him sits half out of the water at his side. It's a squared block of white stone, bigger than a cartwheel, too regular for rubble. It must have stood against the wall once. Now it has tipped forward off a low ledge and come to rest across his shin. Its face is tilted up toward the hole, and the light from above shows something cut into it. It isn't pick-marks. It's a disc with rays round it, worn soft by water and salt, and a ring of small notched marks runs round the rays like a tally.

Behind the block, where it used to stand, the wall is a different colour. It's flat, smooth and grey, like plaster laid over a hollow.

A long timber lies across the gallery near him, half in the water. It's an old prop, black with wet and still sound at the core.

The air down here is still and has a faint sweet smell, like the inside of a bread oven an hour after baking. It doesn't choke him. It just sits on him.

Up above, the square of sky is quiet. The splash and the crack of rotten timber went up into the bright air over the lower cut, and after that the quarry is as silent as before, except for the trickle down the crack and the water lapping against Pell's chest.

 (Out of game) None of these needed a roll:
1) Done as declared. Pell came back onto the crew's packed path and kept well clear of the planks; that's ordinary care, no roll.
2) Done as declared. He looked at the brazier from the shed step, touched nothing, took no salt and didn't breathe over it; looking needs no roll.
3) This couldn't happen. The shed step gave way under him before he set off, and he's pinned in the flooded working.
4) This couldn't happen either. He fell before he reached the house, so Bram and Sefa haven't heard his report. What they caught of the crash is for their own scene.

He stops by the shed door long enough for one more look at the brazier and its rose-coloured crust, and fixes the picture in his head. He doesn't touch it, doesn't breathe over it, and doesn't take a pinch. It isn't his salt, and he doesn't know yet what it does when it's burned.

Then he walks back up to the house at an easy pace, a man done stretching his legs, and keeps half an eye on the sun.

At the door, quietly to Bram and Sefa:

"Nothing down there but honest scraping. Weeks of it, all the crew's own boots, nobody sneaking salt out the back. Planks over old shafts, water underneath. Nobody should stand on them." A small tilt of the head toward the slope. "One odd thing. The brazier in the drying-shed has pink ash fused in the pan. Somebody's burned the stuff."

Then, to Osric, with no edge to it, just a courier's question:

"Master Hale, the brazier in the drying-shed. You heat the slates to dry the salt, or has someone been burning it on purpose? Thorn's buyer will ask what it does in a fire, and I'd rather not find out on the road."

He glances at the page to see how far the letter has got, and at the sun through the doorway.

"When that's read back and sealed, we'll take the case and go. If you're walking to town at noon anyway, you're welcome on the road with us. Safer in four, and Thorn can hear it from your own mouth."

Your narration:
<<<
Pell keeps his heel off the soft spoil and goes back the way he came, onto the hard white mat the crew's boots have packed down. The drip under the planks fades behind him. At the lower cutting-shed he stops at the door with his weight on the flat stone step outside it, the strip of ground the crew must have crossed ten thousand times. He looks in through the hand's-width gap at the brazier and its rose-coloured crust, and keeps his face back from it.

The step moves.

It doesn't crack like a board. It sinks, the whole slab tilting slowly under his boots, and the white mat around it splits along a seam he couldn't have seen. Under the dust there's no rock, only an old timber lid gone soft as bread with damp. Then it falls in, and Pell goes with it in a slide of grit and rotten wood and stone.

He drops about eight feet and hits water. It's so cold it knocks the breath out of him. Under the water his boots slam into a stone floor, his hip and shoulder scrape down a rough wall, and the slab from the step comes down behind him. His body takes a bruising and his shoulder is grazed raw. Then the falling stone stops. The water settles, and Pell is standing in it up to his chest.

His left leg won't come up.

It's caught at the shin, under the water, between the floor and something heavy and square. It isn't crushing the bone. It's holding him, the way a door holds a coat caught in it. He can wiggle his toes in his boot, but he can't pull the foot back an inch.

Light comes down from the ragged hole above, a square of bright noon sky with dust still drifting through it. In that light Pell can see he's in a cutting: a square gallery worked by hand, the walls scored with old pick-strokes and furred white with salt crust. Darkness runs off one way, past the edge of the light. On the near wall a water-mark shows a hand's breadth above the surface, a band of darker stone, and above it a fainter one higher still. A thin trickle runs down one crack from the seep and slips into the water without a sound. The water is so still the light lies on it like a sheet.

The thing pinning him sits half out of the water at his side. It's a squared block of white stone, bigger than a cartwheel, too regular for rubble. It must have stood against the wall once. Now it has tipped forward off a low ledge and come to rest across his shin. Its face is tilted up toward the hole, and the light from above shows something cut into it. It isn't pick-marks. It's a disc with rays round it, worn soft by water and salt, and a ring of small notched marks runs round the rays like a tally.

Behind the block, where it used to stand, the wall is a different colour. It's flat, smooth and grey, like plaster laid over a hollow.

A long timber lies across the gallery near him, half in the water. It's an old prop, black with wet and still sound at the core.

The air down here is still and has a faint sweet smell, like the inside of a bread oven an hour after baking. It doesn't choke him. It just sits on him.

Up above, the square of sky is quiet. The splash and the crack of rotten timber went up into the bright air over the lower cut, and after that the quarry is as silent as before, except for the trickle down the crack and the water lapping against Pell's chest.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Not lately,” I repeat, quietly. “Then when? Did they recover?”

I look towards Pell and call, “The salt makes men drowsy. Worse when heated—don't light anything in there.”

Then I turn back to Osric. “We'll keep the case sealed. But if there's a danger Thorn needs to hear, send that warning with the wages letter. Whoever opens it may not know what your lads learned.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa meets his hard look and does not flinch from it.

“Forgive the word, Master Hale. I had only the three of us in mind, and Pell walking down there. I said ‘fourth’ without counting it. No count meant against your crew.”

She lets it lie there — not apology carried too far, just a correction offered plainly. As he tears the page out, she doesn’t crowd him. When he lays it beside the case, she says quietly, “May I?” and takes it up only when he doesn’t object.

She reads it back word for word, exactly as it’s written, her voice even and unhurried; where the list of names begins, she reads each one and each sum, her finger following the line beneath the paper, not skipping. Then she sets it down again beside the case.

“That’s word for word, Master Hale. Nothing added, nothing rounded. Your mark, if you’ll make it, and one of us will witness it. Then the case, and we’ll put this in Maela’s hand before the coach leaves.”

As she speaks, she glances once toward the doorway, where Bram keeps sight of the slope.

“Is Pell still in the open? I won’t shout again unless he’s gone off the boards.”

scenes.narration:
Bram says it again, quietly: "Not lately." Osric's pen stops. He doesn't look up at once. When he does, he looks past Bram, out through the door to where the slope drops toward the lower cut.

"Three year back." He sets the pen down in the fold of the book. "Most come up right by supper. One didn't."

That's all he gives. His mouth closes on it.

Bram turns in the doorway and calls down the slope. "Pell! The salt makes men drowsy. Worse when it's heated. Don't light anything in there!"

His voice crosses the white yard and reaches the lower cut, and nothing comes back. The crew's path runs empty down to the shelf. The shed stands where it stood, its warped door a hand's width open. Bram can't see Pell on the path, on the shelf or at the low face. Low over the shed step, where the white mat meets the door, a haze of dust hangs in the still noon air, thicker than anything a man's boots would raise. It hasn't settled. Under it, where the flat stone of the step ought to show pale, Bram sees a dark ragged patch instead.

Behind him the kettle sits off its hook, and the coals still spit where it boiled over.

Bram turns back to the table and says what he meant to say: keep the case sealed, and send the warning with the wage letter, because whoever opens it may not know what Osric's lads learned. Osric hears him out. He picks the pen up again and turns the torn page round.

"Drowsy's not a danger. Not up top." He writes anyway. He bears down hard on a short line squeezed in under the names, above the blank for his mark. "There. Don't say I didn't."

Sefa doesn't look away from his hard stare. She tells him plainly that she said "fourth" with only the three of them in mind, and Pell walking down there, and meant no count against his crew. Osric's fingers ease off his sleeve. He gives a single grunt, which is as near to "aye" as he gets, and goes back to blotting the new line.

When he lays the page down by the case, Sefa asks, "May I?" He doesn't stop her, so she takes it up and reads it back to him word for word in her even voice: the greeting to Maela Thorn; Osric Hale, warden at Whitestone for House Vandarren of the Gate; fourteen men, three weeks unpaid; Pryce the factor's runner on the first and the fifteenth, who didn't come, twice; *You paid for this salt. Ask him where it went.* Then the names. She follows each one with her finger under the line: a cutter, four gold and two silver; another the same; the boys at less; Hob the carter at the bottom of the list with the largest sum, *and the mule's keep*. Last she reads the line Osric squeezed in at Bram's word:

*Salt makes men sleepy if they work it long. Do not dry it over a fire in a shut room.*

Osric listens with his eyes shut, as though he's checking her against the words in his head. When she sets the page down he opens them.

"That's it." He takes the pen and scratches his mark on the line: the W with the hammer through it, the same mark as on the wax. Then he lays the pen crosswise on the page beside it, where a witness's hand would go.

Sefa glances toward the doorway and asks whether Pell is still out in the open. At that, Osric's head comes up. He looks at Bram's back, framed in the door. Then he pushes himself up from the table, comes and stands beside Bram, and looks down the slope.

He sees the dust over the shed step, and his face changes. It isn't anger now.

"Shed step." His voice is low and flat. "There's an old cut under it. Under the whole shelf." His hand has gone to the doorframe and is gripping it. "Water in it. Always."

No sound comes up from the lower cut. The haze over the step is thinning in the windless air, and the dark patch under it is plain to see. The sun stands almost straight overhead. On the table behind them, the case sits beside the marked letter with its wax unbroken. The pen still lies across the blank where a witness's mark should go.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops trying to yank the leg. Wrenching against a block that size only tears the shin, and he knows it. He keeps his chin up, breathes slowly through his nose, and doesn't gulp the sweet air.

First he shouts, as loud and flat as a runner calling across rooftops, aimed straight up at the square of sky:

"BRAM! SEFA! Lower shed! I'm down a hole under the step! Leg's pinned, water to my chest! Don't run in! The ground's hollow round the shed door, the step's just a lid! Come along the crew's path and stay off the flagstone! Bring Hale! And tell him the air down here smells sweet!"

While he waits for an answer, he works with what he has. He shrugs the pack round to his front, holding it above the water, and digs out the silk rope. He ties a loose loop in one end so it's ready to throw up the moment a face shows at the hole. He doesn't drop the pack. The potions are in it.

Then he reaches for the old prop timber. He doesn't mean to free himself with it. A man with arms like his won't shift that block alone. He wants to drag it close and wedge one end under the edge of the block nearest his shin, the other end against the floor or the ledge, ready for Bram to lean on from above or beside him. If he can get the end under without straining, he also feels down his own leg with his free hand: where exactly the block bears, whether there's a gap he could slide the boot sideways through if the stone lifted even an inch, and whether the boot laces could come loose to give him that inch.

He keeps an eye on the water-marks on the wall. Is the surface creeping toward the dark band? He doesn't touch the smooth grey plaster or the carved disc. Whatever is walled up behind it can wait until he has two working legs.

Quietly, to himself, teeth already chattering: "Honest scraping. Nobody sneaking. Brilliant, Dunmore."

? Can they hear me from the house at this distance? And does the sweet air call for any saves I should know about?

Close this scene on the world as it stands: no question, offer, demand or wait put to one character, and no out-of-game note — the table asks every player what they do next.)

Pell Dunmore: Pell stops trying to yank the leg. Wrenching against a block that size only tears the shin, and he knows it. He keeps his chin up, breathes slowly through his nose, and doesn't gulp the sweet air.

First he shouts, as loud and flat as a runner calling across rooftops, aimed straight up at the square of sky:

"BRAM! SEFA! Lower shed! I'm down a hole under the step! Leg's pinned, water to my chest! Don't run in! The ground's hollow round the shed door, the step's just a lid! Come along the crew's path and stay off the flagstone! Bring Hale! And tell him the air down here smells sweet!"

While he waits for an answer, he works with what he has. He shrugs the pack round to his front, holding it above the water, and digs out the silk rope. He ties a loose loop in one end so it's ready to throw up the moment a face shows at the hole. He doesn't drop the pack. The potions are in it.

Then he reaches for the old prop timber. He doesn't mean to free himself with it. A man with arms like his won't shift that block alone. He wants to drag it close and wedge one end under the edge of the block nearest his shin, the other end against the floor or the ledge, ready for Bram to lean on from above or beside him. If he can get the end under without straining, he also feels down his own leg with his free hand: where exactly the block bears, whether there's a gap he could slide the boot sideways through if the stone lifted even an inch, and whether the boot laces could come loose to give him that inch.

He keeps an eye on the water-marks on the wall. Is the surface creeping toward the dark band? He doesn't touch the smooth grey plaster or the carved disc. Whatever is walled up behind it can wait until he has two working legs.

Quietly, to himself, teeth already chattering: "Honest scraping. Nobody sneaking. Brilliant, Dunmore."

? Can they hear me from the house at this distance? And does the sweet air call for any saves I should know about?

scenes.narration:
Pell hits the thick air at the surface still gasping, and the cold gets into his chest before anything else. Through the hole he can just hear a voice from up the slope. It's Bram, small and flattened by the stone, and only pieces of it reach him: "*…drowsy… don't light…*"

(Pell: sound carries both ways in a quarry this quiet. Bram and Sefa's own scene settles whether your shout reaches the house. The sweet air needs no save while nothing down here is burning. If that changes, I'll warn you before it bites.)

Pell fills his lungs and sends his shout straight up at the square of sky, flat and loud. The gallery throws it back at him off the wet walls, so for a moment the whole working is full of his voice: Bram, Sefa, the lower shed, the hollow step, the crew's path, bring Hale, the sweet air. Then the shout is gone up into the bright noon, and the only sound left is the trickle running down its crack.

He keeps his chin up and breathes slowly through his nose. He swings the pack round to his chest and holds it clear of the water with one forearm, the satchel still buckled inside it. Working one-handed by feel, he gets the silk rope out and ties a loose loop in the end. His fingers are already stiff. He drapes the coil over his shoulder, where it stays dry and is ready to throw.

The old prop lies close enough to reach if he stretches. He hooks it with his fingertips, then gets a hand round it and pulls it in through the water. It's heavy with wet, but it floats low and comes easily. The block tipped forward off its ledge, and on the near side its lower edge rests on the rubble that came down with it. There's a gap there, an inch or two of loose stone and silt. Pell feeds the end of the prop into it, slowly, until the timber bites. The other end he settles against the foot of the ledge. He doesn't lean on it. It's wedged and waiting.

Then he slides his free hand down his own leg underwater.

The block bears just below his knee and across the whole front of the shin, and presses his leg back against the ledge's broken edge. Rubble from the fall has packed in round the boot on both sides like mortar. No gap lets the foot slip sideways, and the shin itself is caught above the boot, so loosening the laces wouldn't give him his inch. His fingertips tell him what the job is. Before anyone can lever, they have to dig the packed stone out from round the block, under water, by hand, with someone bailing. That takes two people up here working without a break, and it isn't quick. At that pace the block comes free about when the light goes, around sunset. One person alone can't shift it at all, prop or no prop.

He looks at the wall. The dark band is still a hand's breadth above the surface, and he can't see the water climbing toward it. The seep never pauses, though, and it has nowhere to go but in.

He doesn't touch the carved disc or the smooth grey plaster behind it. Pell's teeth have started to chatter. Overhead the sky in the ragged hole is empty and blue, and a little dust is still sifting down through it.

 (Out of game) None of the four needed a roll: Pell did each one just as declared, and the narration shows it. The shout went up, the rope is looped and coiled on his shoulder, the prop is wedged under the block's near edge, and feeling down his leg told him the block is pressing on his shin itself, so neither slipping the boot nor loosening the laces will free him.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa is already moving before Osric finishes the word *Always*. She steps past him and Bram into the daylight, calling down the slope as she goes:

“Pell! Answer if you can hear us!” Then, off that shout, to no one in particular: “Not a sound — come on.”

She doesn’t wait for a plan. She turns her head back only far enough to fix Bram with a look that says *with me*, then starts down toward the lower cut at a walk that’s almost a run, keeping to the rutted track where the ground has been packed hard by the cart.

“Stay off the boards where you can,” she calls to Bram over the white glare. “And don’t get between me and him once we’re in.” There is no command in it now, only the intensity of someone who has worked through worse in a ward and knows what the first moments matter.

As her boots leave the last flat ground, she closes one hand around her prayer beads and speaks a single word, soft as a vigil:

“Light.”

A clear, pale radiance rises from the worn beads at her neck, bright enough for the shadows under the shed but throwing no heat, no cracked wood, no spark. She keeps it low by her chest, where it won’t blind her.

Her stride slows only at the edge of the lower cut, where the ground begins to look shelved and unsettled. There she pauses a heartbeat, searching the dark under the shed for any shape, any stirring, any gleam of Pell’s gear — and for where the old working might have swallowed a man.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell's out of sight. Step may have given way.”

I pull the rope from my pack and head down the crew's path, stopping well short of the shelf and any cracked ground or boards.

“Osric, show us where solid ground ends. Sefa, I'll need you with the rope.”

I call, “Pell! Can you hear me?”

From firm ground, I look for Pell through the broken step and for a stout anchor for the rope. I keep off the shelf—no sense putting another man through it.

scenes.narration:
Sefa is out of the door before Osric has finished the word, into the white glare. "Pell! Answer if you can hear us!" Her voice goes out across the yard and down the slope. Bram is a step behind her, already pulling the coil of hempen rope from his belt, with his own call and his sharp word over his shoulder to Osric: show us where the solid ground ends.

Halfway down the crew's path, Sefa closes her hand round the prayer beads at her neck and says the one word. A pale, even light rises from the wooden beads, a light with no heat in it and no spark. It's faint in the noon sun, but it'll be enough under the shed's shadow. She holds it low against her chest.

Then the ground answers them.

A voice comes up out of the shelf ahead of them, flat and broken by the stone it has to climb through. They catch it in pieces, the way you hear a shout from a cellar:

"*…BRAM! SEFA!… lower shed!… under the step!… pinned… water to my chest!… don't run in!… hollow… door… crew's path… off the flagstone!… bring Hale!… smells sweet!…*"

Then nothing but the drip from somewhere under the planks, and the dust still settling over the dark patch where the step used to be.

Osric has come out after them with his coat left on the peg. He doesn't hurry, but he doesn't stop either, and when Bram halts well short of the shelf he comes up beside him and points with two fingers, the way a man points at stone he has cut.

"Path's rock as far as that brown stone." It's a rust-coloured boulder sunk in the white mat about fifteen feet short of the shed door. "Past it, it's spoil laid over old timber. The whole shelf. Thirty years we walked it." His mouth sets. "Step was a lid. Nobody knew."

He turns his hand to the left, toward the foot of the low face, where the grey stone comes down to the shelf in a ridge of bare rock dark with seep. "Rock runs along the face. Gets you within five, six feet of the hole on that side. No closer." Set into that ridge, a little above the mat, is an iron ring as thick as a man's thumb, brown with rust and leaded into the stone. "Lowering ring. Older than me. It'll hold a cart."

Sefa's light picks out the ragged lip of the hole beyond. It's a gap about four feet across, edged with soft black timber and broken white crust. Below it there's only the glint of still water.

"Cut runs back under the face," Osric says, lower now. "Water stands four foot in summer. Five after rain." He stays on the path behind the brown stone with his feet planted. He doesn't step onto the rock ridge, and he doesn't look at the hole for long.

The sun stands almost straight overhead. The ring waits in its stone. Bram's rope is in his hands, and the hole lies six feet past the end of the good rock.

 (Out of game) None of the three needed a roll, since each was certain: Sefa cast Light, a cantrip, onto her beads; Bram took the rope out (it was coiled at his belt) and stopped short of the shelf; and Sefa called out to Pell and walked down to the lower cut. The narration showed all three happening as declared.

“Stay off the boards where you can,” she calls to Bram over the white glare. “And don’t get between me and him once we’re in.” There is no command in it now, only the intensity of someone who has worked through worse in a ward and knows what the first moments matter.

As her boots leave the last flat ground, she closes one hand around her prayer beads and speaks a single word, soft as a vigil:

“Light.”

A clear, pale radiance rises from the worn beads at her neck, bright enough for the shadows under the shed but throwing no heat, no cracked wood, no spark. She keeps it low by her chest, where it won’t blind her.

Her stride slows only at the edge of the lower cut, where the ground begins to look shelved and unsettled. There she pauses a heartbeat, searching the dark under the shed for any shape, any stirring, any gleam of Pell’s gear — and for where the old working might have swallowed a man.

I pull the rope from my pack and head down the crew's path, stopping well short of the shelf and any cracked ground or boards.

“Osric, show us where solid ground ends. Sefa, I'll need you with the rope.”

I call, “Pell! Can you hear me?”

From firm ground, I look for Pell through the broken step and for a stout anchor for the rope. I keep off the shelf—no sense putting another man through it.

<<<
Sefa is out of the door before Osric has finished the word, into the white glare. "Pell! Answer if you can hear us!" Her voice goes out across the yard and down the slope. Bram is a step behind her, already pulling the coil of hempen rope from his belt, with his own call and his sharp word over his shoulder to Osric: show us where the solid ground ends.

Halfway down the crew's path, Sefa closes her hand round the prayer beads at her neck and says the one word. A pale, even light rises from the wooden beads, a light with no heat in it and no spark. It's faint in the noon sun, but it'll be enough under the shed's shadow. She holds it low against her chest.

Then the ground answers them.

A voice comes up out of the shelf ahead of them, flat and broken by the stone it has to climb through. They catch it in pieces, the way you hear a shout from a cellar:

"*…BRAM! SEFA!… lower shed!… under the step!… pinned… water to my chest!… don't run in!… hollow… door… crew's path… off the flagstone!… bring Hale!… smells sweet!…*"

Then nothing but the drip from somewhere under the planks, and the dust still settling over the dark patch where the step used to be.

Osric has come out after them with his coat left on the peg. He doesn't hurry, but he doesn't stop either, and when Bram halts well short of the shelf he comes up beside him and points with two fingers, the way a man points at stone he has cut.

"Path's rock as far as that brown stone." It's a rust-coloured boulder sunk in the white mat about fifteen feet short of the shed door. "Past it, it's spoil laid over old timber. The whole shelf. Thirty years we walked it." His mouth sets. "Step was a lid. Nobody knew."

He turns his hand to the left, toward the foot of the low face, where the grey stone comes down to the shelf in a ridge of bare rock dark with seep. "Rock runs along the face. Gets you within five, six feet of the hole on that side. No closer." Set into that ridge, a little above the mat, is an iron ring as thick as a man's thumb, brown with rust and leaded into the stone. "Lowering ring. Older than me. It'll hold a cart."

Sefa's light picks out the ragged lip of the hole beyond. It's a gap about four feet across, edged with soft black timber and broken white crust. Below it there's only the glint of still water.

"Cut runs back under the face," Osric says, lower now. "Water stands four foot in summer. Five after rain." He stays on the path behind the brown stone with his feet planted. He doesn't step onto the rock ridge, and he doesn't look at the hole for long.

The sun stands almost straight overhead. The ring waits in its stone. Bram's rope is in his hands, and the hole lies six feet past the end of the good rock.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell gives it a slow count of twenty. Then he shouts again, shorter this time, the way you call a dropped line across a roof:

"DOWN HERE! LOWER SHED! HOLE BY THE STEP!"

He waits, listening for boots on the path or a face in the square of sky.

He doesn't stand idle while he waits. Cold water wins faster against a man who's still. He keeps the pack hugged high on his chest with one forearm, draws a dagger with the other hand, and starts on the job his fingertips described. He works the point into the packed rubble round his boot on the outer side, away from the ledge, and pries the stones loose one at a time. Each loose one he lets roll off into the silt beyond his foot. He moves slowly and steadily. He doesn't wrench and he doesn't touch the prop, so nothing shifts the block's weight onto his shin. It keeps his blood moving, and every stone he clears is one fewer for whoever comes down to help.

He has already sorted out what he'll say when a face appears, and he mutters it to himself so the chattering doesn't steal it:

"Sunset to dig me out. Sunset for the coach. Can't do both with three."

When someone does show at the hole, he calls up the plan plainly:

"Leg's pinned, not broken. Block's too heavy to lift. The stones round it have to be dug out first, under water, before anyone can lever it. Two of you for that, working steady, and you'll have me out about dusk. Rope's ready." He lifts the looped coil off his shoulder to show them. "Somebody has to take the case and Hale's letter and walk now, or none of us gets paid and Hale gets nothing. Sefa, you read it back to him, so you carry it. Bram and Hale dig. Hale knows these workings and how long the air stays decent. Bring a bucket, and don't anybody light a lamp down here."

Then, a little quieter, with a thin grin:

"And tell Thorn I fell into her salt mine personally. She can take it off my share."

He keeps an eye on the water-mark between stones. If it starts to creep toward the dark band, he'll shout that up too.

Somewhere past the rim of the hole a woman's voice carries across the shelf, nearer than Bram's was and broken up by the stone: "...Pell!... answer if you..." A lower, flatter man's voice follows, saying something about rock. Both voices come from off to the side, out on the shelf, not from right overhead.

You shout up into the square of sky, short and hard, like a runner calling a dropped line across a roof. The gallery throws it back at you off the wet walls. The square of sky stays empty and blue, and a few grains of grit sift down through it onto the water.

You don't wait idle. You keep the pack hugged high on your chest with one forearm. With your free hand you draw a dagger and find the outer side of your boot underwater, away from the ledge and away from the prop. You set the point into the packed rubble there and start prying, one stone at a time, slowly, never wrenching.

scenes.narration:
Pell counts to twenty slowly, with his chin up and his breath going in and out through his nose. Somewhere up past the rim of the hole a woman's voice carries across the shelf, nearer than Bram's was and broken up by the stone: "*…Pell!… answer if you…*" After it comes a lower, flatter man's voice, saying something about rock. Both voices come from off to the side, out on the shelf, not from right overhead.

He shouts up into the square of sky, short and hard, like a runner calling a dropped line across a roof:

"DOWN HERE! LOWER SHED! HOLE BY THE STEP!"

The gallery throws it back at him off the wet walls. The square of sky stays empty and blue, and a few grains of grit sift down through it onto the water.

He doesn't wait idle. With one forearm he keeps the pack hugged high on his chest. With his free hand he draws a dagger and finds the outer side of his boot underwater, away from the ledge and away from the prop. He sets the point into the packed rubble there and starts prying, one stone at a time, slowly, never wrenching.

The dagger point goes in by feel, finds the seam between two stones and turns. The first stone comes loose and he nudges it off into the silt beyond his foot. Then a second. He keeps every movement small and pulls nothing toward himself, and the block above his shin stays exactly where it is. He can't feel it settle at all. After a few minutes the outer side of the boot is clear down to the stone floor. His fingertips find bare leather where the rubble was packed like mortar, and there's a hand's width of empty water between the boot and the next stones out.

That's as far as one hand can go. The rest is on the far side of his leg, packed against the broken edge of the ledge, and under the block's own near edge beside the prop. That's where the weight sits, and he can't reach it without leaning on the stone that's holding him. It's still work for two, with bailing. What he's cleared takes a little off their job. It doesn't change when the job ends.

Working has put a little warmth back into his arms. His teeth go on chattering anyway, and he mutters through them, to himself, to keep hold of the words:

"Sunset to dig me out. Sunset for the coach. Can't do both with three."

The rope stays coiled over his shoulder with the loop ready. He keeps the rest of what he means to say to himself, because no face has come to the hole to hear it yet.

Between stones he checks the wall. The dark band is still a hand's breadth above the surface, and the water hasn't visibly moved in the quarter hour. The trickle in the crack keeps running, thin and silent. The sweet smell sits in the still air the way it has all along, the smell of an oven an hour after the bread came out. Up past the rim the voices on the shelf have dropped lower, talking among themselves, and the square of noon sky stays empty.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't run. The ground has told them what it thinks of running. She moves forward only as far as the rock along the low face, one hand on the damp stone, her light held low and her eyes on the hole.

"Pell! We hear you. Keep your voice every little while. We're not coming in over the boards. Bram is going to anchor on the old lowering ring and send a line in. Don't strike a light in there — my light's cold; no spark from it."

She looks back at Bram, and the words come quick, each one pointed at the ground between them.

"Anchor it to the ring and belay from there. I'll carry the end to him with my hand — my mage hand, not a flame. It'll do the reaching; my feet stay on good rock. If he's hurt, I can reach him with healing from here. But I can't haul, Bram. That's your rope and your back."

She turns half toward Osric, never turning her light from the hole. "Master Hale, stay behind the brown stone. If the shelf so much as whispers, you call, and we all come off. You know the ground better than we do. Watch it for all of us."

Then she raises one hand, and the air just beyond the hole stirs: a small, translucent hand shaped of pale light, unhurried, visible as a heatless shimmer. She directs it not into the hole yet, but toward the rope's free end, meaning to guide a loop down to Pell without putting anything living onto the collapsed step.

Her own feet stay on the bare rock ridge, within sight of the glint of water, and well short of the black timber lip.

scenes.narration:
Bram's voice goes out flat and loud across the shelf. "Heard you, Pell! We're on solid ground. Rope coming!" Before the echo has died against the low face, an answer comes up out of the ground, short and hard, broken by the stone it climbs through: "*…DOWN HERE!… LOWER SHED!… HOLE BY THE STEP!…*"

Bram goes left along the ridge of bare rock at the foot of the face, the way Osric pointed. The stone is slick with seep and crusted pink in the cracks. He keeps his boots on the grey and off the white mat. At the lowering ring he crouches and takes the iron in both hands. He twists it, pulls it toward him, then puts his weight on it sideways. It's brown with rust, but under the rust it's as thick as his thumb. The lead around its foot is sunk flush into the rock and doesn't give a hair. It was set by someone who meant it to hold a cart, and it still will.

He runs the hempen rope through the ring and ties it off with two turns and a knot he's used on wagon loads a thousand times. Then he works a wide loop into the free end, big enough to go over a man's head and shoulders, and ties it so it won't close under strain.

Sefa comes along the ridge behind him without hurrying, one palm flat on the wet stone of the face. Her beads glow pale and cold against her chest. She calls down toward the hole in an even voice: they hear him, they're not coming over the boards, Bram is anchoring on the old ring, and nobody should strike a light, because hers has no spark in it. Over her shoulder she gives Osric his job: stay behind the brown stone, watch the shelf, and call if it so much as whispers.

Bram has given Osric a different job, a long pole or a timber, and Osric picks that one first.

"Poles at the frame." He's already turning back up the path. "Mind that shelf till I'm back."

He goes up toward the yard with his heavy walk, coatless, and doesn't look back at the hole.

Sefa raises her hand. Just past the end of the good rock the air thickens into a hand of pale, translucent light, the size of a real one, with no heat and no flicker to it. It drifts to the rope and closes its fingers on the loop. Bram feeds the line out hand over hand from his crouch, and the spectral hand carries the loop over the six feet of spoil the rock doesn't cover, slowly, never touching the mat. It reaches the black edge of the hole, where soft timber and broken crust ring the opening. There it lowers the loop, and the rope pays down through Bram's fists after it.

From down on the ridge, bent low with the rope across his knee, Bram can see into the hole at a slant. The noon sun stands almost straight above the opening and drops a square of light onto still water. In it he sees the top of a man: Pell's dark head and his shoulders, a coil of thin rope over one of them, the water up around his chest. Beside him a corner of pale squared stone breaks the surface, too even to be rubble. The loop comes down into the light a foot from Pell's face and hangs there, turning slowly on the end of the line. Sefa lets the hand of light open and fade.

Bram's questions go down the hole after it, loud and plain: what's pinning him, can he move his arms, get the loop under his arms if he can, and say what's trapped before anyone pulls.

A few minutes later Osric comes back down the path with a long larch pole on his shoulder, peeled and grey, fourteen feet of it, the kind used to brace the lifting frame. In his other hand he carries a quarryman's iron pinch-bar as long as his arm, with one end flattened to a chisel. He stops behind the brown stone, as Sefa asked, and goes no closer. He lays the pole down along the rock ridge and pushes it toward Bram until it reaches him. The bar he sets on the rock where the ridge begins.

"Bar's for stone. Pole's for reach." Then his eyes go to the shelf, the long white mat between the brown stone and the shed. He watches it the way Sefa told him to, and he doesn't look at the hole.

Overhead the sun has almost reached the top of the sky. Osric glances up at it once and then back at the shelf. The rope runs taut from the iron ring across six feet of rotten ground and down into the dark square, where the loop hangs in the light beside Pell.

 (Out of game) None of the four needed a roll, because each was certain for a man who has tied wagon loads for sixteen years and a cantrip working 6 feet off: the ring held, the knots held, and Sefa's spectral hand carried the loop down into the hole. One correction: Bram meant to toss the loop himself, but the narration had him paying out the line to Sefa's hand instead, and it shouldn't have changed how he did it. A toss of 6 feet into a 4-foot opening, crouched on good rock, needs no roll either, and the loop ends up in the same place.
