messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slides the dagger back into its sheath by feel. One blade loose in murky water is one blade lost. He shifts the pack higher on his chest.

The voices are off to the side and talking low. That means they can't find the hole, or they don't trust the ground. Pell decides to give them something to see.

He takes the rope coil off his shoulder, keeps a firm grip on the standing end, and swings the looped end in a short underarm arc up through the square of sky. He means it to land over the rim and lie out on the dust where anyone on the shelf will spot it. If it falls back, he gathers it in and tries again, keeping the throws small so he isn't twisting against the pinned leg.

Then he shouts toward where the voices came from, slowly, one piece at a time so the stone doesn't swallow it:

"SEFA! Follow the ROPE! I'm under the SHED STEP, right at the DOOR! Hole's the size of a cart bed!"

He takes a breath.

"Ground round it's HOLLOW! Come on your BELLIES, spread your weight! Or come through the SHED and look out the door! Don't stand on the edge!"

Another breath, through teeth that won't stop chattering.

"I'm all right! Pinned, NOT broken! Water's NOT rising! Air's sweet but DECENT! Nobody light ANYTHING!"

Then he goes quiet and listens: for scraping on the shelf, for a tug on the rope, for a face at the rim. He keeps his free hand working, clenching and opening, and rocks his weight on his good leg to keep the blood moving. His eyes go back to the dark band on the wall between breaths.

Under his breath: "Come on. Look at the pretty rope."

scenes.narration:
Pell slides the dagger back into its sheath by feel and hitches the pack higher on his chest. Water runs off his forearm in a thin sheet. He takes the silk coil off his shoulder, keeps a firm grip on the standing end, and swings the looped end in a short underarm arc up through the square of sky. He keeps the throw small so it doesn't twist him against the leg.

The first throw is good. A roof-runner has thrown a line across a gap more times than he can count, and this is only eight feet straight up. The loop clears the ragged rim, catches on the soft black timber at the edge for a heartbeat, then slithers over and lies out of sight on the dust. Only the standing end stays in his fist, running taut up the wall, over the lip and away into the white glare.

He fills his lungs and sends the words up a piece at a time: follow the rope, under the shed step, right at the door, a hole the size of a cart bed. Hollow ground, come on your bellies, or come through the shed and look out the door. Don't stand on the edge. Pinned, not broken. Water's not rising. Air's sweet but decent. Nobody light anything. The gallery throws each piece back off the wet walls before the next one goes up.

Then he goes quiet and listens.

This time an answer comes, and it's closer. Bram's voice reaches him from off to the left, low down, as if from a man crouching. The stone still flattens it, but the words come through whole: "*Heard you, Pell! We're on solid ground. Rope coming!*"

The light at the rim changes a moment later. A hand comes into the square of sky, pale and see-through, about the size of a real one. It gives off no heat and doesn't flicker, and the sun shows through it like light through thin horn. Its fingers are closed on a loop of brown hempen rope. It doesn't come down into the hole. It hangs at the edge and lets the loop go, and the rope pays down after it in small even jerks, the way a line comes when someone is feeding it hand over hand. The loop drops into the shaft of light and stops about a foot from Pell's face. It's a wide fixed loop, tied by someone who meant it not to close, and it hangs there turning slowly over the water. Above it the pale hand opens and fades.

At the left-hand edge of the square, low down, a sliver of a man's head and shoulder shows against the sky at a slant, dark against the glare. It's too far to the side to be right over the hole. Bram's voice comes down from there, louder now and plain: what's pinning him, can he move his arms, get the loop under his arms if he can, and tell them what's trapped before anyone pulls.

Pell's free hand keeps clenching and opening under the water. He rocks his weight onto his good leg and back. The block doesn't stir against his shin. On the wall the dark band is still a hand's breadth above the surface, and the thin seep runs down its crack into the water without a sound. Two ropes now hang in the light: his silk line runs taut up and over the rim, and Bram's hempen loop turns slowly in front of his face. The sweet, oven-warm air sits on the water around him. High above, the sun stands almost straight over the hole.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her light steady over the hole and her feet planted on the wet rock. She doesn't take her eyes from Pell for long.

"Pell, it's Sefa. The loop's beside you. Can you get it under either arm — one's enough to start, we won't haul until you say. Tell me what's holding you: stone, timber, your leg. And whether you're bleeding anywhere."

Her voice is calm, each word given a clean edge, as if the water and the smell and the rotten shelf can't have the last word while she's above it.

"I've healing light here. Not fire — warmth. It'll find you if I send it. I'm sending a little now to keep your hands working. Hold still, don't waste breath."

As she says it, she lets the Lantern's power move through her and down through the square of sunlight on the water: a soft, golden warmth, no flame and no spark, settling around Pell's head and shoulders like a breath from a summer window. It carries no haze, no smoke. It only gives what she gives — restoring health and steadiness.

She spends two dice of her healing light on him.

[Healing Light: spend 2 dice — 2d6 — on Pell. Update counter: Healing Light 4/6.]

Then, without turning far, she says lower to Bram:

"When you pull, I'll keep the mage-hand on the rope above the splinters and hold it off the broken edge — ten pounds is all it can carry, but it can keep the line from fouling. We take his weight only on your rope, not on my hand. And if he's wedged, you've the bar to lever, not the line."

She watches the water for Pell's answer, listening for any change in his voice that might mean the sweet air has begun to do its slow work on him.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep the rope steady without pulling on Pell.

“Pell, loop's beside your face. Can you get it under your arms? Tell me what's pinned—your boot, your leg, or something else?”

I draw the larch pole along the ridge, keeping its weight on solid rock, ready to extend it if he needs something to grip.

“Sefa, keep him talking. If he's trapped under stone, hauling blind could hurt him worse.”

I watch Pell for a response and the broken lip for any movement.

scenes.narration:
Sefa stays planted on the wet rock with her light held low. Before she can call down, the hole sends something up first. Pell's voice comes out of the ground, loud and slow, one piece at a time, each piece flattened by the stone it has to climb through:

"*…follow the ROPE!… under the SHED STEP… right at the DOOR!… size of a cart bed!… HOLLOW… come on your BELLIES… or through the SHED… look out the door!… don't stand on the EDGE!… pinned, NOT broken!… water's NOT rising!… sweet but DECENT!… nobody light ANYTHING!…*"

Then the drip again.

From the ridge Bram can see a second line now, which wasn't there before. It's thin pale silk, running taut up out of the hole and over the soft black lip. Its looped end lies out on the white dust of the shelf, past the rim and well beyond the good rock, where nobody can reach it without standing on the hollow ground.

Sefa calls down anyway, in her even voice. The loop is beside him, under one arm is enough to start, nobody will haul until he says. What's holding him, stone, timber or his leg, and is he bleeding anywhere. She has healing light, warmth and not fire, and she's sending some now.

She lets it go. A soft gold warmth slides down out of her open hand into the square of sun, with no haze and no spark in it, and settles round the dark head and shoulders in the water.

The light finds him. Sefa feels it land the way she always does, a give like a hand taken. Whatever the fall did to Pell's body, the scraped shoulder and the bruising down his hip, closes under it, and all of it heals. There was less to mend than she sent, and the last of the warmth has nothing left to do.

It doesn't come back to her empty, though. For the space of a breath, as the gold thins out over the water, it feels drawn on, the way a cold room draws on a lamp held in its doorway. It's a pull from somewhere lower than Pell and to one side of him. Then it lets go, and her palm is only her palm again, warm in the noon air.

Low and without turning, she tells Bram the rest. When he pulls, her mage hand will hold the line off the splintered edge so it doesn't foul. It can't carry more than ten pounds, so Pell's weight goes on Bram's rope and nowhere else. And if Pell's wedged, the bar is for levering, not the line.

Bram keeps the hempen line steady across his knee without drawing it in an inch. He sends his own questions down after hers: get the loop under his arms, and say what's pinned, boot, leg or something else. Then he hauls the larch pole along the ridge behind him, hand over hand, keeping its weight on the rock. He lays it beside him with its end pointing at the hole, ready to run out across the six feet of spoil. "Sefa, keep him talking. If he's under stone, hauling blind could hurt him worse."

Behind the brown stone, Osric has been watching the shelf as he was told. He heard the whole shout come up out of the ground, and he isn't looking at the shelf now. He's looking at the corner of pale stone that shows in the water beside Pell's head, where the sun falls straight down the hole.

"That's dressed." He says it to nobody in particular. "Squared. Not fall-rubble." His jaw works. "Nobody dressed stone down there in my time."

Then he squints up at the sun. It stands straight overhead, and the shadows of the three of them have shrunk to nothing round their boots.

"Noon."

He doesn't move yet. He looks from the corner of stone to Bram's pole, then to the pinch-bar lying on the rock where the ridge begins.

"If it's a block on his leg, you don't lift it. Can't. Rubble packs in round it in the fall, tight as mortar. You dig that out first, under water, by hand, and somebody bails the whole time. Then you bar it." He holds up two fingers, the way he pointed at the ground. "Two men, steady, no stopping. You'd have him by sundown. One man won't shift it at all." His hand drops. "Seen it done once. Took the day."

His eyes go up the slope to the house. Its door still stands open, and inside, on the scrubbed table, the case sits by the letter with the pen still lying across the blank line.

"I'm for the town. Lads need finding, and that won't keep." He doesn't take a step toward the hole, and he doesn't take one toward the house. "Letter wants its witness and the wax. Then the case is yours. I'll not leave it lying unsealed for whoever walks up the track."

Down in the square of light the hempen loop still turns slowly over the water, and the silk line runs taut up over the lip to its loop on the dust. The seep trickles down the low face behind them, dark against the grey.

<<<
Sefa stays planted on the wet rock with her light held low. Before she can call down, the hole sends something up first. Pell's voice comes out of the ground, loud and slow, one piece at a time, each piece flattened by the stone it has to climb through:

"*…follow the ROPE!… under the SHED STEP… right at the DOOR!… size of a cart bed!… HOLLOW… come on your BELLIES… or through the SHED… look out the door!… don't stand on the EDGE!… pinned, NOT broken!… water's NOT rising!… sweet but DECENT!… nobody light ANYTHING!…*"

Then the drip again.

From the ridge Bram can see a second line now, which wasn't there before. It's thin pale silk, running taut up out of the hole and over the soft black lip. Its looped end lies out on the white dust of the shelf, past the rim and well beyond the good rock, where nobody can reach it without standing on the hollow ground.

Sefa calls down anyway, in her even voice. The loop is beside him, under one arm is enough to start, nobody will haul until he says. What's holding him, stone, timber or his leg, and is he bleeding anywhere. She has healing light, warmth and not fire, and she's sending some now.

She lets it go. A soft gold warmth slides down out of her open hand into the square of sun, with no haze and no spark in it, and settles round the dark head and shoulders in the water.

The light finds him. Sefa feels it land the way she always does, a give like a hand taken. Whatever the fall did to Pell's body, the scraped shoulder and the bruising down his hip, closes under it, and all of it heals. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets go of his own silk line. It's anchored over the rim, so it can stay where it is. He catches the hempen loop and works it down over his head and under both arms, one arm at a time so the pack never drops below his chin. He settles the knot at his back, where a pull would lift him by the chest and not the throat.

Then he tips his head back toward the sliver of Bram at the edge and shouts slowly, one piece at a time:

"DON'T PULL! Not yet! Loop's on. Keep it for if the water comes up. NOT for hauling!"

A breath.

"Left shin's under a BLOCK, cut stone, bigger than a cartwheel. Fell off a ledge. Leg's pressed against the ledge edge. Not broken. If you haul, you'll take the leg off at the knee!"

Another breath. His teeth rattle through it, but the words stay whole.

"Arms are fine! I've cleared the outer side. Rubble's packed on the INNER side and under the near edge. There's an old prop wedged under it, ready to lever. Somebody has to come down, dig out that side, bail, then lean on the prop while you lift me on the rope. Two of you, steady work. Hale reckons the air holds if nobody lights anything. I reckon dusk."

He lets that sink in, then says the part that matters:

"Which means somebody walks NOW with the case and Hale's letter, or the coach goes and nobody's paid. Decide it up there. Don't argue it over my head for an hour!"

Quieter, almost to himself, with a crooked grin up at where the pale hand faded: "And whoever's got the floating hand, thank you. Very civilised."

He keeps working his free hand, keeps his weight rocking on the good leg, and watches the dark band on the wall.

? My HP went back to 33. Did someone heal me from up there, or is that a correction?

scenes.narration:
Pell lets go of the silk. The line sags against the wet wall and its end slips into the water beside him, but the loop up on the dust holds it and nothing more comes over the rim. He catches the hempen loop on its next slow turn. One arm at a time, keeping the pack hugged above his chin, he works it down over his head and under both armpits, then reaches back and shifts the knot round between his shoulder blades. It's a good fixed loop and it doesn't close on him. If anyone pulls, the rope will take him by the chest.

While he's settling the knot, Sefa's voice comes down the hole, clearer than the shouting from the shelf has been: *"…the loop's beside you… under either arm… what's holding you… bleeding anywhere… healing light… sending a little now…"*

Something comes down after the words. A soft gold warmth slides into the square of sun with no smoke and no spark, and it settles round his head and shoulders like the air from a window in summer. The raw graze down his shoulder stops stinging. The deep ache in his hip, where it hit the floor, goes out of it all at once, the way a cramp lets go. His hands, stiff a moment ago, close and open easily under the water. The cold is still there, but his body has stopped arguing with it.

(Pell: that was Sefa's Healing Light, sent down from the ridge, so your hit points are right and nothing was corrected.)

As the gold thins out over the water, it doesn't fade evenly. For a breath it seems to lean to one side, past his shoulder, toward the block and the flat grey plaster in the wall behind it. Then it's gone, and the plaster is just grey again in the reflected light. Under the surface his fingers find the stone there no warmer than the rest of the wall.

He tips his head back toward the dark sliver of Bram at the left edge of the hole and shouts it up a piece at a time. Don't pull, not yet. The loop's on, and it's there in case the water rises, not for hauling. His left shin is under a block of cut stone bigger than a cartwheel that fell off a ledge, and the leg is pressed against the ledge's edge. It isn't broken, but if they haul they'll take it off at the knee. His arms are fine. He's cleared the outer side. The rubble is packed on the inner side and under the near edge, and there's an old prop wedged under the block, ready to lever. Somebody has to come down, dig out that side and bail, then lean on the prop while the rope lifts him. That's two people, steady work, and he reckons dusk. So somebody walks now with the case and Hale's letter, or the coach goes and nobody gets paid. Decide it up there, and don't argue it over his head for an hour.

The gallery throws every piece of it back off the wet walls. His teeth rattle between the pieces, but each one goes up whole.

Up past the rim, a flatter, heavier man's voice says something off to the side. It's Osric, further away than Bram and pitched low, and only scraps reach the water: *"…dressed… squared…"* and later *"…two men… sundown…"* and *"…took the day."* Then Bram's voice, closer and lower, says something about Sefa keeping him talking.

Pell's grin comes up crooked at the place where the pale hand faded, and he tells the hand's owner thank you, very civilised, quietly enough that it's mostly for himself.

The rope runs from his back up the wall and over the lip toward the ring, slack but straight. His free hand keeps clenching and opening. He rocks onto the good leg and back, and the block doesn't stir. On the wall the dark band is still a hand's breadth above the water, and the seep goes on threading down its crack without a sound. The sun stands straight over the hole, and the square of light on the water hasn't moved.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:

messages.text:
Sefa does not take her eyes from the square of light over the water, but her voice carries to both men.

"Pell, there's something else down there with you — lower, to your left. My healing didn't all stay with you. It caught on it, the way a cold room pulls at a lamp in a doorway. Don't go reaching into the dark for anything. Tell me if you feel the water moving around your legs, or any change in it."

She turns her head just enough to speak to Bram without losing her place.

"Keep the load line exactly as it is. Pell's silk loop's lying out on the spoil where we can't step. I'll fetch it with the hand — it weighs next to nothing — and you can make it fast to something on this side. The more lines to him, the more we can do without putting a boot on the shelf."

As she says it, the translucent hand forms again in the air just beyond the good rock. It crosses the six feet of rotten ground low and slow, never touching the white crust, closes its fingers around the silk loop, and carries it back to Bram's free side.

Then, without turning her head fully, she addresses Osric:

"Master Hale, you'll not leave either of those things at the house unwitnessed. Fetch the letter and the case down here to the good rock. I'll put my mark and we'll seal it with the wax as it stands. Then go for the lads, and for strong backs. But if you know of any tale about a dressed stone set down in that cut, say it before you take the road. There's a tenant in that water, and I won't have you meet it on your way into town."

She keeps the healing light low and steady, and her feet do not leave the wet ridge. Her weight is braced, as if the stone under her ought to be enough.

scenes.narration:
Bram says it flat and plain across the shelf: they're not leaving Pell under there for a delivery. Osric should fetch the bar over, and if they need the crew, he should tell them where to find them.

Osric looks at him for a long moment from behind the brown stone. It's the first time he has looked at Bram and not at the shelf.

"Your coin," he says. He doesn't make it sound like a fault.

He walks the three steps to where the ridge begins, stoops for the pinch-bar and sets it on the wet rock. Then he shoves it along the ridge hard and low, the way a man sends a stone down a chute. It skids over the grey stone with an iron scrape and stops against Bram's boot.

"Crew's in Beregost. Some alehouse. Wherever Hob drinks, they drink." He straightens. "Half a day there. Half back. Not before dark, and not down that hole. I'd not ask it of them."

Bram braces on the ridge and runs the larch pole out across the spoil, hand over hand. He keeps the butt clamped down on the rock under his knee, and the grey length reaches over the six feet of rotten ground without touching it. At the black lip he lowers the far end into the opening at a slant, slowly, until it dips into the shaft of sunlight above the water. He calls down after it: the pole's coming within reach, don't climb yet, Osric thinks there's a block on his leg, can he feel with his hands what's holding him.

Before the last of it has gone down the hole, Pell's voice comes up, flattened by the stone and broken into pieces:

"*…DON'T PULL!… not yet… loop's on… for if the water comes up… NOT for hauling!… left shin… under a BLOCK… cut stone… bigger than a cartwheel… against the ledge… not broken… haul, you'll take the leg off at the knee!… arms fine… cleared the outer side… inner side… under the near edge… old prop… wedged… to lever… somebody come down… dig… bail… lean on the prop… two of you… dusk…*"

He stops for breath, then goes on.

"*…somebody walks NOW… case… letter… or the coach goes… nobody paid… decide it up there… don't argue it over my head… for an hour!…*"

Then comes a last piece, quieter, which barely clears the rim: "*…very civilised.*"

Osric's mouth tightens when he hears *two of you* and *dusk*. It's his own count coming back to him out of the ground.

Under that, Bram says quietly to Sefa: can her light get any lower, so they can see what Pell's caught on.

Sefa doesn't take her eyes off the square of light. She sends her warning down in the same even voice. Something else is down there, lower and to his left. Her healing didn't all stay with him; it caught on something, the way a cold room pulls at a lamp in a doorway. He's not to reach into the dark for anything, and he's to tell her if he feels the water moving round his legs.

Then she lifts her hand again. The pale hand forms in the air just past the end of the good rock. It crosses the spoil low and slow, never touching the white crust, and closes its fingers on the loop of Pell's silk line where it lies in the dust. It draws the loop back toward the ridge. The light silk slides over the soft black lip after it, and its slack end comes up dripping from the water below. The hand lays the loop on the wet rock at Bram's free side and opens. Now two lines cross the six feet of rotten ground. The hemp runs taut from the iron ring and the silk lies loose, and both go down into the hole beside the grey slant of the pole.

She speaks to Osric without fully turning her head. He's not to leave the letter or the case up at the house unwitnessed. He should bring them both down to the good rock; she'll make her mark and they'll seal it as it stands. Then he can go for the lads and strong backs. But if he knows any tale about a dressed stone set down in that cut, he should tell it before he takes the road. There's a tenant in that water, and she won't have him meet it on his way into town.

Osric takes the first part like an order from a foreman he doesn't mind.

"Bring the lot down. Aye." He glances up the slope at the open door. "Wax wants a flame. I'll bring a candle-end. Up here, in the open air, not down there." He jerks his chin at the hole. "That's what the letter says, isn't it."

Then he hears *tenant*. He doesn't laugh at it.

"Water's water." He looks past her at the hole, and the look stays there longer than he means it to. "Those galleries were cut before the house had the place. Before anybody I knew had it. Whoever squared that stone never wrote it in my book." His fingers find his sleeve and press. "Only thing that was ever in that water was one of mine."

He stops there. His mouth closes on whatever comes after.

He turns and goes up the crew's path toward the yard with his heavy, coatless walk. He keeps to the packed white mat, and his boots raise small puffs of dust that hang behind him in the windless air. The sun stands straight overhead. Sefa's beads still glow pale against her chest, faint in the glare. On the ridge the iron bar lies against Bram's boot, the silk loop lies coiled at his side, and the pole's far end hangs in the shaft of light a foot or two above the dark head in the water.

 (Out of game) None of these needed a roll:
1) Done as Bram declared: he lowered the pole into the shaft of light from the good rock and told Pell not to climb. Nothing about it was uncertain.
2) Bram asked his question, and Pell's shout answered it: a cut block on his left shin, pressed against the ledge.
3) Bram put that question to Sefa, so it waits for Sefa's player. The light stays where it is until she says otherwise.
4) Done as Sefa declared. Mage Hand is a cantrip, not healing magic, and carrying a few pounds of silk six feet with nobody opposing it can't fail.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his free hand working under the water and his weight rocking on the good leg. Sefa's light has bought him time against the cold, and he means to spend it carefully.

He tips his face up toward where her voice came from, and pitches it lower now that someone's listening close:

"Thank you. That's the first time I've been warm since dawn."

A breath, then, plainly, because she ought to know:

Beside him the silk line he let go stirs. It slides up the wet wall in small even pulls, and its slack end comes dripping out of the water, over the soft black lip and away. Up there someone is reeling it in by a hand that isn't a hand.

He tips his face up toward Sefa's voice and pitches it lower, now that someone close is listening. He thanks her, the first warmth since dawn. Then, plainly, he tells her what he saw: as her light faded it leaned past him toward the wall behind the block, where there's a flat grey patch like plaster laid over a hollow. The block stood against that patch before it tipped. The block is carved, too, not just dressed: a disc with rays and a ring of little notches like a tally. He hasn't touched either and he won't. If her patron has an interest in something down here, he'd rather she knew before anyone starts digging round it. His teeth catch on the words, but each one gets out whole and goes up the hole.

While he talks he studies the carving in the slanting noon light, with his eyes only. The block's face is tilted up toward the hole, half out of the water. Its top corner is dry and its lower edge is lost in the dark water round his shin.

Recognising a temple's mark worn soft by three feet of water and years of salt isn't something a roof-runner does every day, so it gets a card.

Pell can't tell, and he looks a long while. The disc is plain enough and the rays round it are plain enough, but the salt has eaten the cut edges down to soft ridges. Wherever a door-painter's sun would sit on its horizon line, the bottom of this one runs down under the water and into the crust. It might be a sunrise or the noon sun. It might be a cartwheel some mason liked the look of. He can't say which.

The notches are easier. Counting is a ledger man's job. He makes it twenty-eight that he can see, running round the rays in a ring. They aren't evenly spaced. They bunch, three here and one there and then a gap, the way letters bunch into words on a page. Some are single strokes, some have a short cross-cut through them, and a few are doubled. Every one of them is worn exactly as soft as the disc. Not one is sharper or newer than the rest. Whoever cut the ring cut it all at once, and nobody has added to it since.

He lifts his voice toward the heavier man's voice off to the side, the one that said *dressed* and *squared*: did Hale know this stone was down here, whose working is it, how old, and how far does the dark band climb when the seep runs bad?

The answer had come before his question went up, and it wasn't meant for him. Osric's flat voice, pitched at someone on the shelf, drops into the hole in pieces: *"…cut before the house had the place… before anybody I knew… never wrote it in my book…"* Then, lower and barely clearing the rim: *"…only thing that was ever in that water was one of mine."*

After that he hears heavy boots on packed stone, going away up the slope, then nothing. Pell's question goes up into the bright air over the shelf and no flat voice comes back down.

Last he calls the practical part up to Sefa. Whatever the three of them decide, someone should tell him who's carrying the case, so he knows who to curse if Thorn shorts them. If anyone's coming down, the bucket comes first and the boots after. The floor down here is stone and the rim by the step is rotten, so come down the rope, not over the edge.

Then he goes quiet and listens. The hemp runs slack from his back up over the lip. The pole hangs dry in the light above his head. The silk is gone up the wall. On the stone the dark band is still a hand's breadth above the water, and the fainter mark sits higher, where it always has. The seep threads down its crack without a sound. His eyes go from the band to the grey plaster and back again. The plaster is flat and grey and gives nothing away. The sweet air sits on the water, and the sun has started, just barely, to lean west of the hole.

 Pell searches the worn rays for the sign Lathander's priests paint over their doors, and he can't find it. He doesn't know enough of temple marks to pick out a dawn sun from what the salt has left. So the carving stays what it was when he first saw it: a disc with rays round it, and nobody's name on it that he can read.

His eyes go from the band to the grey plaster and back again. The plaster is flat and grey and gives nothing away. The sweet air sits on the water, and the sun has started, just barely, to lean west of the hole.

So the carving stays what it was when he first saw it: a disc with rays round it, and nobody's name on it that he can read.

<<<
Bram's voice comes down the hole, low and plain: the pole is coming within reach, and you're not to climb yet. Sefa follows, even and careful. She says there's something else down there, lower and to your left, and that her healing didn't all stay with you but caught on it. She warns you not to reach into the dark and asks you to tell her if you feel the water moving round your legs.

The grey end of the larch pole comes down into the square of light at a slant and stops a foot or two above your head. It's bone-dry and peeled smooth, close enough to grab.

The water round your legs is as still as it has been all along. Cold lies on your shins and nothing pulls at them.

Beside you the silk line you let go stirs. It slides up the wet wall in small even pulls, and its slack end comes dripping out of the water, over the soft black lip and away. Up there someone is reeling it in by a hand that isn't a hand.

You tip your face up toward Sefa's voice and pitch your own lower, now that someone close is listening. You thank her for the first warmth since dawn. Then you tell her plainly what you saw: as her light faded it leaned past you toward the wall behind the block, where there's a flat grey patch like plaster laid over a hollow. The block stood against that patch before it tipped. The block is carved, too, not just dressed: a disc with rays and a ring of little notches like a tally. You haven't touched either and you won't. If her patron has an interest in something down here, you'd rather she knew before anyone starts digging round it. Your teeth catch on the words, but each one gets out whole and goes up the hole.

- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her eyes on the hole as she gives Pell back his calm, word by word.

“Pell, no hauling. The loop stays for the water, and only for the water. The silk’s up with us, the bar’s at Bram’s foot, and the pole’s in the shaft. We hear you. Hold quiet.”

Then, without turning toward Bram, she says just loud enough to carry to him alone:

“We won’t argue it over his head. I’ll walk the case and letter to Beregost now — not with his leg still under the block. I’ll find Thorn and the crew if they’re in a place an alehouse can point to. That leaves the coach handled and a road-messenger already on the move.”

She turns enough then to look Bram in the eye.

“You and Hale go down together, if he will. That’s two pairs of hands to dig and lever, and the ring holds the line. No flame down there. I can fix a cold light to the end of the pole before I go—the Lantern’s kind, not a spark—so you can see without kindling anything.” A pause, full of care. “He lost a man in that water three years back. If you go down with him, let him work with his head, not his grief. And mind the tenant my light caught. Don’t turn your back on the deep side of that block. If the water moves like something in it is awake, you put yourselves on the line and call.”

She looks out once toward the open house where Osric has gone, and then back to the square of sun on the still water below.

“Pell, you’re not to be civilised. You’re to stay awake and tell us if your leg starts to go cold where the stone meets it. You’ll be asking for a hot meal by dark, not a barge.”

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, understood. No hauling. I'm coming down to clear the block.”

I turn to Sefa. “Will you stay above and tend my line? Keep your light on his left, where you felt that thing.”

I call after Osric: “Bring a bucket as well! If you're going to Beregost, will you take the case and witnessed letter to Thorn? Tell her where we are. Rescue first; we can settle payment later.”

I set my shield on the solid rock and secure Pell's silk line to the lowering ring without pulling on him. Before trusting it with my weight, I check with Pell that it's sound rope.

Then, with Sefa's help tending the line, I prepare to lower myself from the anchored rope into the opening, keeping my weight off the rotten shelf. I'll take the pinch-bar down secured to a line, not loose in my hand.

“Pell, talk me onto a safe footing beside you. Then we'll clear the packed rubble before we try shifting anything.”

scenes.narration:
The quarry is so quiet that Pell's voice reaches the ridge before Sefa has finished drawing breath. It comes up out of the ground in pieces, flattened by the stone:

"*…thank you… first time I've been warm since dawn…*" Then, more plainly: "*…Sefa… your light… leaned past me… toward the wall behind the block… flat grey… like plaster over a hollow… block stood against it… carved… a disc with rays… ring of little notches… like a tally… haven't touched either… won't… if your patron's interested… before anybody digs round it…*"

There's a pause, and then, louder and aimed off to the side where nobody stands any more: "*…Master Hale!… whose working… how old… how far does that dark band go up…*" Nobody answers from the shelf. Last comes the practical part: "*…who's carrying the case… so I know who to curse… bucket first… boots after… floor's stone… rim's rotten… come down the ROPE, not the rim…*"

Sefa sends her answer down in the same even voice. No hauling. The loop stays round him for the water and only for the water. The silk is up with them, the bar is at Bram's foot, the pole is in the shaft. They hear him, and he should hold quiet. While she speaks, the pale glow fades out of the prayer beads at her neck. The hour of the cantrip is spent, and nobody would have noticed the change in the noon glare if they hadn't been looking at her hands.

Then she says, low enough to reach Bram and nobody else, that they won't argue it over Pell's head. She'll walk the case and the letter to Beregost now, find Thorn, and find the crew if an alehouse can point to them. She turns and meets his eyes. Bram and Hale should go down together, if Hale will, with two pairs of hands to dig and lever and the ring holding the line, and no flame. She could fix a cold light to the end of the pole before she goes, the Lantern's kind, with no spark in it. Hale lost a man in that water three years back, so Bram should let him work with his head and not his grief. And Bram should keep his eyes on the deep side of the block. If the water moves as though something in it has woken, they get on the line and call.

Last, she sends one more line down the hole: Pell isn't to be civilised. He's to stay awake and tell them if his leg starts going cold where the stone meets it.

Bram sends his own words straight down after hers: understood, no hauling, he's coming down to clear the block. To Sefa he says, plainly, will she stay up top and tend his line, with her light on Pell's left where she felt that thing? Then he turns his head up the slope and lets his voice go across the yard, the way it went before:

"Hale! Bring a bucket as well! If you're for Beregost, will you take the case and the witnessed letter to Thorn? Tell her where we are. Rescue first. Payment can wait."

Up at the house, Osric is already in the doorway with his arms full. The call reaches him, and he stops on the step for a moment. Then he ducks back inside. When he comes out again he has a wooden bucket with a rope handle hooked over one wrist. He walks down the crew's path with his heavy, unhurried tread. The oak case is under his arm, its red wax catching the sun. The torn page is folded once over his fingers, and a pen, a horn of ink, a stub of red wax and a candle-end are bunched in his fist.

He stops behind the brown stone, as he was told, and sets the case down on the rock with the letter beside it. He weights the page with the ink-horn and lays the candle-end by it, unlit. The bucket goes down last. He gives it a shove along the ridge, as he did the bar, and it rattles over the wet stone and fetches up a stride short of Bram.

"Bucket." He straightens. "Her door I'll pass. I'll tell her you're down a hole at Whitestone. That much."

He looks at the case on the rock, not at Bram.

"Her salt I'll not carry. I'm warden here, not the house's carter. Salt goes out of Whitestone in the buyer's man's hands, and that's how it'll stand in my book when Pryce comes asking who took it." His jaw sets. "She hired you for it. Your coin to earn. Or not."

Bram sets his round shield down flat on the good rock beside the ring. He picks up the coil of Pell's silk where the spectral hand laid it, runs a length through his fingers and looks it over. It's fine, close-laid silk, dry where it never touched the water, with no fraying and no soft places. It's better rope than his own. He takes it round the iron ring beside the hemp with two turns and a knot, and doesn't let it take any tension that could reach Pell. Then he loops the spare end round the pinch-bar's middle and hitches it tight, so the iron can go down on a line and not loose in his fist.

From where he crouches, he can see what going down will mean. The ring sits on the last of the good rock. Between it and the hole lie six feet of white spoil over old timber, the same stuff the step was made of. The lip of the hole is soft and black. The rope will carry his weight, but it will run across that spoil and over that lip, and he'll be on it in chain mail. Below the lip the water stands chest-deep on a stone floor. The larch pole's grey length reaches over the spoil beside the ropes, its butt still clamped on the rock and its far end hanging dry in the shaft of light.

Bram's question goes down the hole after the rest, asking Pell to talk him onto safe footing beside him before they clear the packed rubble.

The sun has slipped just past the top of the sky. The shadows of the three of them have come out from under their boots again, short, and they lean a little toward the east. The case sits on the rock in the open air, sealed with wax, and the pen lies beside the folded letter. The candle-end lies unlit beside them.

 1) Sefa can't take the case yet. Osric hands it over only after she makes her witness mark and he seals the letter, and she hasn't done that. Once she witnesses it, she can set off.
2) Thorn and the crew are in Beregost, half a day's walk away, so Sefa finds them when she gets there. Nothing about that happens this round.
3) Sefa said she *could* put a cold light on the pole, so I read it as an offer and didn't cast for her. If she casts Light on the pole's end, it needs no roll, and her beads stay dark.
4) Tending the line was Bram's request, not something Sefa did, and it conflicts with her leaving with the case. It's her player's call next round.

Last comes the practical part: "*…who's carrying the case… so I know who to curse… bucket first… boots after… floor's stone… rim's rotten… come down the ROPE, not the rim…*"

Sefa sends her answer down in the same even voice. No hauling. The loop stays round him for the water and only for the water. The silk is up with them, the bar is at Bram's foot, the pole is in the shaft. They hear him, and he should hold quiet. While she speaks, the pale glow fades out of the prayer beads at her neck. The hour of the cantrip is spent, and nobody would have noticed the change in the noon glare if they hadn't been looking at her hands.

Then she says, low enough to reach Bram and nobody else, that they won't argue it over Pell's head. She'll walk the case and the letter to Beregost now, find Thorn, and find the crew if an alehouse can point to them. She turns and meets his eyes. Bram and Hale should go down together, if Hale will, with two pairs of hands to dig and lever and the ring holding the line, and no flame. She could fix a cold light to the end of the pole before she goes, the Lantern's kind, with no spark in it. Hale lost a man in that water three years back, so Bram should let him work with his head and not his grief. And Bram should keep his eyes on the deep side of the block. If the water moves as though something in it has woken, they get on the line and call.

Last, she sends one more line down the hole: Pell isn't to be civilised. He's to stay awake and tell them if his leg starts going cold where the stone meets it.

Bram sends his own words straight down after hers: understood, no hauling, he's coming down to clear the block. To Sefa he says, plainly, will she stay up top and tend his line, with her light on Pell's left where she felt that thing? Then he turns his head up the slope and lets his voice go across the yard, the way it went before:

"Hale! Bring a bucket as well! If you're for Beregost, will you take the case and the witnessed letter to Thorn? Tell her where we are. Rescue first. Payment can wait."

Up at the house, Osric is already in the doorway with his arms full. The call reaches him, and he stops on the step for a moment. Then he ducks back inside. When he comes out again he has a wooden bucket with a rope handle hooked over one wrist. He walks down the crew's path with his heavy, unhurried tread. The oak case is under his arm, its red wax catching the sun. The torn page is folded once over his fingers, and a pen, a horn of ink, a stub of red wax and a candle-end are bunched in his fist.

He stops behind the brown stone, as he was told, and sets the case down on the rock with the letter beside it. He weights the page with the ink-horn and lays the candle-end by it, unlit. The bucket goes down last. He gives it a shove along the ridge, as he did the bar, and it rattles over the wet stone and fetches up a stride short of Bram.

"Bucket." He straightens. "Her door I'll pass. I'll tell her you're down a hole at Whitestone. That much."

He looks at the case on the rock, not at Bram.

"Her salt I'll not carry. I'm warden here, not the house's carter. Salt goes out of Whitestone in the buyer's man's hands, and that's how it'll stand in my book when Pryce comes asking who took it." His jaw sets. "She hired you for it. Your coin to earn. Or not."

Bram sets his round shield down flat on the good rock beside the ring. He picks up the coil of Pell's silk where the spectral hand laid it, runs a length through his fingers and looks it over. It's fine, close-laid silk, dry where it never touched the water, with no fraying and no soft places. It's better rope than his own. He takes it round the iron ring beside the hemp with two turns and a knot, and doesn't let it take any tension that could reach Pell. Then he loops the spare end round the pinch-bar's middle and hitches it tight, so the iron can go down on a line and not loose in his fist.

From where he crouches, he can see what going down will mean. The ring sits on the last of the good rock. Between it and the hole lie six feet of white spoil over old timber, the same stuff the step was made of. The lip of the hole is soft and black. The rope will carry his weight, but it will run across that spoil and over that lip, and he'll be on it in chain mail. Below the lip the water stands chest-deep on a stone floor. The larch pole's grey length reaches over the spoil beside the ropes, its butt still clamped on the rock and its far end hanging dry in the shaft of light.

Bram's question goes down the hole after the rest, asking Pell to talk him onto safe footing beside him before they clear the packed rubble.

The sun has slipped just past the top of the sky. The shadows of the three of them have come out from under their boots again, short, and they lean a little toward the east. The case sits on the rock in the open air, sealed with wax, and the pen lies beside the folded letter. The candle-end lies unlit beside them.

 1) Sefa can't take the case yet. Osric hands it over only after she makes her witness mark and he seals the letter, and she hasn't done that. Once she witnesses it, she can set off.
2) Thorn and the crew are in Beregost, half a day's walk away, so Sefa finds them when she gets there. Nothing about that happens this round.
3) Sefa said she *could* put a cold light on the pole, so I read it as an offer and didn't cast for her. If she casts Light on the pole's end, it needs no roll, and her beads stay dark.
4) Tending the line was Bram's request, not something Sefa did, and it conflicts with her leaving with the case. It's her player's call next round.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes hold of the larch pole with his free hand. He doesn't haul on it and he doesn't climb. He holds it so he's braced against something dry and solid, and so that whoever is on the other end can feel through the wood that he's still there and steady.

Sefa warned him about something lower and to the left, so he keeps his eyes off that side. He doesn't turn his body toward the dark or put a hand anywhere he can't see. He keeps his legs still apart from the slow rocking on the good one, and he pays attention to the water round them. If it so much as stirs, he'll say so.

He tips his face up toward Sefa's voice and keeps his own low and even:

"Water's still. Nothing's pulling. I'm not reaching for anything."

A breath, teeth rattling.

"About the carving. I can't tell whose sun it is. The salt's eaten it soft. But the notches aren't a tally. Twenty-eight of them, bunched like words. Single strokes, some with a cross-cut, some doubled. All cut at once, all equally worn. It's writing, or near enough. Somebody meant it to be read, by someone who'd know how." He lets that settle. "If your patron leaned toward it, that's two things down here pointing at the same wall. I'd like to be up the rope before anyone finds out what for."

Then, quieter, because he heard it go over the rim:

"And Hale said someone of his went into this water once. If he's gone off up the slope with that in his head, somebody ought to go after him. Not to fetch him back, just so he isn't on his own with it. Bram's better at that than me."

Last, practical, with half a glance at the sun leaning off the hole:

"Sun's past noon. Whoever's carrying the case should go before it leans much further. I'll still be here. I'm very reliable that way."

He settles his grip on the pole and goes quiet, watching the dark band, the grey plaster, and the still water. He doesn't look into the dark on his left.

scenes.narration:
Pell closes his free hand on the larch pole. The upper length has been in the sun and the wood is dry and faintly warm. He doesn't pull on it. He feels the other end through the grain. It doesn't give at all, because someone is holding it clamped hard on the rock up there. Once it shifts a little, as if the man holding it has moved his knee, and then it settles again.

He keeps his eyes off the left-hand dark and his body square to the light. Below the surface the water lies cold and still round both legs. Nothing brushes them or pulls at them. The shin under the block has gone dull with the cold, but when he tries his toes inside the boot they still move.

He sends his words up the hole low and even, and the wet walls throw each piece back: the water's still, nothing's pulling, he isn't reaching for anything. He can't name the sun. The notches aren't a tally but something close to writing: twenty-eight of them, bunched like words, all cut at once. That makes two things down here pointing at the same wall. Someone ought to go after Hale. The sun's past noon. He's very reliable.

Answers come down, and the first was already on its way before his own words had cleared the rim. Sefa's voice is even and close: *"…Pell, no hauling… the loop stays for the water… only for the water… the silk's up with us… the bar's at Bram's foot… the pole's in the shaft… we hear you… hold quiet."* Bram's comes after, lower and blunter: *"…understood… no hauling… I'm coming down to clear the block."*

Then Bram turns away and his voice goes big and flat across the yard, the way it carried earlier: *"…Hale!… bucket as well!… take the case… the witnessed letter… to Thorn… rescue first…"*

For a while nothing comes but the drip. Then Pell hears a heavy, unhurried tread on stone, coming nearer. Something wooden rattles and scrapes over rock off to the side of the rim and stops. Osric's flat voice comes down in pieces from close to where Bram is crouching. Hale hasn't gone anywhere:

*"…Bucket… her door I'll pass… down a hole at Whitestone… that much… her salt I'll not carry… warden here, not the house's carter… your coin to earn… or not."*

Sefa's voice comes last, pitched for the hole: *"…Pell… you're not to be civilised… stay awake… tell us if your leg starts going cold where the stone meets it."*

Iron scrapes on the rock above, and then he hears the soft hiss of rope running through somebody's hands. The pole stays steady in his grip. On the wall the dark band is still a hand's breadth above the water, and the seep goes on threading down its crack without a sound. The grey plaster behind the block is flat and gives nothing away. Overhead the square of sky has started to lean west, and the slant of light on the water has crept a finger's width toward the far wall.

 (Out of game) None of the four needed a roll, because each one was certain. Pell grips the pole and feels Bram holding the other end, keeps still with his eyes off the dark, and calls both his report and his description of the carving up the hole, so they reach Bram and Sefa in their next scene.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“All right, Sefa. Take the case once you've witnessed the letter. Cold light on the pole before you go, please.”

I call down, “Pell, bucket first, as ordered. Sefa's carrying the case. I'm staying.”

I lower the bucket on the bar's line, keeping the iron up here for now, then start taking off my chain mail on the solid rock. No sense wrestling underwater in it.

“Osric, I'll need your help here before you leave. That rotten lip won't safely bear a loaded rope. Can we brace the larch pole across sound stone, or is there another way into this cut? I've a bedroll for padding the line, but that won't hold rotten timber together.”

I keep my sword belted on and watch the water while I work. I won't put my weight over the lip until we've made the descent safe.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa picks up the pen without ceremony and kneels beside the letter, using the flat rock as a desk.

"I'll witness it now. Hold the page steady, Master Hale."

She signs in a clear, unhurried hand beneath his mark: *Sefa Marrin, courier by hire of Maela Thorn, witnessed at Whitestone this day.* Then she sets the pen down, opens her tinderbox, and strikes a light for the candle-end — up on the rock, well away from the hole, exactly as he said. She lets Osric tip the wax and set his seal with his own hand.

When the seal has cooled, she folds the letter carefully and places it in her belt pouch. The oak case she takes up and holds under one arm.

"I'll carry both to Thorn. She'll have them before the coach leaves, or none of us has earned anything." She looks from Bram to Osric. "Pell said somebody must walk now. That's me."

Her voice turns practical, not hard.

"So while I'm gone, Hale stays up here on the ring and the ridge. You, Bram, go down. Pell's arms are sound — two of you can clear the near edge of the block and work the prop while Hale tends the line and lowers the bucket and the bar. That keeps a man at the rope and a clear road for help."

She turns to the larch pole and touches it near its upper end. A pale, heatless light kindles there, the colour of starlight under water.

"I'll leave this light on the pole for you. It lasts an hour — not a breath more — so set the first work inside that hour. No flame down there. And listen for the water. If you see movement behind that flat grey wall Pell spoke of, you call Hale and both come up the line at once. The rayed disc and tally-marks are not ours to open. Don't touch them. Don't tap the wall to see if it's hollow. Dig only at the near edge of the block, and let the block answer."

She settles the case over her shoulder as best she can, checks the letter's folded edge in her pouch, and readies herself at the edge of the good rock.

"I'll ask after Hob in every alehouse on the way to Thorn's and send the crew out as soon as they're found. Keep the track clear in case I meet them coming back."

scenes.narration:
Sefa kneels at the flat rock beside the brown stone and picks up the pen without any ceremony. "I'll witness it now. Hold the page steady, Master Hale."

Osric crouches and lays two thick fingers on the top corner of the page. Under his W with the hammer through it, she writes in a clear, unhurried hand: *Sefa Marrin, courier by hire of Maela Thorn, witnessed at Whitestone this day.* Osric reads it upside down, moving his lips a little, and gives a short nod.

Sefa opens her tinderbox and strikes the light up on the rock, well back from the hole, as the letter itself says to do. The candle-end catches. There's no wind, so the flame stands straight and pale in the noon glare. She holds it out to him and leaves the sealing to his hand. Osric holds the stub of red wax over the flame until it drips, lets a coin-sized pool fall across the fold, and presses the end of his iron key-ring into it. It's the same mark as on the case. He holds it there a moment, then pinches out the candle with a wet thumb.

When the wax has gone dull, Sefa folds the letter along its crease and slides it into her belt pouch. Osric picks up the oak case with both hands and holds it a breath longer than he needs to. Then he puts it into her arms.

"Ask her who she paid." He doesn't let go of her eyes. "Then tell me. That's the price of it."

While the wax cools, Bram gets on with his own work. He calls down the hole, flat and clear: "Pell! Bucket first, as ordered. Sefa's carrying the case. I'm staying." He unhitches the silk from the pinch-bar, lays the bar down on the rock, and knots the line through the bucket's rope handle. He pays the bucket out over the six feet of spoil and down past the soft black lip. It goes into the dark square knocking softly against the wall, and the line goes slack in his hands once it settles on the water below.

After that he sits down on the good rock and starts on the chain mail. It isn't quick work. He gets the buckles at the side undone, pulls the coat of rings off over his head, then works out of the padded coat under it, which is dark with sweat. It takes about five minutes. When he's done the mail lies in a grey heap beside his shield, and Bram crouches by the ring in shirt and breeches with his sword still on his belt. He feels lighter, and the sun bites at his shoulders.

He puts his question to Osric while he works. The rotten lip won't take a loaded rope, so can they brace the larch pole across sound stone, or is there another way into the cut?

Osric looks at the hole for longer than he likes to.

"No other way. Not that I know." He points at the pole, which still slants down into the shaft of light. "Lay it flat. Butt here on the rock, head clean across the hole onto the far side. Spread the weight. Then the rope runs over larch, not over that lip." He jerks his chin at Bram's pack. "Bedroll goes where the rope bites the pole. Far side's spoil too, mind. Pole spreads it. Doesn't make it rock."

Then Sefa gives her plan. Hale stays on the ring and the ridge and tends the line, and Bram goes down, and the two of them, Bram and Pell, clear the near edge and work the prop. When she gets to Hale at the ring, Osric shakes his head once.

"Not me on that ring till dark." He says it without heat. "Lads need finding. That won't keep."

He hesitates, then adds the part she won't want to hear, plainly, the way he'd tell them a face was bad.

"And the man under the block's no pair of hands. You heard him. Far side's packed against the ledge. He can't reach it without leaning on what's holding him. Two men, I said. Two that go down to him. Not him and one."

He leaves it there.

Sefa turns to the larch pole and lays her fingers on the grey wood near the butt, where it rests on the ridge under Bram's knee. A pale light kindles under her hand. It's as cold as starlight under water and gives off no heat or spark, and it stays there glowing on the peeled larch after she lifts her hand away. She gives her warnings in the same even voice: it lasts an hour and not a breath more, so get the first of the work done inside it. No flame down there. Listen for the water. If anything moves behind the flat grey wall, call and come up the line. The rayed disc and the marks aren't theirs to open, so don't touch them and don't tap the wall. Dig only at the near edge, and let the block answer.

Osric hears it all through. "Don't tap the wall" makes him look at her sharply. Then he collects his pen and ink-horn and the stub of wax, leaves the candle-end lying on the rock, and straightens up.

"I'll pass Thorn's door. Tell her where you are." He looks once more at the glowing pole and the slack lines running down into the dark. "Road's the road. Mine goes the same way yours does."

He turns and goes up the crew's path toward the house, keeping to the white mat, with his heavy coatless walk. His coat and his blackthorn stick are still waiting on the peg inside the door. By the iron ring Bram crouches without his mail. Sefa stands at the end of the good rock with the oak case under one arm and the sealed letter in her pouch. Six feet of spoil lie between the ring and the hole, and the bucket's line runs down over the black lip. The sun has moved a little west of the cut.

 1) Bram's chain mail: this was done as he declared, with no roll, because getting out of armour on solid rock takes about five minutes and can't fail.
2) The pole: Bram asked Osric whether it could be braced, and Osric explained how. Bram hasn't laid it across the hole yet, and he can't until Pell lets go of the far end, which is up to Pell's player.
3) The descent: Bram said he won't put his weight over the lip until the descent is made safe, and it isn't yet, so he hasn't gone down. When he does, it'll be an Athletics check, with advantage if the pole is laid flat across the hole first.
4) The bucket: this was done as he declared, with no roll, because lowering a bucket on a tied-off line into still water is certain.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his grip on the pole and answers Sefa first, honestly, since she asked:

"Shin's gone dull where the stone sits. Not dead, just numb, like a foot you've slept on. Toes still wiggle. I'll tell you the moment they stop."

Then he turns his attention to the hiss of the rope and the man coming down it. He keeps his voice low now that Bram will be close enough to hear without shouting:

"Bram. Come down on the right side, my right, where the prop is. Keep off the left and don't put a foot into the dark there. Sefa says something's down that way and I believe her."

He frees his hand from the pole just long enough to point under the water, so Bram can follow the line of his arm:

"Outer side's clear, down to the floor. What's left is the inner side, between my leg and the ledge edge, and under the near edge of the block beside the prop. That's where the weight sits. Dig there first, a stone at a time, and push them away from me, not toward me. Don't lean on the block while you're digging. When there's a gap under the near edge, you take the prop, Sefa takes the rope, and I'll pull the leg back the moment it lifts. A finger's width is all I need."

A breath, teeth rattling, then quieter, with no grin this time:

"And Bram. Hale won't carry it. So it's Sefa walks with the case, or nobody does. I'd rather it was her. She's the one who heard the letter read. Tell her I said so, if she argues."

He shrugs the pack a little higher on his chest and settles back against the pole. He keeps his weight on the good leg, his free hand clenching and opening, and his eyes on the dark band, the grey plaster and the still water. He doesn't look left.

scenes.narration:
Pell keeps his hand on the pole and answers Sefa first, since she asked. His shin has gone dull where the stone sits, numb like a foot slept on, but not dead. His toes still move, and he'll tell her the moment they stop. The wet walls throw each piece of it back at him as it goes up.

The rope's hiss stops, and something knocks against the wall above him, once and then again, softly. A wooden bucket comes down into the square of light, turning on Pell's own silk line. It knocks against the crusted stone a third time, settles on the water a foot from his shoulder, rocks, and floats. The silk is knotted through its rope handle, and the line runs taut back up the wall, over the black lip and away to the left.

Nobody comes down after it.

Pell turns to the hole anyway, keeping his voice low as if a man will be beside him in a moment. He tells Bram to come down on his right, where the prop is, keep off the left and not put a foot into the dark there, because Sefa says something's that way and he believes her. He takes his hand off the pole just long enough to point under the water, the line of his arm showing the way. The outer side is clear to the floor. What's left is the inner side, between his leg and the ledge edge, and under the near edge of the block by the prop, where the weight sits. Dig there first, one stone at a time, and push them away from him. Don't lean on the block while you're digging. When there's a gap, Bram takes the prop, Sefa takes the rope, and Pell pulls the leg back the moment it lifts. A finger's width is all he needs. Then, quieter and with no grin: Hale won't carry the case, so it's Sefa walks with it or nobody does. He'd rather it was her, because she heard the letter read. messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa turns once more at the end of the good rock, her light left burning pale at the pole's upper end, a still, cold star above the shaft.

"Pell, Sefa again. I have the case and the witnessed letter under my arm, and I'm walking them to Thorn now. Bram is coming down to you. Master Hale stays by the ring. You speak every little while, even if it's only your breath. Tell them if the water moves, if your foot goes cold, if anything touches the line. I'll find Hob and the crew, and I'll send them up the track."

She lets her eyes rest a moment on the black rim and the rope.

"Keep him at it, Bram. And you take no fire into that dark, whatever it offers."

Then she is gone up the crew's path with the oak case against her side and the folded letter in her pouch, not running, but setting each step as if the whole afternoon were the cart-track and the sun's shadow were a clock laid out behind her. At the top of the yard she glances once toward the open house, then walks on, toward the road to Beregost.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Sefa, he says it needs two able bodies below. I'd sooner lose the fee than Pell. Will you stay and help me? Your call.”

I raise my voice towards Osric. “If you're leaving, send help from Beregost. Tell Thorn a man's trapped, not merely down a hole.”

Then I lay the pole across as Osric described, with its butt well supported on rock and the bedroll padding where the hemp will bear. I secure it against rolling and gradually load the rope from my position on solid stone, watching the far support for settling.

“Pell, we're rigging the descent. Any change in your leg or the water?”

If the support holds firm, I lower the pinch-bar separately, then descend the anchored hemp slowly, without setting foot on the rotten rim. If the pole or spoil shifts under the test, I stop rather than trust it with my weight.

scenes.narration:
Pell's voice comes up out of the ground before Sefa has taken her last step along the ridge. It's flattened by the stone, but it's steadier than it was, the voice of a man who has stopped shouting because someone is now close enough to hear him:

"*…shin's gone dull… where the stone sits… not dead… like a foot you've slept on… toes still wiggle… I'll say when they stop…*" There's a breath, and then: "*…Bram… come down on my RIGHT… where the prop is… keep off the left… don't put a foot in the dark there… inner side… between my leg and the ledge… under the near edge… push them away from me… don't lean on the block…*" Another breath. "*…Hale won't carry it… so it's Sefa walks, or nobody… I'd rather it was her… she heard the letter read… tell her I said so…*"

Sefa turns once more at the end of the good rock, with the oak case against her side. She sends her words down past the pole with its pale, cold light: it's Sefa again, she has the case and the witnessed letter and is walking them to Thorn now, Bram is coming down, Master Hale stays by the ring. Pell is to speak every little while, even if it's only his breath, and say if the water moves, if his foot goes cold, if anything touches the line. She'll find Hob and the crew and send them up the track. Her eyes rest a moment on the black rim and the rope. Then, to Bram: keep him at it, and take no fire into that dark, whatever it offers.

She goes up the crew's path on the packed white mat. She doesn't run. Her steps are even, and her shadow lies short and a little east of her on the dust.

Bram's voice follows her up the slope, and the quarry is quiet enough that every word reaches her. Pell says it needs two able bodies below. He'd sooner lose the fee than Pell. Will she stay and help him? Her call.

Then Bram turns his head toward the house and raises his voice to carry the whole way. "Hale! If you're leaving, send help from Beregost. Tell Thorn a man's trapped. Not just down a hole."

Up at the house, Osric is in the doorway, one arm in his coat and the blackthorn stick hooked over his wrist. He works the other arm in before he answers. His voice comes down across the yard flat and heavy.

"Trapped. I'll say it." He settles the coat on his shoulders. "Fist keeps a post in the town. I'll knock there too." There's a pause, the length of a man looking at the sun. "Not before dark. Whoever comes."

He pulls the door to behind him. It won't latch, and it swings back a hand's width onto the cold hearth. He comes down the step onto the cart track. Sefa has reached the top of the yard, and when she glances toward the house he's already there, ten paces behind her on the same road, with his stick and his heavy walk. He doesn't hurry to catch her up and he doesn't hang back.

On the ridge, Bram sets about the rig. He pulls the bedroll out of his pack and unrolls it on the rock beside the ring, ready to fold double where the hemp will bear on the larch. He prises loose stones out of the seep-cracks along the ridge, fist-sized lumps of grey crusted pink, and packs them round the pole's butt on both sides, so it can't roll once it lies flat. Then he takes the butt in both hands and starts to draw the pole up out of the hole, slowly, a few inches at a time, to bring the head over and lay it across.

The pole doesn't come. A few inches up, the far end holds. It isn't caught on stone. Through the grain Bram can feel a hand closed on the wood down there, and the small, living give of a man braced against it in the water. He keeps his grip without hauling, and the larch stays where it is, slanting down past the soft black lip into the shaft of light.

He sends his voice down after it: they're rigging the descent. Is there any change in his leg or the water?

The drip comes up out of the hole. Out on the cart track, two figures go down toward the Way, a woman with a case under her arm and a heavy man with a stick a little behind her, getting smaller in the white glare. The cold light glows on the larch. The bucket's silk line runs taut from the ring over the lip, and the hemp runs slack beside it. The sun has moved a hand's breadth west of the top of the sky.

Your narration:
<<<
Pell's voice comes up out of the ground before Sefa has taken her last step along the ridge. It's flattened by the stone, but it's steadier than it was, the voice of a man who has stopped shouting because someone is now close enough to hear him:

"*…shin's gone dull… where the stone sits… not dead… like a foot you've slept on… toes still wiggle… I'll say when they stop…*" There's a breath, and then: "*…Bram… come down on my RIGHT… where the prop is… keep off the left… don't put a foot in the dark there… inner side… between my leg and the ledge… under the near edge… push them away from me… don't lean on the block…*" Another breath. "*…Hale won't carry it… so it's Sefa walks, or nobody… I'd rather it was her… she heard the letter read… tell her I said so…*"

Sefa turns once more at the end of the good rock, with the oak case against her side. She sends her words down past the pole with its pale, cold light: it's Sefa again, she has the case and the witnessed letter and is walking them to Thorn now, Bram is coming down, Master Hale stays by the ring. Pell is to speak every little while, even if it's only his breath, and say if the water moves, if his foot goes cold, if anything touches the line. She'll find Hob and the crew and send them up the track. Her eyes rest a moment on the black rim and the rope. Then, to Bram: keep him at it, and take no fire into that dark, whatever it offers.

She goes up the crew's path on the packed white mat. She doesn't run. Her steps are even, and her shadow lies short and a little east of her on the dust.

Bram's voice follows her up the slope, and the quarry is quiet enough that every word reaches her. Pell says it needs two able bodies below. He'd sooner lose the fee than Pell. Will she stay and help him? Her call.

Then Bram turns his head toward the house and raises his voice to carry the whole way. "Hale! If you're leaving, send help from Beregost. Tell Thorn a man's trapped. Not just down a hole."

Up at the house, Osric is in the doorway, one arm in his coat and the blackthorn stick hooked over his wrist. He works the other arm in before he answers. His voice comes down across the yard flat and heavy.

"Trapped. I'll say it." He settles the coat on his shoulders. "Fist keeps a post in the town. I'll knock there too." There's a pause, the length of a man looking at the sun. "Not before dark. Whoever comes."

He pulls the door to behind him. It won't latch, and it swings back a hand's width onto the cold hearth. He comes down the step onto the cart track. Sefa has reached the top of the yard, and when she glances toward the house he's already there, ten paces behind her on the same road, with his stick and his heavy walk. He doesn't hurry to catch her up and he doesn't hang back.

On the ridge, Bram sets about the rig. He pulls the bedroll out of his pack and unrolls it on the rock beside the ring, ready to fold double where the hemp will bear on the larch. He prises loose stones out of the seep-cracks along the ridge, fist-sized lumps of grey crusted pink, and packs them round the pole's butt on both sides, so it can't roll once it lies flat. Then he takes the butt in both hands and starts to draw the pole up out of the hole, slowly, a few inches at a time, to bring the head over and lay it across.

The pole doesn't come. A few inches up, the far end holds. It isn't caught on stone. Through the grain Bram can feel a hand closed on the wood down there, and the small, living give of a man braced against it in the water. He keeps his grip without hauling, and the larch stays where it is, slanting down past the soft black lip into the shaft of light.

He sends his voice down after it: they're rigging the descent. Is there any change in his leg or the water?

The drip comes up out of the hole. Out on the cart track, two figures go down toward the Way, a woman with a case under her arm and a heavy man with a stick a little behind her, getting smaller in the white glare. The cold light glows on the larch. The bucket's silk line runs taut from the ring over the lip, and the hemp runs slack beside it. The sun has moved a hand's breadth west of the top of the sky.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell catches the bucket's rope handle before it can drift, checks the silk knot through it by feel, and hooks the handle over the end of the prop so it sits beside him and stays put.

He tips his face up toward the rim and keeps his voice level:

"Bucket's here, thanks. Tied off on the prop so it won't wander." A breath, teeth rattling. "Who's gone up the slope? Hale, or Sefa with the case? Somebody tell me who's still on the rim. I'd like to know who I'm talking to."

He waits a moment, then goes on, practical:

"If two are coming down, the bucket's for the stones as well as the water. Dig them out, drop them in, haul them up. If you pile them round the block, they just pack back in where they were. Send the bar down on the rope, not over the edge, and send it before the men."

Then he says what Sefa asked for, plainly:

"Toes still move. Shin's numb, no worse than before. No cold creeping past the knee."

He gives the pole a slow, deliberate squeeze, two pulses, so whoever holds the far end feels he's still there. He glances once at the faint cold paleness at the top of the slant, then back down.

"And whoever's holding the pole up there, with the hand that isn't a hand: don't let go of it on my account. I'm not climbing. I just like something dry to hang on to."

He settles back, weight on the good leg, free hand clenching and opening under the water. He counts the notches on the block again in his head to stay awake: three, one, gap. His eyes keep going from the dark band to the grey plaster and back. He doesn't look left.

Under his breath: "An hour. Fine. I've waited longer for worse company."
