scenes.narration:
Pell reaches out with his free hand and catches the bucket's rope handle on its next slow turn. By feel he finds the silk knot through it: two turns and a hitch, pulled hard, wet now and holding. He pushes the bucket along the surface toward the prop, finds the black timber with his fingertips where it slants down to the block, and hooks the rope handle over it. The bucket bumps once against the wood and stays there by his hip, floating and tethered. The prop doesn't shift under it.

As he lets go, Sefa's voice comes down past the cold light, even and clear, aimed into the hole: *"…Pell, Sefa again… I have the case… the witnessed letter… walking them to Thorn now… Bram is coming down to you… Master Hale stays by the ring… speak every little while… if the water moves… your foot goes cold… anything touches the line… I'll find Hob and the crew… send them up the track."* After that she says something lower and further off, not meant for the hole. Then he hears nothing more from her.

He tips his face up and sends his words after hers, level and one piece at a time. The bucket's here, thanks, tied off on the prop so it won't wander. Who's gone up the slope, Hale or Sefa with the case? Somebody tell him who's still on the rim. If two are coming down, the bucket's for the stones as well as the water: dig them out, drop them in, haul them up, because if they're piled round the block they'll pack straight back in. Send the bar down on the rope, not over the edge, and before the men. His toes still move. The shin's numb and no worse, and the cold isn't creeping past the knee. The wet walls throw each piece back at him as it goes.

Bram's voice comes next. It doesn't come down the hole. It's aimed up the slope, big and flat, and from the bottom of the working Pell gets only pieces of it: *"…Sefa… needs two able bodies below… sooner lose the fee than Pell… will you stay… your call."* Nothing comes back down that Pell can hear. Then Bram sends it the other way, louder: *"…Hale!… send help from Beregost… tell Thorn a man's trapped… not just down a hole."*

The answer is a long way off, a heavy voice carrying down across the yard from the house end of the quarry. By the time it reaches the water there's almost nothing left of it: *"…trapped… I'll say it… Fist… not before dark…"*

Then the pole moves.

It slides upward through his fist, slowly, an inch, then another, as somebody draws it up from the rock. Pell's hand is closed on it and the wood stops against his grip. He feels the small give of the man at the other end feeling for him, the larch hanging still between them. Pell squeezes it twice, slowly, two pulses through the grain. Nothing pulls on it after that.

Bram's voice comes down the hole again, close and low over the ring: *"…rigging the descent… any change in your leg… or the water?"*

The last of Pell's words go up after it, quieter. Whoever's holding the pole up there with the hand that isn't a hand shouldn't let go of it on his account. He isn't climbing. He just likes something dry to hang on to.

Then he settles back, weight on the good leg, his free hand clenching and opening under the water. He counts the notches round the rays in his head to keep his mind awake: three, one, gap. The sweet, oven-warm air sits on the surface the way it has since he fell.

His eyes go to the wall. The dark band is still there, but it isn't a full hand's breadth above the water any more. A finger of it has gone. The water hasn't moved in a way he could see, but it is higher now than it was when he first measured it against the stone. The seep threads down its crack without a sound and slips into the water. The grey plaster behind the block is flat and grey. The bucket knocks softly against the prop. High above, the square of sky leans a little further west, and the slant of light has crept another finger's width across the far wall.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I stop moving the pole.

“Pell, are you holding the larch? I need it across the hole to carry my rope clear of the rotten edge. Can you let go safely? You've still got the rescue loop under your arms.”

I keep it steady until he answers. If he can release it, I tell him before moving it, then finish laying and bracing it across the opening, pad the rope's bearing point, and test the rig gradually from solid rock.

If it holds, I lower the bar on a separate line and descend slowly on his right, towards the prop.

“Sefa's taking the case, as you asked. Help's being sent. Now let's see what we can clear without shifting that block onto you.”

You ask whether Pell is holding the larch, since you need it laid across the hole to carry your rope clear of the rotten edge, and whether he can let go safely with the rescue loop still under his arms. In the same breath you tell him Sefa is taking the case, as he asked, that help is being sent, and that you'll see what can be cleared without shifting the block onto him.

Before you've finished, Pell's voice is already climbing the other way, words he must have sent up a moment before you began. The stone flattens them and breaks them into pieces. He says the bucket has reached him, thanks, and he's tied it off on the prop so it won't wander. He asks who has gone up the slope, Hale or Sefa with the case, and who is still on the rim. The bucket is for the stones as well as the water, he says: dig them out, drop them in, haul them up and pile them round the block, where they'll pack back in. The bar goes down on the rope, not over the edge, before the men come.

Then, plainer: his toes still move, his shin is numb, it's no worse, and there's no cold past the knee.

The last piece is the quietest, and it barely clears the black lip. Whoever is holding the pole up there shouldn't let go of it on his account. He isn't climbing, he just likes having something dry to hang on to.

Through the wood you feel the grip at the far end tighten once and settle, the hold of a man who has found the one dry, solid thing in a cold place and isn't letting go. The pole stays where it is, slanting down past the soft black lip into the shaft of light. Sefa's cold paleness glows faintly near the butt under your knee.

The rig waits on the ridge beside you: the bedroll unrolled on the rock, the pink-crusted stones packed round the pole's butt, the pinch-bar lying loose where you set it down. The silk that was to carry the bar runs taut from the ring over the lip and down to the bucket below. The hemp beside it runs slack to the loop round Pell's chest. messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stops on the cart track, the case against her side, and turns all the way back so Bram can see she isn't continuing.

"Don't go below alone. I'm coming back to the rope. Wait for me before you put a foot into that water."

Then she closes the ten paces to Osric, not to block his road but to meet him on it.

"You said it takes two men by dusk. Bram is one. You are the other, if you can be made to stay. But you won't carry the salt, and you won't go down, and one woman can't be both on the road and under the ground." Her voice is not raised; it has the clarity of someone making a division of labour out of a bad day.

"So I'll make it plain. I'm staying to hold the line, keep the light, and heal. You walk to Beregost—not to the Fist and past Thorn's door, but into Thorn's shop, with this case and the witnessed letter in your hand. Tell her Sefa Marrin stayed at Whitestone on her hire, to keep a man alive until more hands come, and that you are not cartering the house's salt—you're carrying the buyer's goods because the buyer's courier is standing over a hole."

She holds the oak case out, not yet letting go, the red wax catching the midday sun.

"Put it in her hands before the coach leaves, and your crew's wage-letter goes with it. Refuse, and I leave the case on the rock and we all lose the coin—but I won't lose Pell to a contract. Choose, Master Hale."

scenes.narration:
Sefa stops in the middle of the cart track. She turns all the way round, with the oak case against her hip, so that anyone looking up from the low face can see she has stopped walking. Then she sends her voice back down across the white yard: don't go below alone, she's coming back to the rope, wait for her before he puts a foot in that water. The quarry is so quiet that it carries the whole way down.

Osric has stopped too, ten paces behind her, with the blackthorn stick planted in the dust. He watches her walk the distance back to him. He doesn't step aside and he doesn't step forward.

She lays it out for him in her clear, level voice. Two men by dusk, and Bram is one. Hale won't carry the salt and won't go down, and one woman can't be on the road and under the ground at once. So she'll stay to hold the line, keep the light and heal. He walks into Thorn's shop, not just past her door, with the case and the witnessed letter in his hand. He tells her Sefa Marrin stayed at Whitestone on her hire to keep a man alive, and that he isn't carting the house's salt. He's carrying the buyer's goods because the buyer's courier is standing over a hole. She holds the case out but keeps hold of it. If he refuses, the case goes back on the rock and everyone loses the coin, because she won't lose Pell to a contract.

Osric hears her out without moving. When she gets to *the buyer's courier standing over a hole*, his eyes drop to the case and its red wax, his own mark, and stay there. He runs it through in his head once, the way he would recount a column of figures.

"Your hire. Your hand to mine." He says it slowly, so it will stick. "Thorn's courier gave it me to carry, at her asking. That's how it goes in my book." He looks up at her. "That I can stand behind when Pryce comes."

He hooks the stick over his wrist and takes the case in both hands, the way he gave it to her. Then he holds out a broad, split-knuckled palm for the letter. She takes it from her pouch and lays it there, and he pushes it inside his coat, flat against his chest, and buttons the coat over it.

"Into her shop. In her hands. And I'll ask her myself who she paid." That part he seems to like. "Saves you the telling."

Before he turns, he looks past her down the slope, at the shelf, the ring and the little dark square beyond it.

"Fist post I'll still knock at. And the alehouses." His jaw works. "Water's on the rise in the afternoons. Slow. Mind it."

He turns and goes down the cart track toward the Way with the case under one arm and the stick swinging in the other hand. His heavy walk is no faster than before and no slower. He doesn't look back. The dust he kicks up hangs behind him in the still air.

Sefa stands alone on the track at the top of the yard. Her hands are empty now, and the whole white bowl of Whitestone lies open below her: the cold house with its door hanging open, the lifting frame, the long shed by the lower cut, the rust-brown stone, and the grey ridge along the low face where the ropes run out to the hole. The sun has moved a little past the top of the sky. Her shadow has come out from under her feet and lies short on the dust, pointing back down toward the low face.

 Sefa's words do their work. Her case reaches him on the one ground he had stood on, the house's book and his own name in it, and it leaves him with nothing left to refuse, so Osric gives way and takes the errand as his own. The salt is on the road to Beregost in the warden's arms. The road back to the rope is hers.

He's carrying the buyer's goods because the buyer's courier is standing over a hole. She holds the case out but keeps hold of it. If he refuses, the case goes back on the rock and everyone loses the coin, because she won't lose Pell to a contract.

Osric hears her out without moving. When she gets to *the buyer's courier standing over a hole*, his eyes drop to the case and its red wax, his own mark, and stay there. He runs it through in his head once, the way he would recount a column of figures.

"Your hire. Your hand to mine." He says it slowly, so it will stick. "Thorn's courier gave it me to carry, at her asking. That's how it goes in my book." He looks up at her. "That I can stand behind when Pryce comes."

He hooks the stick over his wrist and takes the case in both hands, the way he gave it to her. Then he holds out a broad, split-knuckled palm for the letter. She takes it from her pouch and lays it there, and he pushes it inside his coat, flat against his chest, and buttons the coat over it.

"Into her shop. In her hands. And I'll ask her myself who she paid." That part he seems to like. "Saves you the telling."

Before he turns, he looks past her down the slope, at the shelf, the ring and the little dark square beyond it.

"Fist post I'll still knock at. And the alehouses." His jaw works. "Water's on the rise in the afternoons. Slow. Mind it."

He turns and goes down the cart track toward the Way with the case under one arm and the stick swinging in the other hand. His heavy walk is no faster than before and no slower. He doesn't look back. The dust he kicks up hangs behind him in the still air.

The sun has moved a little past the top of the sky. Her shadow has come out from under her feet and lies short on the dust, pointing back down toward the low face.

Her case reaches him on the one ground he had stood on, the house's book and his own name in it, and it leaves him with nothing left to refuse, so Osric gives way and takes the errand as his own. The salt is on the road to Beregost in the warden's arms. The road back to the rope is hers.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets the pole go slack in his fist so whoever is drawing it can have it back if they need it for the descent. He keeps his fingers resting on the wood all the same.

He tips his face up toward Bram's voice and gives it to him straight, without dressing it up:

"Bram. One thing's changed. The water's up a finger on the wall. I measured it against the dark band when I fell, a hand's breadth clear. Now it's a hand less a finger. Slow, but it isn't standing still." A breath through rattling teeth. "Leg's the same. Numb, toes moving. Nothing's touched the line."

He works it through out loud, plainly, the way he'd lay out a job:

"So don't waste the bucket on bailing. That seep will beat a bucket all afternoon. Use it for the stones and keep the water for later. If it gets near my chin before the block's off, that's when you haul, and you haul gently. A ruined leg's better than a drowned man. But we're hours off that. Come down on my right, by the prop. The rim's rotten on the step side, so come over where your rope's anchored, not near the door."

Then, quieter, because Hale said something and Pell heard it:

"And if Hale's sending to the Fist, tell him thank you from me. Even if it's not before dark."

He pushes the bucket a hand's width closer along the prop, so it'll sit by Bram's hand when he lands. With his free hand he feels along the cleared outer side of his boot to check nothing has slid back into the gap.

Then he settles. Weight on the good leg, hand clenching and opening, counting under his breath: three, one, gap. His eyes go to the dark band and stay there a while, as if staring might hold the water still. He doesn't look left.

"A finger an hour," he mutters. "I can do sums. Come on, Bram."

scenes.narration:
Pell lets his fist go loose on the larch. The wood stays where it is, but his fingers lie open on it now instead of closed, and nothing at his end is holding it any more. Up at the far end the grip doesn't move. The pole hangs at its slant, dry and still. Near the top, where it crosses the rim, it gives off a faint cold paleness against the glare.

Bram's voice comes down before Pell has finished drawing breath. It's close and low over the ring, and the stone flattens it: *"…Pell… are you holding the larch?… need it across the hole… carry my rope clear of the rotten edge… can you let go safely?… you've still got the rescue loop…"* Then: *"…Sefa's taking the case… as you asked… help's being sent… let's see what we can clear… without shifting that block onto you."*

Pell tips his face up and sends his own words up a piece at a time, and the wet walls throw each one back at him. One thing's changed: the water is up a finger on the wall. It was a hand's breadth clear of the dark band when he fell, and now it's a hand less a finger, slow but not standing still. His leg is the same, numb, toes moving, and nothing has touched the line. So the bucket shouldn't go on bailing, because the seep will beat a bucket all afternoon. It's for the stones, and the water can wait. If the water gets near his chin before the block is off, that's when they haul, gently, because a ruined leg is better than a drowned man, but they're hours off that. Bram should come down on his right, by the prop. The rim on the step side is rotten, so he should come over where his rope is anchored, not near the door. Last, quieter: if Hale is sending to the Fist, tell him thank you from Pell, even if it's not before dark.

The words go up and stay up.

Then another voice comes, from much further off, high across the yard and broken to pieces by the time it drops into the hole. It's a woman's voice, clear and level, and nobody would mistake it for Bram's:

*"…don't go below alone… I'm coming back to the rope… wait for me… before you put a foot… in that water."*

After that comes only the drip.

Pell pushes the bucket a hand's width further along the prop with his free hand, until it bumps against the black timber on the right-hand side where a man coming down the rope would land. Its rope handle stays hooked fast, and the silk runs taut from it up the wall. Then he slides his hand down under the water along the outside of his boot. The gap he cleared is still there, a hand's width of open water between the leather and the next stones out. A skin of fine silt has settled into it, soft as flour under his fingertips, and nothing has slid back. The block above his shin sits exactly where it sat.

He settles his weight onto his good leg. His hand clenches and opens under the water. *Three, one, gap.* His eyes go to the dark band on the wall and stay there.

The water lies flat and cold round his chest. The seep threads down its crack and slips into the surface without a sound. The grey plaster behind the block is just grey. The square of sky overhead has leaned a little further west, and the slant of light now lies across the far wall a finger's width higher than when he first looked.

"A finger an hour," he mutters. "I can do sums. Come on, Bram."

Above him the pole hangs slack in his open fingers. Nothing draws on it yet.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Pell, it's Bram alone up here. Sefa has the case; Hale's gone to send help. Listen: I need you to let go of the pole for a minute so I can make a safe way down. Can you do that?”

I hold the pole steady while he answers.

“Keep the chest loop on. Once I've braced the pole across the hole, I'll lower the bar, then come down on your right. You'll have company instead of a stick.”

I don't tug against his grip. Once he releases it, I proceed with bracing, padding and testing the crossing from solid rock.

opening.narration:
The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind them, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life — a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 23 gp; 14 sp; 30 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: in the quarry yard, a few paces from the house doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You leave the doorway clear and keep your sword sheathed, waiting on the man's answer. You look over his apron and hands, then past him into the house.

Sefa holds her ground and watches the warden. When he says nothing at once, she keeps her voice level and doesn't press. She says the three of you have no wish to make his trouble yours unless you must, that you are here for the case, and that if anything stands between you and it, you had best know now while the sun is still high enough to act. She glances once at the smoke, then back at him.

Pell answers for the group. He calls the man master Hale and says you are couriers, paid ninety on delivery and nothing before, much like the man's own crew. He asks who carries the wages out from the Gate and whose house that factor or clerk serves. If someone is skimming both ends, he says, Thorn will want the name, since a buyer's coach leaves at sunset and she will be shouting by suppertime. He offers to carry a written statement of the three weeks unpaid, sealed with the man's own mark, to her hand along with the case, while the man keeps a copy. Then he asks about the long shed down the lower cut with its door standing open, and whether one of the crew left in a rush or the mule went in there.

Osric does not answer straight away. His hands are a cutter's hands: broad, split at the knuckles, the nails worn to the quick, and no weapon anywhere near them. White dust is ground into the creases of his apron like flour. Near the pocket a faint smear of grit shows a different colour, pinkish, the shade of a rose gone pale, where something was wiped off once and not brushed away.

Past his shoulder you can see part of one room. A kettle hangs over the hearth coals, and a scrubbed table holds a fat book bound in stained canvas with a pen stuck through its strap. Beside it sits a small case of dark oak, banded in brass, about the size of a loaf, with a disc of red wax across the clasp. A coat hangs on a peg just inside the door, and a blackthorn stick leans under it.

"Something between you and the case," Osric says to Sefa. "Aye. The money."

He hears Pell out, and his jaw works at the comparison with his lads as if he'd like to argue it and can't.

"House is Vandarren. In the Gate. Patriar house, or used to be." He says the name like a stone he's been carrying in his pocket. "Their man's Pryce. Factor. Salt goes out of here sealed, and the money for it goes to Pryce. Pryce sends the wages back by runner, first of the month and the fifteenth." A beat. "Didn't. Twice now."

He thinks about the letter longer than about anything else Pell said.

"Write it. Aye." He nods once, slowly. "Witnessed. That I'll do. You read it out to her, in front of her, not after." His eyes go to the sun, high over the white faces, and then to the coat on its peg. "I'm for the town at noon myself. Lads'll be drinking it out somewhere. Want them to hear it from me, not from a broadsheet."

On the shed, his hand doesn't go to the keys. It stays pressed flat against his sleeve. He looks past Pell, not at the shed but below it, at the lower face where the terraces drop away into stone stained dark with damp.

"Lower cutting-shed. Nobody in it. Door's warped. Won't shut. Mule went with Hob, the carter. He was owed the most."

Then Osric unfolds his arms, turns into the house and sits heavily at the table, leaving the door open behind him. He slides the pen free of its strap, opens the canvas-bound book to a clean page at the back and starts to write, slowly, pressing hard, his lips moving over the words. The oak case sits at his elbow with its red wax catching the hearth light. The kettle starts to tick as it comes to the boil.

Where you are: yard outside Osric's house at the quarry · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You stayed by the open doorway while Osric wrote. You said you would witness what he put down and see Thorn heard it, but that you wouldn't promise she'd pay another man's debts. You asked whether he'd release the case along with the letter, and how much he and the crew were owed.

Before that, Pell had stepped up to the threshold, leaned a shoulder on the frame with his hands in view, and asked Osric whose seal was on the wax and whether the stain on him was the salt. Then he told you and Sefa to stay with Osric while he wrote, and asked Sefa to read the letter back before it was sealed. He said he'd be a quarter of an hour at most, and walked down toward the lower cut.

Osric didn't look up when Pell's shadow fell across the threshold. The pen kept scratching. The seal was his, he said: a quarry mark, a W with a hammer through it. The house never sent one and never asked for one. The colour was the salt, which grows on the wet walls down the low cuts, rose-white like frost that won't melt. You scrape it, dry it on slates, and it goes in the case. Nothing had leaked, and he had sealed it himself the day before yesterday. He brushed at the smear on his apron and it didn't come off. "Thirty years it's been on those walls. Nobody wanted it till the spring."

As Pell started down the slope Osric raised his voice, flat and carrying. "Mind the boards down there. Old workings under. And don't stand about at the low face. Air's thick." Then he bent back to the page.

Sefa spoke next, quietly. She said she had once been a novice in a hospice in the Gate, and that she knew the look of a man who had been told he'd done everything possible and still hadn't believed it. She asked what work the crew did before they were shut in, and whether the rose-coloured dust on their gear came from the new salts or had always been there. Osric's pen stopped and stayed stopped while she talked. "Didn't do all I could," he said. "Did what the house paid for." Nobody was shut in, he said. They worked the faces, upper and lower, same as any year: cut, split, cart, and scrape the salt when there was an order. He glanced at her, brief and dry. "And I never said the shed changed. Shed's just a shed. Door's warped."

To you he said she needn't pay it, only know it. Fourteen men, three weeks, two silver a day for a cutter and less for the boys. Forty-two gold, near enough. Hob was owed more, having fed the mule out of his own purse. That didn't count Osric's own. The case would go when the letter was sealed and Sefa had read it back to him, and not before.

From the doorway you follow Osric's earlier look down the slope. The lower face is a different stone from the rest: greyer, streaked dark where water seeps from the cracks, and spotted with a pale crust that catches the sun faintly pink. Below it the ground flattens into a shelf of trodden spoil. Grey planks lie across it here and there, laid flat over something.

Pell reaches the lower shed and looks in at the gap without crossing the sill. You can't make out what he sees from here.

Up at the house the kettle boils over with a hiss onto the coals. Osric reaches out and swings it off the hook without looking, and keeps writing.

Where you are: in the doorway of Osric's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 4 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Beside you in the doorway, Sefa had turned at Osric's warning and called after Pell herself, telling him to mind the boards because of old workings under them and not to stand about at the low face. As Pell walked on she added, low and as if to herself, a remark that bad air like that doesn't save its warnings for strangers. She then went back into the house and pressed Osric, before the letter was sealed, on what he meant by the low face air: had he been down since his crew stopped, and had the men complained of headaches, guttering lamps or a sweetness in the air before they were gone. She said that if it was foul air pooling in old workings, Pell ought to know how far it reaches, and that she didn't want to bring Thorn word of a fourth man overcome before sundown.

Your call and hers carry out over the white yard and down the slope toward the lower cut. The quarry is quiet enough that every word goes the whole way.

Inside, Osric's pen doesn't stop for the shouting. It stops when Sefa comes back in and asks her questions, and it stays stopped while you ask yours from the doorway.

"Not coughing." He sets the pen down crosswise on the page. "Sleepy. Man works the low face a long stretch, he gets heavy in the eyes, slow in the hands. Send him up into the sun, he's right by supper." He rubs a thumb along the edge of the table. "Headaches, some. Lamps burn fine. That's why I said it. Air's thick down there. It doesn't choke you. It just sits on you."

He thinks about the sweetness longer.

"Shed's the same when the brazier's going. Wet weather we dry the salt on the slates over a bit of fire. Room smells like a bakehouse. Lads used to nod off over the racks." He says it like any other fact about the place, the way he'd tell them the faces get slick in rain. "Haven't been down since they went. No call to."

Then Sefa's last line lands, and his head comes up.

"Fourth." He looks at her for the first time since he sat down, flat and hard. "Nobody's been overcome. Nobody said three." His fingers have found his sleeve and pressed in. A moment passes. When he picks up the pen again he says, to the page and not to her, "Not lately."

He writes the rest quickly, with no lip-moving now, and blots it with the heel of his hand. Then he takes the page by its top corner and tears it out of the canvas book along the fold, slowly, so it comes away clean. The book stays open on the table with its stub showing, and behind the stub are the ruled pages of earlier years, columns of names and days in the same heavy hand.

He lays the torn page beside the oak case. From the doorway you can read the first lines without trying, the letters pressed nearly through the paper:

*To Maela Thorn, apothecary, Beregost. From Osric Hale, warden at Whitestone for House Vandarren of the Gate. Fourteen men three weeks unpaid by the house. Wages to come by Pryce the factor's runner on the first and the fifteenth. Did not come, twice. You paid for this salt. Ask him where it went.*

Below that the hand gets smaller, a list of names with a sum against each, and at the bottom a blank space with a short line drawn for a mark.

The kettle has stopped ticking. The hearth settles. Out past your shoulder the sun stands nearly at the top of the sky over the white faces, and the coat on its peg sways a little in the draught from the open door.

Where you are: Doorway of Osric's house at the Whitestone quarry · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 5 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa meets Osric's hard look without flinching. She tells him she said "fourth" with only the three of you in mind, and Pell walking down there, and that she meant no count against his crew. She takes the page only after asking and getting no objection, then reads it back to him word for word, names and sums included, a finger following the line under the paper. She asks him for his mark, with one of you to witness it. She also asks you whether Pell is still in the open.

When you said it again, quietly, "Not lately," Osric's pen stopped. He didn't look up at once, and when he did, he looked past you, out the door toward the lower cut.

"Three year back." He set the pen in the fold of the book. "Most come up right by supper. One didn't." He gave nothing more, and his mouth closed on it.

You turned in the doorway and called down the slope to Pell: the salt makes men drowsy, worse when heated, don't light anything in there. Your voice crossed the white yard to the lower cut, and nothing came back. The crew's path runs empty down to the shelf. The shed's warped door stands a hand's width open. You can't see Pell on the path, on the shelf or at the low face. Over the shed step, where the white mat meets the door, a haze of dust hangs in the still noon air, thicker than boots would raise, and it hasn't settled. Under it, where the flat stone of the step should show pale, there is a dark ragged patch. Behind you the kettle sits off its hook, and the coals still spit where it boiled over.

You turned back and told Osric to keep the case sealed and to send the warning with the wage letter, since whoever opens it may not know what his lads learned. He heard you out, picked up the pen and turned the torn page round.

"Drowsy's not a danger. Not up top." He wrote anyway, bearing down on a short line squeezed in under the names, above the blank for his mark. "There. Don't say I didn't."

His fingers eased off his sleeve at Sefa's words, and he gave a single grunt, as near to "aye" as he gets. When she read the page back, she read the line he added at your word last: salt makes men sleepy if they work it long, do not dry it over a fire in a shut room. Osric listened with his eyes shut. "That's it." He scratched his mark on the line, the W with the hammer through it, the same as on the wax, and laid the pen crosswise on the page where a witness's hand would go.

At Sefa's question about Pell, Osric's head came up. He looked at your back in the door, pushed himself up from the table and came to stand beside you, looking down the slope. He saw the dust over the shed step, and his face changed. It wasn't anger now.

"Shed step." His voice was low and flat. "There's an old cut under it. Under the whole shelf." His hand gripped the doorframe. "Water in it. Always."

No sound comes up from the lower cut. The haze over the step is thinning in the windless air, and the dark patch beneath it is plain to see. The sun stands almost overhead. On the table behind you, the case sits beside the marked letter with its wax unbroken, and the pen still lies across the blank where a witness's mark should go.

Where you are: in the doorway of the warden's hut at Whitestone, looking down the slope · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 6 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa is out of the door before Osric has finished speaking, into the white glare, and calls down the slope for Pell to answer if he can hear. You follow a step behind, already pulling the coil of hempen rope from your belt. You call out yourself and tell Osric sharply to show you where the solid ground ends.

Halfway down the crew's path, Sefa closes her hand round the prayer beads at her neck and says a single word. A pale, even light rises from the wooden beads, with no heat in it and no spark. It's faint in the noon sun, but it'll be enough under the shed's shadow. She holds it low against her chest.

Then the ground answers you.

A voice comes up out of the shelf ahead, flat and broken by the stone it has to climb through. You catch it in pieces, the way you hear a shout from a cellar:

"*…BRAM! SEFA!… lower shed!… under the step!… pinned… water to my chest!… don't run in!… hollow… door… crew's path… off the flagstone!… bring Hale!… smells sweet!…*"

Then nothing but the drip from somewhere under the planks, and the dust still settling over the dark patch where the step used to be.

Osric has come out after you with his coat left on the peg. He doesn't hurry, but he doesn't stop either. When you halt well short of the shelf he comes up beside you and points with two fingers, the way a man points at stone he has cut.

"Path's rock as far as that brown stone." It's a rust-coloured boulder sunk in the white mat about fifteen feet short of the shed door. "Past it, it's spoil laid over old timber. The whole shelf. Thirty years we walked it." His mouth sets. "Step was a lid. Nobody knew."

He turns his hand to the left, toward the foot of the low face, where the grey stone comes down to the shelf in a ridge of bare rock dark with seep. "Rock runs along the face. Gets you within five, six feet of the hole on that side. No closer." Set into that ridge, a little above the mat, is an iron ring as thick as a man's thumb, brown with rust and leaded into the stone. "Lowering ring. Older than me. It'll hold a cart."

Sefa's light picks out the ragged lip of the hole beyond. It's a gap about four feet across, edged with soft black timber and broken white crust. Below it there's only the glint of still water.

"Cut runs back under the face," Osric says, lower now. "Water stands four foot in summer. Five after rain." He stays on the path behind the brown stone with his feet planted. He doesn't step onto the rock ridge, and he doesn't look at the hole for long.

The sun stands almost straight overhead. The ring waits in its stone. The rope is in your hands, and the hole lies six feet past the end of the good rock.

Where you are: on the crew's path above the lower shed, short of the brown stone · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 7 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa came along the ridge behind you, one palm on the wet face, her beads glowing pale and cold. She called down to Pell in an even voice: they could hear him, nobody would come over the boards, you were anchoring on the old ring, and no one should strike a light, because hers had no spark in it. She told you to belay from the ring, said she would carry the end to him with a spectral hand of hers while her feet stayed on good rock, and that she could not haul, since the rope and the back were yours. She told Osric to stay behind the brown stone, watch the shelf, and call if it so much as whispered.

Your shout goes out flat and loud across the shelf. Before the echo dies against the low face, an answer climbs up out of the ground, short and hard, broken by the stone: "...DOWN HERE!... LOWER SHED!... HOLE BY THE STEP!..."

You go left along the ridge of bare rock at the foot of the face, the way Osric pointed. The stone is slick with seep and crusted pink in the cracks. You keep your boots on the grey and off the white mat. At the lowering ring you crouch and take the iron in both hands. You twist it, pull it toward you, then put your weight on it sideways. It's brown with rust, but under the rust it's as thick as your thumb. The lead around its foot is sunk flush into the rock and doesn't give a hair. It was set by someone who meant it to hold a cart, and it still will.

You run the hempen rope through the ring and tie it off with two turns and a knot you've used on wagon loads a thousand times. Then you work a wide loop into the free end, big enough to go over a man's head and shoulders, tied so it won't close under strain.

Osric picks your job first. "Poles at the frame," he says, already turning back up the path. "Mind that shelf till I'm back." He goes up toward the yard with his heavy walk, coatless, and doesn't look back at the hole.

Sefa raises her hand. Just past the end of the good rock the air thickens into a hand of pale, translucent light, the size of a real one, with no heat and no flicker. It drifts to the rope and closes its fingers on the loop. You feed the line out hand over hand from your crouch, and the spectral hand carries the loop over the six feet of spoil the rock doesn't cover, slowly, never touching the mat. It reaches the black edge of the hole, where soft timber and broken crust ring the opening. There it lowers the loop, and the rope pays down through your fists after it.

Bent low with the rope across your knee, you can see into the hole at a slant. The noon sun stands almost straight above the opening and drops a square of light onto still water. In it you see the top of a man: Pell's dark head and shoulders, a coil of thin rope over one of them, the water up around his chest. Beside him a corner of pale squared stone breaks the surface, too even to be rubble. The loop comes down into the light a foot from Pell's face and hangs there, turning slowly on the end of the line. Sefa lets the hand of light open and fade.

Your questions go down the hole after it, loud and plain: what's pinning him, can he move his arms, get the loop under his arms if he can, and say what's trapped before anyone pulls.

A few minutes later Osric comes back down the path with a long larch pole on his shoulder, peeled and grey, fourteen feet of it, the kind used to brace the lifting frame. In his other hand is a quarryman's iron pinch-bar as long as his arm, one end flattened to a chisel. He stops behind the brown stone and goes no closer. He lays the pole along the rock ridge and pushes it toward you until it reaches you. The bar he sets on the rock where the ridge begins.

"Bar's for stone. Pole's for reach." Then his eyes go to the shelf, the long white mat between the brown stone and the shed. He watches it and doesn't look at the hole.

Overhead the sun has almost reached the top of the sky. Osric glances up at it once and then back at the shelf. The rope runs taut from the iron ring across six feet of rotten ground and down into the dark square, where the loop hangs in the light beside Pell.

Where you are: on the bare-rock ridge by the old lowering ring, rope anchored · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 8 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa holds her light low and stays braced on the wet rock. Before she can call down, Pell's voice comes up out of the hole, loud and slow, broken into pieces by the stone. You catch these: follow the rope under the shed step, right at the door; a hollow the size of a cart bed; come on your bellies or through the shed; don't stand on the edge; he's pinned, not broken; the water isn't rising; the air is sweet but decent; nobody is to light anything. Then only the drip.

From the ridge you see a second line that wasn't there before. It's thin pale silk, running taut up out of the hole and over the soft black lip. Its looped end lies out on the white dust of the shelf, past the rim and well beyond the good rock, where nobody can reach it without standing on the hollow ground.

Sefa calls down in her even voice. The loop is beside him, one arm is enough to start, and nobody will haul until he says. She asks what holds him and whether he's bleeding. She tells him she has healing light, warmth and not fire, and sends it. A soft gold warmth slides from her open hand into the square of sun and settles round his head and shoulders in the water, with no haze and no spark.

Low, without turning far, she tells you the rest. When you pull, her mage hand will hold the line off the splintered edge. It can carry only ten pounds, so Pell's weight goes on your rope alone. If he's wedged, the bar is for levering, not the line.

You keep the hempen line steady across your knee without drawing in an inch, and send your own questions down: get the loop under his arms, and say what's pinned. You haul the larch pole along the ridge, its weight on the rock, and lay it with its end pointing at the hole, ready to run out across the six feet of spoil. You tell Sefa to keep him talking, since hauling blind could hurt him worse if he's under stone.

Behind the brown stone, Osric has been watching the shelf as he was told. He heard the whole shout, and now he's looking at the corner of pale stone showing in the water beside Pell's head, where the sun falls straight down the hole. "That's dressed," he says to nobody in particular. "Squared. Not fall-rubble. Nobody dressed stone down there in my time."

He squints up at the sun, straight overhead, your shadows shrunk to nothing round your boots. "Noon."

He looks from the stone to your pole, then to the pinch-bar on the rock where the ridge begins. If a block is on Pell's leg, he says, you don't lift it. Rubble packs in round it in the fall, tight as mortar. You dig that out first, under water, by hand, with somebody bailing the whole time, and only then bar it. Two men, steady, no stopping, and you'd have him by sundown. One man won't shift it at all. He's seen it done once, and it took the day.

His eyes go up the slope to the house, its door still open, the case on the scrubbed table by the letter with the pen across the blank line. He says he's for the town, because the lads need finding and that won't keep. He takes no step toward the hole or the house. The letter wants its witness and the wax, and then the case is yours. He won't leave it lying unsealed for whoever walks up the track.

Down in the square of light the hempen loop still turns slowly over the water. The seep trickles down the low face behind it, dark against the grey.

Where you are: on the ridge above the hole, with rope and pole · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 9 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa keeps watching the lit patch above the water, yet she speaks so both of you hear. She calls down to Pell that something else shares the water with him, lower and off to his left. Part of her healing, she says, did not stay with him but was pulled away toward it, as a chilly room drags at a lamp set in its doorway. He is not to put a hand into the dark after anything, and he is to tell her if the water stirs around his legs. She tells you to leave the hauling line just as it is. Pell's silk loop lies out on the spoil, she says, and she will bring it with the hand so you can tie it off on this side. More lines down to him, she says, means more you can do without setting a boot on the shelf.

Osric looks at you for a long moment, the first time he has looked at you rather than at the shelf. "Your coin," he says, and he doesn't make it sound like a fault. He walks to where the ridge begins, picks up the pinch-bar and shoves it along the wet rock, hard and low. It skids over the grey stone with an iron scrape and stops against your boot. "Crew's in Beregost. Some alehouse. Wherever Hob drinks, they drink. Half a day there, half back. Not before dark, and not down that hole. I'd not ask it of them."

You run the larch pole out over the spoil, hand over hand, the butt clamped under your knee. The pole spans the rotten ground without touching it. At the black lip you lower the far end into the opening at a slant until it dips into the shaft of sunlight above the water. You call down to Pell: the pole is coming within reach, he's not to climb yet, Osric thinks a block is on his leg, and can he tell by feel what is holding him?

Pell's voice comes up flattened by the stone and broken into pieces: "*...DON'T PULL!... not yet... loop's on... for if the water comes up... NOT for hauling!... left shin... under a BLOCK... cut stone... bigger than a cartwheel... against the ledge... not broken... haul, you'll take the leg off at the knee!... arms fine... cleared the outer side... inner side... under the near edge... old prop... wedged... to lever... somebody come down... dig... bail... lean on the prop... two of you... dusk...*" He stops for breath, then goes on: "*...somebody walks NOW... case... letter... or the coach goes... nobody paid... decide it up there... don't argue it over my head... for an hour!...*" Then, quieter, barely clearing the rim: "*...very civilised.*"

Osric's mouth tightens at *two of you* and *dusk*.

You had quietly asked Sefa whether her light could get lower, so you could see what he's caught on. She doesn't answer that, but lifts her hand again. The pale hand forms in the air past the end of the good rock and crosses the spoil slowly and low, keeping clear of the white crust. It closes its fingers on the silk loop where it lies in the dust and draws it back. The silk slides over the soft black lip, and its slack end comes up dripping. The hand lays the loop on the wet rock at your free side and opens. Now two lines cross the rotten ground, the hemp taut from the iron ring and the silk loose, both going down beside the grey slant of the pole.

Sefa speaks to Osric without fully turning her head. He's not to leave the letter or the case at the house unwitnessed. He should bring both down to the good rock, where she'll put her mark and they'll seal it as it stands. Then he can go for the lads and strong backs. But if he knows any story of a dressed stone being set down in that cut, he should tell it before he goes. There's a tenant in that water, she says, and she won't have him meet it on his way into town.

"Bring the lot down. Aye," Osric says, glancing up the slope at the open door. "Wax wants a flame. I'll bring a candle-end. Up here, in the open air, not down there." He jerks his chin at the hole. "That's what the letter says, isn't it." At *tenant* he doesn't laugh. "Water's water." He looks past her at the hole, longer than he means to. "Those galleries were cut before the house had the place. Before anybody I knew had it. Whoever squared that stone never wrote it in my book." His fingers find his sleeve and press. "Only thing that was ever in that water was one of mine." He stops there, his mouth closing on whatever comes after.

He turns and goes up the crew's path toward the yard with his heavy, coatless walk, keeping to the packed white mat. His boots raise small puffs of dust that hang in the windless air. The sun stands straight overhead. Sefa's beads still glow pale against her chest, faint in the glare. The iron bar lies against your boot, the silk loop is coiled at your side, and the pole's far end hangs in the shaft of light a foot or two above the dark head in the water.

Where you are: On the wet grey ridge of good rock above the shaft, braced beside the iron ring · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 10 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Pell's voice comes up out of the ground in pieces, flattened by the stone. He thanks Sefa for the warmth, the first he has felt since dawn. He says her light leaned past him toward the wall behind the block: flat grey, like plaster over a hollow, and the block stands against it. On it is carved a disc with rays and a ring of little notches like a tally. He hasn't touched either and won't, if the patron is interested, before anybody digs round it. Then he calls off to the side, where nobody stands any more, asking Master Hale whose working this is, how old it is, and how far the dark band goes up. Nobody answers. Last he asks who is carrying the case, so he knows who to curse. He wants the bucket first and the boots after. The floor is stone and the rim is rotten, so you are to come down the rope and not the rim.

Sefa answers him in the same even voice: no hauling, the loop stays round him only for the water, the silk is up with you, the bar is at your foot and the pole is in the shaft. He should hold quiet. The pale glow fades out of her prayer beads as she speaks, the hour of the cantrip spent.

Then, low enough for you alone, she says she won't argue it over Pell's head. She'll walk the case and the letter to Beregost, find Thorn, and find the crew if an alehouse can point to them. She tells you to go down with Hale if he will, so that there are two of you digging and levering, with the ring holding the line and no flame. She offers to put a cold light on the pole's end before she leaves. She says Hale lost a man to that water three years back, so you should let him work with his head and not his grief. She tells you to keep your eyes on the deep side of the block, and if the water moves as though something in it has woken, to get on the line and call. She sends one more line down to Pell about staying awake and telling you if his leg goes cold.

You answer Pell and ask Sefa to stay up and tend your line, her light on Pell's left. Then you call across the yard to Hale for a bucket and ask him to take the case and the witnessed letter to Thorn.

Up at the house, Osric is already in the doorway with his arms full. He stops on the step, then ducks back in and returns with a wooden bucket hooked over one wrist. He walks down the crew's path with his heavy, unhurried tread. Under his arm is the oak case, its red wax catching the sun. The torn page is folded over his fingers, and in his fist are a pen, an ink-horn, a stub of red wax and a candle-end. He stops behind the brown stone as told and sets the case on the rock with the letter beside it. He weights the page with the ink-horn and lays the candle-end by it, unlit. He shoves the bucket along the ridge and it fetches up a stride short of you.

"Bucket." He straightens. "Her door I'll pass. I'll tell her you're down a hole at Whitestone. That much." He looks at the case, not at you. "Her salt I'll not carry. I'm warden here, not the house's carter. Salt goes out of Whitestone in the buyer's man's hands, and that's how it'll stand in my book when Pryce comes asking who took it. She hired you for it. Your coin to earn. Or not."

You set your round shield flat on the good rock beside the ring. You run a length of Pell's silk through your fingers and find it fine, close-laid and dry where it never touched the water, with no fraying and no soft places. It is better rope than your own. You take it round the iron ring beside the hemp with two turns and a knot, letting no tension reach Pell, and hitch the spare end round the middle of the pinch-bar so the iron can go down on a line.

From where you crouch you can see what going down will mean. The ring sits on the last of the good rock. Between it and the hole lie six feet of white spoil over old timber, and the lip of the hole is soft and black. The rope will carry your weight, but it will run across that spoil and over that lip, with you on it in chain mail. Below the lip the water stands chest-deep on a stone floor. The larch pole's grey length reaches over the spoil beside the ropes, its far end hanging dry in the shaft of light.

You ask Pell to talk you onto safe footing before you clear the packed rubble. The sun has just passed its height, and your shadows have come out from under your boots again, short and leaning east. The sealed case sits on the rock with the pen and the folded letter beside it, and the candle-end lies unlit.

Sefa can't take the case yet. Osric hands it over only after she makes her witness mark and he seals the letter, and she hasn't done that. Thorn and the crew are in Beregost, half a day's walk away. Your request that Sefa tend your line conflicts with her leaving with the case, so that is her player's call next round.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Iron Pinch-Bar

Where you are: on the ridge by the lowering ring, about to descend the shaft · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 11 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Sefa kneels at the flat rock, tells Osric to hold the page steady, and signs beneath his mark as courier by hire of Maela Thorn, witnessing it at Whitestone that day. She strikes a light from her tinderbox to kindle the candle stub, set on the rock well back from the hole. Osric drips red wax over the fold and presses his key-ring into it, the same mark as on the case. Sefa folds the letter into her belt pouch and takes up the oak case. Osric holds it a breath longer than he needs to before he puts it into her arms. "Ask her who she paid," he tells her. "Then tell me. That's the price of it."

You call down the hole to Pell: bucket first, as ordered, Sefa is carrying the case, and you're staying. You unhitch the silk from the pinch-bar, lay the bar on the rock, and knot the line through the bucket's rope handle. You pay the bucket out over the six feet of spoil and past the soft black lip. It knocks softly against the wall going down, and the line goes slack in your hands once it settles on the water.

Then you sit on the good rock and work out of your armour. You undo the buckles at the side, pull the coat of rings over your head, and get out of the sweat-dark padded coat beneath. It takes about five minutes. The mail lies in a grey heap beside your shield. You crouch by the ring in shirt and breeches with your sword still belted on, lighter, with the sun biting at your shoulders.

You ask Osric whether the larch pole can be braced across sound stone, or whether there's another way into the cut. He looks at the hole longer than he likes to.

"No other way. Not that I know." He points at the pole, still slanting down into the shaft of light. "Lay it flat. Butt here on the rock, head clean across the hole onto the far side. Spread the weight. Then the rope runs over larch, not over that lip." He jerks his chin at your pack. "Bedroll goes where the rope bites the pole. Far side's spoil too, mind. Pole spreads it. Doesn't make it rock."

Sefa then lays out her plan. Osric would stay on the ring and the ridge to tend the line, and you would go down to join Pell, the two of you clearing the near edge of the block and working the prop. Osric shakes his head once. "Not me on that ring till dark." He says it without heat. "Lads need finding. That won't keep." Then he adds, plainly, the way he'd tell them a face was bad: "And the man under the block's no pair of hands. You heard him. Far side's packed against the ledge. He can't reach it without leaning on what's holding him. Two men, I said. Two that go down to him. Not him and one." He leaves it there.

Sefa lays her fingers on the grey wood of the pole near the butt, where it rests on the ridge under your knee. A pale light kindles under her hand, cold as starlight under water, with no heat or spark. It stays glowing on the peeled larch after she lifts her hand away. She tells you it lasts an hour and not a breath more, so the first work must be done inside it. There must be no flame down there. Listen for the water. If anything moves behind the flat grey wall, call out and come up the line. Don't touch the rayed disc or the marks, and don't tap the wall. Dig only at the near edge, and let the block answer.

Osric listens to it all, and "don't tap the wall" makes him look at her sharply. He collects his pen, ink-horn and wax stub, leaves the candle-end lying on the rock, and straightens. "I'll pass Thorn's door. Tell her where you are." He looks once more at the glowing pole and the slack lines running into the dark. "Road's the road. Mine goes the same way yours does." He goes up the crew's path toward the house, keeping to the white mat, with his heavy coatless walk. His coat and blackthorn stick are still on the peg inside the door.

You crouch by the iron ring without your mail. Sefa stands at the end of the good rock with the oak case under one arm and the sealed letter in her pouch. Six feet of spoil lie between the ring and the hole, and the bucket's line runs down over the black lip. The sun has moved a little west of the cut.

Where you are: by the iron ring on the good rock beside the hole, armour off · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 12 — what does Bram Halloway do?

Pell's voice comes up out of the ground just as Sefa reaches the end of the good rock. It is flattened by the stone, but steadier than it was. He says his shin has gone dull where the stone sits, not dead, like a foot you've slept on, and his toes still move. He will say when they stop. He tells you to come down on his right, where the prop is, and to keep off the left and not put a foot in the dark there, but to go on the inner side between his leg and the ledge, under the near edge, and push them away from him, without leaning on the block. Hale won't carry the case, so either Sefa walks it or nobody does. He would rather it were her, because she heard the letter read, and he asks you to tell her so.

Sefa pauses at the last of the good rock, the oak case held against her side, and sends her voice down past the pole with its pale, cold light. She tells Pell she has the case and the witnessed letter and is walking them to Thorn, that you are coming down, and that Master Hale stays by the ring. He is to keep talking at intervals, even if it's only the sound of his breath, and say if the water moves, if his foot goes cold, or if anything touches the line. She will find Hob and the crew and send them up the track. She looks for a moment at the black rim and the rope. Then she tells you to keep Pell talking, and to carry no flame into that dark, whatever it offers. She goes up the crew's path on the packed white mat, not running, her steps even.

You call after her, and the quarry is quiet enough that every word reaches her. You ask whether she will stay and help you, and tell her the choice is hers.

Then you turn toward the house and raise your voice to carry the whole way. If Hale is leaving, he is to send help from Beregost, and tell Thorn a man is trapped, not just down a hole.

Up at the house Osric stands in the doorway, one arm in his coat and the blackthorn stick hooked over his wrist. He works the other arm in before he answers, his voice flat and heavy across the yard. "Trapped. I'll say it." He settles the coat on his shoulders. "Fist keeps a post in the town. I'll knock there too." He pauses for the length of a man looking at the sun. "Not before dark. Whoever comes."

He pulls the door to behind him, but it won't latch and swings back a hand's width onto the cold hearth. He comes down the step onto the cart track and follows Sefa along the road, ten paces behind her, neither hurrying nor hanging back.

You set about the rig. You pull your bedroll from your pack and unroll it on the rock beside the ring, ready to fold double where the hemp will bear on the larch. You prise loose stones out of the seep-cracks along the ridge, fist-sized lumps of grey crusted pink, and pack them round the pole's butt on both sides so it can't roll once it lies flat. Then you take the butt in both hands and start to draw the pole up out of the hole, slowly, a few inches at a time, to bring the head over and lay it across.

The pole doesn't come. A few inches up, the far end holds. It isn't caught on stone. Through the grain you can feel a hand closed on the wood down there, and the small, living give of a man braced against it in the water. You keep your grip without hauling, and the larch stays where it is, slanting down past the soft black lip into the shaft of light.

You send your voice down after it: you are rigging the descent, and you ask whether there is any change in his leg or the water.

The drip comes up out of the hole. Out on the cart track, two figures go down toward the Way, a woman with a case under her arm and a heavy man with a stick a little behind her, getting smaller in the white glare. The cold light glows on the larch. The bucket's silk line runs taut from the ring over the lip, and the hemp runs slack beside it. The sun has moved a hand's breadth west of the top of the sky.

Where you are: on the ridge at the shaft's rim, rigging the descent · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 13 — what does Bram Halloway do?

You stop drawing on the larch and keep your knee on the butt, your hands loose on the grey wood. Through the grain you can feel the man at the far end, steady and holding.

You bend low over the ring and send your voice down the hole. You ask whether Pell is holding the larch, since you need it laid across the hole to carry your rope clear of the rotten edge, and whether he can let go safely with the rescue loop still under his arms. In the same breath you tell him Sefa is taking the case, as he asked, that help is being sent, and that you'll see what can be cleared without shifting the block onto him.

Before you've finished, Pell's voice is already climbing the other way, words he must have sent up a moment before you began. The stone flattens them and breaks them into pieces. He says the bucket has reached him, thanks, and he's tied it off on the prop so it won't wander. He asks who has gone up the slope, Hale or Sefa with the case, and who is still on the rim. The bucket is for the stones as well as the water, he says: dig them out, drop them in, haul them up and pile them round the block, where they'll pack back in. The bar goes down on the rope, not over the edge, before the men come.

Then, plainer: his toes still move, his shin is numb, it's no worse, and there's no cold past the knee.

The last piece is the quietest, and it barely clears the black lip. Whoever is holding the pole up there shouldn't let go of it on his account. He isn't climbing, he just likes having something dry to hang on to.

Through the wood you feel the grip at the far end tighten once and settle, the hold of a man who has found the one dry, solid thing in a cold place and isn't letting go. The pole stays where it is, slanting down past the soft black lip into the shaft of light. Sefa's cold paleness glows faintly near the butt under your knee.

The rig waits on the ridge beside you: the bedroll unrolled on the rock, the pink-crusted stones packed round the pole's butt, the pinch-bar lying loose where you set it down. The silk that was to carry the bar runs taut from the ring over the lip and down to the bucket below. The hemp beside it runs slack to the loop round Pell's chest. The quarry has gone quiet up the slope. The seep threads down the low face in its dark ribbons, and the sun has slipped a little further west, so the short shadows on the white mat lean a little further east.

Where you are: on the ridge by the hole, kneeling on the larch pole's butt · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 14 — what does Bram Halloway do?

messages.text:
I sheathe my sword and walk into the yard, shield resting at my side. As I approach, I look over the scattered tools and empty sheds for blood or signs of a struggle.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us for a sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?”

I stop a few paces short of the doorway.

“Quiet for a working day. Something happened?”
I wait for the man's answer, leaving the doorway clear and keeping my sword sheathed. From here, I glance at his apron and hands, then into whatever part of the house is visible behind him.

I stay by the open doorway while Osric writes, leaving Pell and Sefa room to join him.

“We can witness what you put down and see Thorn hears it. Won't promise she'll pay another man's debts.”

I nod towards the oak case. “Will you release the case with the letter, then? And how much are you and the crew owed, all told?”

While he answers, I look back towards the damp lower face he glanced at, trying to make out what caught his attention.

“Pell! Old workings under those boards, and bad air at the low face. Keep clear of both.”

I turn back to Osric. “This salt—anyone taken ill scraping it? Coughing, dizzy, anything like that? We ought to know before we carry it.”

I stay at the doorway, keeping Pell in sight while Sefa handles the letter.

“Not lately,” I repeat, quietly. “Then when? Did they recover?”

I look towards Pell and call, “The salt makes men drowsy. Worse when heated—don't light anything in there.”

Then I turn back to Osric. “We'll keep the case sealed. But if there's a danger Thorn needs to hear, send that warning with the wages letter. Whoever opens it may not know what your lads learned.”

“Pell's out of sight. Step may have given way.”

I pull the rope from my pack and head down the crew's path, stopping well short of the shelf and any cracked ground or boards.

“Osric, show us where solid ground ends. Sefa, I'll need you with the rope.”

I call, “Pell! Can you hear me?”

From firm ground, I look for Pell through the broken step and for a stout anchor for the rope. I keep off the shelf—no sense putting another man through it.

“Heard you, Pell! We're on solid ground. Rope coming. What's pinning you, and can you move your arms?”

I follow the bare-rock ridge Osric pointed out, keeping off the spoil. At the lowering ring, I check the iron and its setting for looseness before trusting it.

If it holds firm, I secure one end of the rope to it and tie a broad rescue loop in the free end.

“Sefa, help me get this loop to him from the rock. No stepping onto that shelf. Osric, fetch a long sound pole or timber—we may need the reach.”

Staying low on the good rock, I toss the loop towards the opening, keeping the connecting rope within reach.

“Pell, rope's anchored. If you can, put the loop under your arms. Tell us what's trapped before we pull—we don't want to shift stone onto you.”

I keep the rope steady without pulling on Pell.

“Pell, loop's beside your face. Can you get it under your arms? Tell me what's pinned—your boot, your leg, or something else?”

I draw the larch pole along the ridge, keeping its weight on solid rock, ready to extend it if he needs something to grip.

“Sefa, keep him talking. If he's trapped under stone, hauling blind could hurt him worse.”

I watch Pell for a response and the broken lip for any movement.

“Osric, we're not leaving him under there for a delivery. Fetch the bar here, please. If we need the crew, tell us where to find them.”

I stay braced on the ridge and slide the pole out over the opening, holding its near end firmly on the rock.

“Pell, pole's coming within reach. Don't climb yet. Osric thinks there's a block on your leg—is that right? Can you feel what's holding you with your hands? We need that before we can help.”

To Sefa, quietly: “Can your light get lower so we can see what he's caught on?”

I keep the anchored rescue rope within reach, ready to take up slack if Pell gets the loop around himself, but I don't haul.

“Pell, understood. No hauling. I'm coming down to clear the block.”

I turn to Sefa. “Will you stay above and tend my line? Keep your light on his left, where you felt that thing.”

I call after Osric: “Bring a bucket as well! If you're going to Beregost, will you take the case and witnessed letter to Thorn? Tell her where we are. Rescue first; we can settle payment later.”

I set my shield on the solid rock and secure Pell's silk line to the lowering ring without pulling on him. Before trusting it with my weight, I check with Pell that it's sound rope.

Then, with Sefa's help tending the line, I prepare to lower myself from the anchored rope into the opening, keeping my weight off the rotten shelf. I'll take the pinch-bar down secured to a line, not loose in my hand.

“Pell, talk me onto a safe footing beside you. Then we'll clear the packed rubble before we try shifting anything.”

“All right, Sefa. Take the case once you've witnessed the letter. Cold light on the pole before you go, please.”

I call down, “Pell, bucket first, as ordered. Sefa's carrying the case. I'm staying.”

I lower the bucket on the bar's line, keeping the iron up here for now, then start taking off my chain mail on the solid rock. No sense wrestling underwater in it.

“Osric, I'll need your help here before you leave. That rotten lip won't safely bear a loaded rope. Can we brace the larch pole across sound stone, or is there another way into this cut? I've a bedroll for padding the line, but that won't hold rotten timber together.”

I keep my sword belted on and watch the water while I work. I won't put my weight over the lip until we've made the descent safe.

“Sefa, he says it needs two able bodies below. I'd sooner lose the fee than Pell. Will you stay and help me? Your call.”

I raise my voice towards Osric. “If you're leaving, send help from Beregost. Tell Thorn a man's trapped, not merely down a hole.”

Then I lay the pole across as Osric described, with its butt well supported on rock and the bedroll padding where the hemp will bear. I secure it against rolling and gradually load the rope from my position on solid stone, watching the far support for settling.

“Pell, we're rigging the descent. Any change in your leg or the water?”

If the support holds firm, I lower the pinch-bar separately, then descend the anchored hemp slowly, without setting foot on the rotten rim. If the pole or spoil shifts under the test, I stop rather than trust it with my weight.

I stop moving the pole.

“Pell, are you holding the larch? I need it across the hole to carry my rope clear of the rotten edge. Can you let go safely? You've still got the rescue loop under your arms.”

I keep it steady until he answers. If he can release it, I tell him before moving it, then finish laying and bracing it across the opening, pad the rope's bearing point, and test the rig gradually from solid rock.

If it holds, I lower the bar on a separate line and descend slowly on his right, towards the prop.

“Sefa's taking the case, as you asked. Help's being sent. Now let's see what we can clear without shifting that block onto you.”

“Pell, it's Bram alone up here. Sefa has the case; Hale's gone to send help. Listen: I need you to let go of the pole for a minute so I can make a safe way down. Can you do that?”

I hold the pole steady while he answers.

“Keep the chest loop on. Once I've braced the pole across the hole, I'll lower the bar, then come down on your right. You'll have company instead of a stick.”

I don't tug against his grip. Once he releases it, I proceed with bracing, padding and testing the crossing from solid rock.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: in the quarry yard, near Bram, just outside the doorway's shadow · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram stays clear of the doorway with his sword sheathed. He looks over the man's apron and hands, and past him into the house.

Pell answers for the group before you have to. He tells the man, whom he calls master Hale, that the three of you are couriers, paid ninety on delivery and nothing before, much like the man's own crew. He asks who carries the wages out from the Gate, and whose house that factor or clerk serves. He says that if someone is skimming both ends, Thorn will want the name, because a buyer's coach leaves at sunset and she will be shouting by suppertime. He offers to carry a written statement of the three weeks unpaid, sealed with the man's own mark, to her hand along with the case, while the man keeps a copy. Then he asks about the long shed down the lower cut with its door standing open, wondering whether one of the man's crew left it in a rush or whether the mule went in there.

Osric does not answer straight away. You keep your tone level, as you spoke it, and watch how he takes it.

His hands are a cutter's hands: broad, split at the knuckles, the nails worn to the quick, and no weapon anywhere near them. White dust is ground into the creases of his apron like flour. Near the pocket a faint smear of grit shows a different colour, pinkish, the shade of a rose gone pale, where something was wiped off once and not brushed away.

Past his shoulder you can see part of one room. A kettle hangs over the coals of the hearth, and a scrubbed table holds a fat book bound in stained canvas with a pen stuck through its strap. Next to the book sits a small case of dark oak, banded in brass, about the size of a loaf, with a disc of red wax across the clasp. A coat hangs on a peg just inside the door, and a blackthorn stick leans under it.

Her years at the hospice bedside are hers to draw on. The narration after the die will follow her silence and her patience.

A few things in your paragraph go beyond what the scene has shown, so I'll treat them as Sefa's impressions or as proposals, not as facts of the world yet:
