[Out of game] Thanks, that's a clear move, and Sefa's words and manner are hers. When you press Onward, she says that line aloud just as you wrote it: low, unhurried, no bargain attached, no step closer. She keeps watching his face, his breathing and where his worry goes.

Two parts of it work differently, so I'll handle them separately:

- **"You're not barring the door against us."** That stands as Sefa's own read, said to his face. Osric reacts to it as something she believes about him. Whether it's right is the world's to show. The die you've already seen decides how much of him she can actually read while she says it.

Where you are: yard outside Osric's house at the quarry · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Pell stepped up to the threshold and leaned on the frame with his hands in view. He asked Osric whose seal was on the wax, and whether the rose-coloured stain on the apron was the salt itself. He said Thorn should hear of any leak from Osric's pen rather than find it herself. He told you and Bram to stay with Osric while he wrote, and asked you to read the letter back before it was sealed. He said he would be a quarter of an hour at most, then walked down toward the lower cut in the open.

Bram stayed in the doorway. He told Osric you would witness what he wrote and see that Thorn heard it, but would not promise she'd pay another man's debts. He asked whether Osric would release the case with the letter, and how much he and the crew were owed in all.

Osric did not look up when Pell's shadow fell across the threshold. The pen kept scratching. "Mine," he said of the seal: a quarry mark, a W with a hammer through it. The house never sent a seal and never asked for one. The colour was the salt, he said, which grows on the wet walls of the low cuts, rose-white like frost that won't melt. You scrape it, dry it on slates, and it goes in the case. Nothing had leaked, and he had sealed it himself the day before yesterday. He brushed at the smear on his apron and it didn't come off. "Thirty years it's been on those walls. Nobody wanted it till the spring."

As Pell started down the slope Osric raised his voice, flat and carrying. "Mind the boards down there. Old workings under. And don't stand about at the low face. Air's thick." Then he bent back to the page.

When you spoke, his pen stopped at the words *a novice in a hospice* and stayed stopped while you talked about the not knowing, and the man who was told he did all he could. He sat with that a moment, looking at the wet ink. "Didn't do all I could. Did what the house paid for." He set the pen to the paper again. Nobody had been shut in, he said. They worked the faces, upper and lower, same as any year: cut, split, cart, and scrape the salt when there was an order. He glanced at you, brief and dry. "And I never said the shed changed. Shed's just a shed. Door's warped."

To Bram he answered that she needn't pay the debt, only know it. Fourteen men, three weeks, two silver a day for a cutter and less for the boys. Forty-two gold, near enough. Hob was owed more, having fed the mule out of his own purse. That did not count Osric's own. The case would go when the letter was sealed and you had read it back to him, and not before.

Up at the house the kettle boiled over with a hiss onto the coals. Osric reached out and swung it off the hook without looking, and kept writing.

Where you are: in Osric's house at the quarry, by the table · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 4 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram called out to Pell too, almost at the same moment you did, telling him to keep clear of the old workings and the bad air at the low face. He then turned to Osric from the doorway and asked whether anyone scraping the salt had fallen ill, coughing or dizzy, since you ought to know before carrying it. He stays at the door with Pell in sight.

Your warning, and Bram's, carries out over the white yard and down the slope toward the lower cut. The quarry is quiet enough that every word goes the whole way.

Inside, Osric's pen doesn't stop for the shouting. It stops when you come back in and ask your questions, and it stays stopped while Bram asks his.

"Not coughing." He sets the pen down crosswise on the page. "Sleepy. Man works the low face a long stretch, he gets heavy in the eyes, slow in the hands. Send him up into the sun, he's right by supper." He rubs a thumb along the edge of the table. "Headaches, some. Lamps burn fine. That's why I said it. Air's thick down there. It doesn't choke you. It just sits on you."

He thinks about the sweetness longer.

"Shed's the same when the brazier's going. Wet weather we dry the salt on the slates over a bit of fire. Room smells like a bakehouse. Lads used to nod off over the racks." He says it like any other fact about the place, the way he'd tell you the faces get slick in rain. "Haven't been down since they went. No call to."

Then your last line lands, and his head comes up.

"Fourth." He looks at you for the first time since he sat down, flat and hard. "Nobody's been overcome. Nobody said three." His fingers have found his sleeve and pressed in. A moment passes. When he picks up the pen again he says, to the page and not to you, "Not lately."

He writes the rest quickly, with no lip-moving now, and blots it with the heel of his hand. Then he takes the page by its top corner and tears it out of the canvas book along the fold, slowly, so it comes away clean. The book stays open on the table with its stub showing, and behind the stub are the ruled pages of earlier years, columns of names and days in the same heavy hand.

He lays the torn page beside the oak case. The letters are pressed nearly through the paper:

*To Maela Thorn, apothecary, Beregost. From Osric Hale, warden at Whitestone for House Vandarren of the Gate. Fourteen men three weeks unpaid by the house. Wages to come by Pryce the factor's runner on the first and the fifteenth. Did not come, twice. You paid for this salt. Ask him where it went.*

Below that the hand gets smaller, a list of names with a sum against each, and at the bottom a blank space with a short line drawn for a mark.

The kettle has stopped ticking. The hearth settles. Past Bram's shoulder the sun stands nearly at the top of the sky over the white faces, and the coat on its peg sways a little in the draught from the open door.

Where you are: Osric's house at the Whitestone quarry, by the table · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 5 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram, standing in the doorway, repeated quietly to Osric that it hadn't happened lately, and asked when it had happened and whether the men recovered. Osric's pen stopped. He didn't look up at once, and when he did, he looked past Bram, out the door toward the lower cut.

"Three year back." He set the pen in the fold of the book. "Most come up right by supper. One didn't." He gave nothing more, and his mouth closed on it.

Bram turned and called down the slope to Pell that the salt makes men drowsy, and more so when it is heated, so he shouldn't light anything in there. His voice crossed the white yard to the lower cut, and nothing came back. Bram then told Osric to keep the case sealed and to send the warning along with the wage letter, since whoever opens it may not know what his lads learned. Osric heard him out, picked up the pen and turned the torn page round.

"Drowsy's not a danger. Not up top." He wrote anyway, bearing down on a short line squeezed in under the names, above the blank for his mark. "There. Don't say I didn't."

When you told him plainly that you had said "fourth" with only the three of you in mind, he eased his fingers off his sleeve and gave a single grunt, as near to "aye" as he gets, then went back to blotting the new line.

When he laid the page down by the case, you asked "May I?" and he didn't stop you. You read it back, then set it down. The last line you read was the one he squeezed in at Bram's word: salt makes men sleepy if they work it long, do not dry it over a fire in a shut room. Osric listened with his eyes shut, as though checking you against the words in his head, and opened them when you finished.

"That's it." He took the pen and scratched his mark on the line, the W with the hammer through it, the same mark as on the wax. Then he laid the pen crosswise on the page, where a witness's hand would go.

You glanced toward the doorway and asked whether Pell was still in the open. At that, Osric's head came up. He looked at Bram's back, framed in the door, pushed himself up from the table and went to stand beside Bram, looking down the slope. His face changed. It wasn't anger now.

"Shed step." His voice was low and flat. "There's an old cut under it. Under the whole shelf." His hand went to the doorframe and gripped it. "Water in it. Always."

No sound comes up from the lower cut. The sun stands almost overhead. On the table, the case sits beside the marked letter with its wax unbroken, and the pen still lies across the blank where a witness's mark should go. Behind the men the kettle sits off its hook, and the coals still spit where it boiled over.

Where you are: at the table inside the warden's hut at Whitestone · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 6 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram speaks up just behind you. He says Pell is out of sight and the step may have given way. He draws his rope from his pack and follows the crew's path down, stopping well short of the shelf, cracked ground and boards. He tells Osric to show you both where the solid ground ends, says he'll need you on the rope, and calls Pell's name. He means to keep off the shelf himself.

Halfway down the crew's path you close your hand round the prayer beads and say the one word. A pale, even light rises from the wooden beads, with no heat in it and no spark. It's faint in the noon sun, but it'll be enough under the shed's shadow. You hold it low against your chest.

Then the ground answers you.

A voice comes up out of the shelf ahead, flat and broken by the stone it has to climb through. You catch it in pieces, the way you hear a shout from a cellar:

"*…BRAM! SEFA!… lower shed!… under the step!… pinned… water to my chest!… don't run in!… hollow… door… crew's path… off the flagstone!… bring Hale!… smells sweet!…*"

Then nothing but the drip from somewhere under the planks, and the dust still settling over the dark patch where the step used to be.

Osric has come out after you with his coat left on the peg. He doesn't hurry, but he doesn't stop either. When Bram halts well short of the shelf, Osric comes up beside him and points with two fingers, the way a man points at stone he has cut.

"Path's rock as far as that brown stone." It's a rust-coloured boulder sunk in the white mat about fifteen feet short of the shed door. "Past it, it's spoil laid over old timber. The whole shelf. Thirty years we walked it." His mouth sets. "Step was a lid. Nobody knew."

He turns his hand to the left, toward the foot of the low face, where the grey stone comes down to the shelf in a ridge of bare rock dark with seep. "Rock runs along the face. Gets you within five, six feet of the hole on that side. No closer." Set into that ridge, a little above the mat, is an iron ring as thick as a man's thumb, brown with rust and leaded into the stone. "Lowering ring. Older than me. It'll hold a cart."

Your light picks out the ragged lip of the hole beyond. It's a gap about four feet across, edged with soft black timber and broken white crust. Below it there's only the glint of still water.

"Cut runs back under the face," Osric says, lower now. "Water stands four foot in summer. Five after rain." He stays on the path behind the brown stone with his feet planted. He doesn't step onto the rock ridge, and he doesn't look at the hole for long.

The sun stands almost straight overhead. The ring waits in its stone. Bram's rope is in his hands, and the hole lies six feet past the end of the good rock.

Where you are: on the crew's path above the lower shed, short of the brown stone · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 7 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Bram went left along the bare-rock ridge, keeping off the spoil, and tested the old lowering ring in both hands, twisting it and pulling it and putting his weight on it sideways. He tied the rope through it and worked a wide loop into the free end. He had asked Osric to fetch a long sound pole or timber, and he called down to Pell that the rope was anchored and the loop should go under his arms if he could manage it, and that Pell should say what was trapped before anyone pulled.

Your voice goes down toward the hole in an even tone: they hear him, nobody is coming over the boards, Bram is anchoring on the old ring, and no one should strike a light, because yours has no spark in it. You tell Bram to belay from the ring, and you give Osric his job: stay behind the brown stone, watch the shelf, call if it so much as whispers.

Osric takes Bram's job first. "Poles at the frame." He is already turning back up the path. "Mind that shelf till I'm back." He goes up toward the yard with his heavy walk, coatless, and doesn't look back at the hole.

You raise your hand. Just past the end of the good rock the air thickens into a hand of pale, translucent light, the size of a real one, with no heat and no flicker. It drifts to the rope and closes its fingers on the loop. Bram feeds the line out hand over hand from his crouch, and the spectral hand carries the loop over the six feet of spoil the rock doesn't cover, slowly, never touching the mat. It reaches the black edge of the hole, where soft timber and broken crust ring the opening. There it lowers the loop, and the rope pays down through Bram's fists after it.

The noon sun stands almost straight above the opening and drops a square of light onto still water. The loop comes down into the light, and you see Pell there, dark head and shoulders, a coil of thin rope over one of them, the water up around his chest. Beside him a corner of pale squared stone breaks the surface, too even to be rubble. The loop hangs a foot from his face, turning slowly on the end of the line. You let the hand of light open and fade.

Bram's questions go down the hole after it, loud and plain: what's pinning Pell, can he move his arms, get the loop under his arms if he can, and say what's trapped before anyone pulls.

A few minutes later Osric comes back down the path with a long larch pole on his shoulder, peeled and grey, fourteen feet of it, the kind used to brace the lifting frame. In his other hand is a quarryman's iron pinch-bar as long as his arm, one end flattened to a chisel. He stops behind the brown stone, as you asked, and goes no closer. He lays the pole along the rock ridge and pushes it toward Bram until it reaches him. The bar he sets on the rock where the ridge begins.

"Bar's for stone. Pole's for reach." Then his eyes go to the shelf, the long white mat between the brown stone and the shed. He watches it and doesn't look at the hole.

Overhead the sun has almost reached the top of the sky. Osric glances up at it once and then back at the shelf. The rope runs taut from the iron ring across six feet of rotten ground and down into the dark square, where the loop hangs in the light beside Pell.

Where you are: on the bare-rock ridge near the low face, short of the black timber lip · Time: Day 1 · midday

Round 8 — what does Sefa Marrin do?

Before you can call down, Pell's voice comes up out of the hole, loud and slow, broken into pieces by the stone. You catch these: follow the rope under the shed step, right at the door; a hollow the size of a cart bed; come on your bellies or through the shed; don't stand on the edge; he's pinned, not broken; the water isn't rising; the air is sweet but decent; nobody is to light anything. Then only the drip.

Sefa slows as the quarry opens up before them, and her first thought is not of the case or the gold. It is of the hammers set down in the dust, and the half-loaded cart, and the silence where there should be a working day.

She stops a little distance onto the yard, not yet in the doorway's shadow, and studies the man in the apron. Then she says, quiet enough that only Pell and Bram will hear her plainly:

"That's the warden, I think. He's not acting like a man eager to hand anything over — and no one's working. Keep your hands easy. Let me speak first."

She leaves her own hands open at her sides, the dagger at her belt untouched, and takes a few steps toward the house, stopping well short of arm's reach.

"Morning to you. Maela Thorn sent us from Beregost — she gave us her mark for the sealed case of dye-salts, for the coach that leaves by sunset." She keeps her voice level, without edge, but her eyes move over the yard again, over the scattered tools and the empty trace. "Is your day as strange as it looks?"

Sefa watches him through the space of a few heartbeats, and the picture that comes clear is not the one she first suspected.

He is not playing at grief. The warden is wrung out the way people get when they have stopped sleeping and stopped expecting help — not the large, theatrical sadness of a man performing for witnesses, but the smaller, heavier one of a man who has carried bad news alone for longer than one bad day. Grief, yes. But under it there is fear, not for himself; or not only for himself. The way he stands in the doorway is not the stance of a man guarding a trap. It is the stance of a man who has put his own body in front of something and does not know if that will be enough.

And there is the smear by his pocket. Pink against chalk dust. Not slaughter-red — old, wiped away, but not forgotten. The kind of mark a man gets when his hands have been pressed against a wound, or when he has used them to hold something hurt while it stopped moving.

He leans a little into the doorframe as if the morning weighs on him. His eyes go, without meaning to, toward the long shed down the lower cut. Then back to you. He is not checking for anyone behind you. He is trying to decide whether you are the people he has been dreading, or the ones he gave up hoping for.

Sefa holds very still while Osric speaks, because she knows that kind of answer when she hears it. Not the words only — the way a man shapes them when he has been sitting too long with something too heavy, and has finally set a little of it down in front of strangers.

She keeps her voice low, and unhurried, as though there were all the time in the world before dusk. There isn't. But he doesn't need to know that from her lips yet.

"Master Hale," she says, "the case is why we came. But no man alive could walk in on what you're telling us and ask only for the box." A pause, so he can decide whether that is kindness, or simply the plain truth. "You don't know what it was. That's the worst part of a sickbed, I think — the not knowing. I was a novice in a hospice in the Gate. I know the look of a man who has been told he did all he could, and hasn't yet believed it."

She doesn't say he looks guilty. She doesn't say he looks innocent, either. She lets the words settle and watches.

When it comes to the shed, her gaze follows his to it, and holds there a beat too long before returning to him. There is nothing accusing in it. If anything, her expression has gone careful, the kind of careful a healer wears on a landing where something may still be breathing on the other side of a door.

"What kind of work did they do before they were shut in?" she asks gently, as though the question were small. Her eyes move once toward the smoky air and then back. "And the rose-coloured dust on their gear and aprons — is that from the new salts, or was it always here? You said the shed was the only thing that changed. I'd rather know what 'changed' means before any of us is part of it."

She has not offered her light yet. The Lantern is there, behind her eyes, a warmth at the base of her thought. She holds it banked, ready, but makes no sign. She has seen fear put on a good face before, and she has seen grief do the same. She wants one honest thing, if Hale can give it: the truth about the thing they would be walking into if they go to that shed.

Sefa meets his hard look and does not flinch from it.

“Forgive the word, Master Hale. I had only the three of us in mind, and Pell walking down there. I said ‘fourth’ without counting it. No count meant against your crew.”

She lets it lie there — not apology carried too far, just a correction offered plainly. As he tears the page out, she doesn’t crowd him. When he lays it beside the case, she says quietly, “May I?” and takes it up only when he doesn’t object.

She reads it back word for word, exactly as it’s written, her voice even and unhurried; where the list of names begins, she reads each one and each sum, her finger following the line beneath the paper, not skipping. Then she sets it down again beside the case.

“That’s word for word, Master Hale. Nothing added, nothing rounded. Your mark, if you’ll make it, and one of us will witness it. Then the case, and we’ll put this in Maela’s hand before the coach leaves.”

As she speaks, she glances once toward the doorway, where Bram keeps sight of the slope.

“Is Pell still in the open? I won’t shout again unless he’s gone off the boards.”

messages.text:
Sefa is already moving before Osric finishes the word *Always*. She steps past him and Bram into the daylight, calling down the slope as she goes:

“Pell! Answer if you can hear us!” Then, off that shout, to no one in particular: “Not a sound — come on.”

She doesn’t wait for a plan. She turns her head back only far enough to fix Bram with a look that says *with me*, then starts down toward the lower cut at a walk that’s almost a run, keeping to the rutted track where the ground has been packed hard by the cart.

“Stay off the boards where you can,” she calls to Bram over the white glare. “And don’t get between me and him once we’re in.” There is no command in it now, only the intensity of someone who has worked through worse in a ward and knows what the first moments matter.

As her boots leave the last flat ground, she closes one hand around her prayer beads and speaks a single word, soft as a vigil:

“Light.”

A clear, pale radiance rises from the worn beads at her neck, bright enough for the shadows under the shed but throwing no heat, no cracked wood, no spark. She keeps it low by her chest, where it won’t blind her.

Her stride slows only at the edge of the lower cut, where the ground begins to look shelved and unsettled. There she pauses a heartbeat, searching the dark under the shed for any shape, any stirring, any gleam of Pell’s gear — and for where the old working might have swallowed a man.

messages.text:
Sefa doesn't run. The ground has told them what it thinks of running. She moves forward only as far as the rock along the low face, one hand on the damp stone, her light held low and her eyes on the hole.

"Pell! We hear you. Keep your voice every little while. We're not coming in over the boards. Bram is going to anchor on the old lowering ring and send a line in. Don't strike a light in there — my light's cold; no spark from it."

She looks back at Bram, and the words come quick, each one pointed at the ground between them.

"Anchor it to the ring and belay from there. I'll carry the end to him with my hand — my mage hand, not a flame. It'll do the reaching; my feet stay on good rock. If he's hurt, I can reach him with healing from here. But I can't haul, Bram. That's your rope and your back."

She turns half toward Osric, never turning her light from the hole. "Master Hale, stay behind the brown stone. If the shelf so much as whispers, you call, and we all come off. You know the ground better than we do. Watch it for all of us."

Then she raises one hand, and the air just beyond the hole stirs: a small, translucent hand shaped of pale light, unhurried, visible as a heatless shimmer. She directs it not into the hole yet, but toward the rope's free end, meaning to guide a loop down to Pell without putting anything living onto the collapsed step.

Her own feet stay on the bare rock ridge, within sight of the glint of water, and well short of the black timber lip.

messages.text:
Sefa keeps her light steady over the hole and her feet planted on the wet rock. She doesn't take her eyes from Pell for long.

"Pell, it's Sefa. The loop's beside you. Can you get it under either arm — one's enough to start, we won't haul until you say. Tell me what's holding you: stone, timber, your leg. And whether you're bleeding anywhere."

Her voice is calm, each word given a clean edge, as if the water and the smell and the rotten shelf can't have the last word while she's above it.

"I've healing light here. Not fire — warmth. It'll find you if I send it. I'm sending a little now to keep your hands working. Hold still, don't waste breath."

As she says it, she lets the Lantern's power move through her and down through the square of sunlight on the water: a soft, golden warmth, no flame and no spark, settling around Pell's head and shoulders like a breath from a summer window. It carries no haze, no smoke. It only gives what she gives — restoring health and steadiness.

She spends two dice of her healing light on him.

[Healing Light: spend 2 dice — 2d6 — on Pell. Update counter: Healing Light 4/6.]

Then, without turning far, she says lower to Bram:

"When you pull, I'll keep the mage-hand on the rope above the splinters and hold it off the broken edge — ten pounds is all it can carry, but it can keep the line from fouling. We take his weight only on your rope, not on my hand. And if he's wedged, you've the bar to lever, not the line."

Sefa does not take her eyes from the square of light over the water, but her voice carries to both men.

"Pell, there's something else down there with you — lower, to your left. My healing didn't all stay with you. It caught on it, the way a cold room pulls at a lamp in a doorway. Don't go reaching into the dark for anything. Tell me if you feel the water moving around your legs, or any change in it."

She turns her head just enough to speak to Bram without losing her place.

"Keep the load line exactly as it is. Pell's silk loop's lying out on the spoil where we can't step. I'll fetch it with the hand — it weighs next to nothing — and you can make it fast to something on this side. The more lines to him, the more we can do without putting a boot on the shelf."

As she says it, the translucent hand forms again in the air just beyond the good rock. It crosses the six feet of rotten ground low and slow, never touching the white crust, closes its fingers around the silk loop, and carries it back to Bram's free side.

Then, without turning her head fully, she addresses Osric:

"Master Hale, you'll not leave either of those things at the house unwitnessed. Fetch the letter and the case down here to the good rock. I'll put my mark and we'll seal it with the wax as it stands. Then go for the lads, and for strong backs. But if you know of any tale about a dressed stone set down in that cut, say it before you take the road. There's a tenant in that water, and I won't have you meet it on your way into town."

She keeps the healing light low and steady, and her feet do not leave the wet ridge. Her weight is braced, as if the stone under her ought to be enough.

“Pell, no hauling. The loop stays for the water, and only for the water. The silk’s up with us, the bar’s at Bram’s foot, and the pole’s in the shaft. We hear you. Hold quiet.”

“We won’t argue it over his head. I’ll walk the case and letter to Beregost now — not with his leg still under the block. I’ll find Thorn and the crew if they’re in a place an alehouse can point to. That leaves the coach handled and a road-messenger already on the move.”

She turns enough then to look Bram in the eye.

“You and Hale go down together, if he will. That’s two pairs of hands to dig and lever, and the ring holds the line. No flame down there. I can fix a cold light to the end of the pole before I go—the Lantern’s kind, not a spark—so you can see without kindling anything.” A pause, full of care. “He lost a man in that water three years back. If you go down with him, let him work with his head, not his grief. And mind the tenant my light caught. Don’t turn your back on the deep side of that block. If the water moves like something in it is awake, you put yourselves on the line and call.”

She looks out once toward the open house where Osric has gone, and then back to the square of sun on the still water below.

“Pell, you’re not to be civilised. You’re to stay awake and tell us if your leg starts to go cold where the stone meets it. You’ll be asking for a hot meal by dark, not a barge.”

Sefa picks up the pen without ceremony and kneels beside the letter, using the flat rock as a desk.

"I'll witness it now. Hold the page steady, Master Hale."

She signs in a clear, unhurried hand beneath his mark: *Sefa Marrin, courier by hire of Maela Thorn, witnessed at Whitestone this day.* Then she sets the pen down, opens her tinderbox, and strikes a light for the candle-end — up on the rock, well away from the hole, exactly as he said. She lets Osric tip the wax and set his seal with his own hand.

When the seal has cooled, she folds the letter carefully and places it in her belt pouch. The oak case she takes up and holds under one arm.

"I'll carry both to Thorn. She'll have them before the coach leaves, or none of us has earned anything." She looks from Bram to Osric. "Pell said somebody must walk now. That's me."

Her voice turns practical, not hard.

"So while I'm gone, Hale stays up here on the ring and the ridge. You, Bram, go down. Pell's arms are sound — two of you can clear the near edge of the block and work the prop while Hale tends the line and lowers the bucket and the bar. That keeps a man at the rope and a clear road for help."

She turns to the larch pole and touches it near its upper end. A pale, heatless light kindles there, the colour of starlight under water.

"I'll leave this light on the pole for you. It lasts an hour — not a breath more — so set the first work inside that hour. No flame down there. And listen for the water. If you see movement behind that flat grey wall Pell spoke of, you call Hale and both come up the line at once. The rayed disc and tally-marks are not ours to open. Don't touch them. Don't tap the wall to see if it's hollow. Dig only at the near edge of the block, and let the block answer."

She settles the case over her shoulder as best she can, checks the letter's folded edge in her pouch, and readies herself at the edge of the good rock.

"I'll ask after Hob in every alehouse on the way to Thorn's and send the crew out as soon as they're found. Keep the track clear in case I meet them coming back."

He lost a man, perhaps reluctant; but he can be persuaded to help. He is warden, knows cut. Two below: Bram and Osric. Sefa stays up top tending line, as Bram asked. But Osric is leaving for town to find crew and Fist. Maybe persuade him to stay and work, because crew won't arrive before dark and Pell needs two now. But Sefa is weakest, not good digger; Bram needs able body. Osric is strong, knows rock. Let Sefa deliver case? Osric refuses. Maybe Sefa can persuade Osric that if they get Pell out by dusk, then he can take the case and letter? But he won't carry case. Could Sefa leave case with Osric while she goes down? He won't carry it but could guard it? The case can wait. Contract says case must be in Thorn's hands by sunset. If no deliver, pay lost. Could ask Osric to carry only the case to Thorn, no letter, while Sefa stays. He said no. Maybe he can be persuaded? "Not as warden, but as a man trying to save one of his own: take it." But maybe too much.

Need respond to Bram's call. We can stop, look back down the slope, and decide. Maybe speak to Osric: "I need you to tell me where Hob drinks before I go further. And if you mean to knock at the Fist, tell them two men are below and one pinned—they might send a patrol quicker than the crew." But also answer Bram: "I'll be back with help; I'm no digger. If I stay, I can't haul, only hold light and heal. You need Hale with you. Master Hale, if you won't carry the salt, carry the letter and send help, but stay with Bram until more hands come." Yet that could be bossy.

Let's think of Sefa's voice: calm, decisive, practical. She doesn't plead. She knows her strengths: healing and light, not digging. She can walk fast, negotiate with Thorn, find crew. Bram can dig with Osric if Osric stays, but Osric is heading to town. She can say: "I am not the second pair of hands. Hale is." Maybe ask Osric: "Your man is under your own stone, on your own ground. You said two men by dusk. You are one. Are you leaving him?" That would challenge him. But he lost a man and may be too afraid. Could be powerful. Sefa can set it before him. Also deliver case? Maybe she can ask Bram to come up and walk case? No. Could give case to Osric to guard? Hmm.

Maybe Sefa doesn't yet leave. She can turn and call down to Bram: "I'm coming back. Hold, don't go alone." Then to Osric: "We settle this now. There are three of us. Pell needs two below, one on the line. I can be the one on the line and healing, but I won't be any use moving stone. That leaves you and Bram below. Unless you'd rather take my case down the road and send the Fist, while I hold his head?" That lays out options. She can ask Osric to choose: go for help or go down. But she still has case. She can leave it on the rock while they work; Thorn's pay may be lost, but lives first. She might accept that. This is likely the heroic choice. But contract is important. Could still try to get crew later.

The GM gave "you offered a cold light... Bram asked you to tend his line, and that conflicts with leaving. It's your call next round." So we need make call. Maybe I should choose to stay, and ask Osric to go for help/case? But Osric won't carry case. Could ask him to carry letter only and get Fist/crew. Then Sefa stays with Bram/Pell. That seems best: she stays on rope/light/healing; Osric walks to Beregost anyway. But then case not delivered by sunset; pay lost, but Pell saved maybe. Another option: Sefa gives Osric case despite his refusal and says "I release it into your hand as Thorn's hired courier; the salt still leaves in buyer's man's hands? You are not house carter, but you'd be a man helping his people." Maybe he won't. We can attempt Persuasion. If he refuses, decide. The player may want to ask game master? No. We can roleplay.

We need write one message. Could have Sefa call to Bram: "Don't go below alone. I'm coming back." Then to Osric: "Hale, I am going to hand you the case and the letter, and you will carry them to Maela Thorn. I'll witness this: the salt goes from your hand to hers, not Pryce's. You are not the house's carter. You are the man walking off this quarry to save his crew's wages. I will stay and be the second pair at the rope and the third hand with a bucket. If you refuse, I'll leave the case on the rock and we all lose." Hmm. But this is pressuring. Sefa can do that.

Alternatively, she can take case back, put it on rock, and say to Osric: "Then we save Pell first, case after. Tell Thorn why. We'll lose the fee but not the man." But Bram has no way to rescue with only one below. Maybe Osric can stay and work; Sefa delivers case and returns with crew. But by then too late. The most logical is: send Osric to town with case/letter, since he's already walking; Sefa stays. That covers both goals: case delivered, help fetched (Osric says he'll knock Fist and pass Thorn's door). But Osric refuses to carry case. We can try to persuade him. We have +7 Persuasion. This is a good moment to use it. Since this is a meaningful social check with uncertain outcome, GM may ask roll? But as player, we can attempt and roleplay; GM will card. Need not roll ourselves? We should make persuasive argument. Could mention "I'll sign your book that it went from you to her in the buyer's man's absence; no one can fault the warden." But still maybe DC 15.

Sefa stops on the track. She turns all the way round, so Bram can see she isn't leaving. "Bram, you don't go below alone. I'm coming back. Hold where you are."

Then she walks not toward Bram but to Osric, closing the ten paces, case against her side.

"Master Hale, you are already on the road. You said you would knock at the Fist and pass Thorn's door. Do more. Walk to Thorn's shop with this case and the letter in your own hand, and tell her I remained at the quarry as her hire: to keep Pell alive and to see the salt got to her, even if it isn't by her chosen hand. Bram stays clear of the doorway with his sword sheathed. He looks over the man's apron and hands, and past him into the house.

Pell answers for the group before you have to. He tells the man, whom he calls master Hale, that the three of you are couriers, paid ninety on delivery and nothing before, much like the man's own crew. He asks who carries the wages out from the Gate, and whose house that factor or clerk serves. He says that if someone is skimming both ends, Thorn will want the name, because a buyer's coach leaves at sunset and she will be shouting by suppertime. He offers to carry a written statement of the three weeks unpaid, sealed with the man's own mark, to her hand along with the case, while the man keeps a copy. Then he asks about the long shed down the lower cut with its door standing open, wondering whether one of the man's crew left it in a rush or whether the mule went in there.

Osric does not answer straight away. You keep your tone level, as you spoke it, and watch how he takes it.

His hands are a cutter's hands: broad, split at the knuckles, the nails worn to the quick, and no weapon anywhere near them. White dust is ground into the creases of his apron like flour. Near the pocket a faint smear of grit shows a different colour, pinkish, the shade of a rose gone pale, where something was wiped off once and not brushed away.

Past his shoulder you can see part of one room. A kettle hangs over the coals of the hearth, and a scrubbed table holds a fat book bound in stained canvas with a pen stuck through its strap. Next to the book sits a small case of dark oak, banded in brass, about the size of a loaf, with a disc of red wax across the clasp. A coat hangs on a peg just inside the door, and a blackthorn stick leans under it.

Sefa's card stands as it is: an Insight check against an easy difficulty, with her own Insight added. Her paragraph shapes what she watches for, Osric's eyes while he answers rather than his anger, and the narration after your roll will follow that.

Two things in your text aren't in the scene yet, so I'll treat them as proposals:

- **The pinkish smear.** I haven't described any mark on Osric's apron. I'll take it as Sefa looking closely at the apron and its pocket. What she actually sees there, if anything, comes after the die.
- **Pell's offer.** In the scene as I have it, Pell hasn't offered the warden anything aloud. If Pell says something this round, it comes in his player's paragraph. Sefa's nod will land on whatever he actually says, and if he says nothing, her nod lands on nothing.

When you're ready, roll the die.

Thank you, that's a vivid read, and it tells me exactly where Sefa's attention goes. I'll keep that part as hers: she is watching the weight he carries, not the anger. She wants to know whether he is performing or worn down, and whether he stands in that doorway to guard a trap or to shield something.

What she finds there is the world's to say, though, so these stay proposals until the narration settles them:

- **What Osric feels.** Grief, fear, and for whom. The die you've seen decides how far her read gets. Who Osric really is decides what's there to find.
- **The pink smear and what made it.** It still isn't on the apron in the scene as I've described it. If there's any mark there, the narration will show it after the die, and it won't come with an explanation.
- **His glance toward the lower shed.** In the scene so far he has only looked past Bram at the cart. Where his eyes go next is his, and I'll show it in the narration if it happens.

When you're ready, press Onward or use one of your rerolls. Either way, the narration picks up from Sefa watching him exactly as you wrote it.

Thanks, that gives me Sefa's stance clearly. She waits, says nothing, keeps her weight back and her hands easy, and watches Osric's face for what sits under his words. Her years at the hospice bedside are hers to draw on. The narration after the die will follow her silence and her patience.

A few things in your paragraph go beyond what the scene has shown, so I'll treat them as Sefa's impressions or as proposals, not as facts of the world yet:

- **"A man who has sat with the dead."** That stands as Sefa's first impression of him. Whether anyone has died, and whether that is what weighs on Osric, is still the world's to show. Your die decides how far her read gets toward it.
- **"The hand that waited outside his door."** Nothing in the scene matches this yet. If you mean someone Sefa suspects is out of sight, I'll read it as her watching for anyone else at the house. If you meant something you think was described, tell me and I'll check.
- **"Pell's lead."** In the scene as it stands, Pell stepped back and let Bram take the front. He kept to the side, about twenty feet from the door, reading the yard. Sefa will register that, and Bram's stillness, and that nobody is crowding Osric.
- **"Where death has already been."** So far the yard shows no blood, no struggle and nothing knocked over. Bram looked for exactly that and found nothing. If Sefa feels death in the place, that is her feeling, and I'll write it as hers.

The card still waits. Press Onward to go with the die as it fell, or use one of Sefa's allowed rerolls if you want it.

Thanks, that's a clear move, and Sefa's words and manner are hers. When you press Onward, she says that line aloud just as you wrote it: low, unhurried, no bargain attached, no step closer. She keeps watching his face, his breathing and where his worry goes.

Two parts of it work differently, so I'll handle them separately:

- **"You're not barring the door against us."** That stands as Sefa's own read, said to his face. Osric reacts to it as something she believes about him. Whether it's right is the world's to show. The die you've already seen decides how much of him she can actually read while she says it.
- **The offer of steady hands.** It's on the table now, said plainly. Osric answers it his own way, and he may take it, turn it, or ignore it. Pell and Bram act in that same moment as their players decide.

Press Onward when you're ready, or ask for one of your rerolls if you want one.

Got it. Onward it is, and both of Sefa's rerolls stay unspent. You read the table right: the card was all that stood between Sefa's silence and what comes next, and nothing more was needed from you. When the scene goes on, the narration opens with what Sefa reads in Osric as she holds that quiet. After that come Osric's answer to her offer and to Bram's question, and whatever Pell and Bram do in the same breath.

You stop in the middle of the cart track with the oak case against your hip and turn all the way round, so that anyone looking up from the low face can see you have stopped walking. Your voice carries back down across the white yard, and the quarry is so quiet that it reaches the bottom: he is not to go below alone, you are coming back to the rope, and he should wait for you before he puts a foot in that water.

Ten paces behind you, Osric has stopped too, with the blackthorn stick planted in the dust. He watches you walk back to him. He doesn't step aside and he doesn't step forward.

You lay it out for him in a clear, level voice. It takes two men by dusk, and Bram is one. Hale won't carry the salt and won't go down, and one woman can't be on the road and under the ground at once. So you will stay to hold the line, keep the light and heal. He is to walk into Thorn's shop, not just past her door, with the case and the witnessed letter in his hand. He is to tell her that you stayed at Whitestone on your hire to keep a man alive, and that he isn't carting the house's salt but carrying the buyer's goods because the buyer's courier is standing over a hole. You hold the case out but keep hold of it. If he refuses, the case goes back on the rock and everyone loses the coin, because you won't lose Pell to a contract.
Go ahead and roll. The card stands as called: Persuasion +7 against DC 15, with advantage. When the turn goes on, the story will show how Osric answers on the road.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Pell Dunmore — Human, rogue 5 (Thief), Lower City roof-runner turned hireling, level 5
HP 33/33 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 10 · DEX 17 · CON 13 · INT 13 · WIS 12 · CHA 12
Skills: Stealth +9 (expertise); Sleight of Hand +6; Acrobatics +6; Perception +4; Investigation +4; Insight +4; Tools: thieves' tools +9 (expertise)
Saves: Dexterity saving throw +6 (proficient); Intelligence saving throw +4 (proficient); Strength saving throw +0; Constitution saving throw +1; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +1
Attacks: Shortsword +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing; Dagger +6 to hit, 1d4+3 piercing, thrown 20/60; Shortbow +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 80/320; Sneak Attack: +3d6 once a turn with advantage or an ally beside the target
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Sneak Attack 3d6; Cunning Action: Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action; Uncanny Dodge: a reaction halves the damage of an attack he can see; Fast Hands (Thief): a bonus action to use an object — a potion on another, a lock, a lamp; Second-Story Work: climbs at full speed; Thieves' Cant
Limits: Light armour; 33 hit points — he cannot stand at the front for long; Sneak Attack needs advantage or an ally beside the target
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 31 gp; 2 ep; 6 sp; 55 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Thieves' Tools; Main hand: Shortsword
Pack: Arrow ×20; Bedroll and Rations; Dagger ×2; Flask of Oil ×2; Hooded Lantern; Potion of Healing ×3; Shortbow; Silk Rope (50 feet)

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 1 — what does Pell Dunmore do?

You hang back a step and let Bram go ahead of you. As you walk, you say quietly to both of them that the picks are down and the mule is loose, and that the warden isn't coming out to meet paying folk. You say either the crew ran or someone has told him to stand there and look ordinary. You ask Bram to do the talking while you keep watch.

Bram sheathes his sword, shield at his side, and walks into the yard, looking over the scattered tools and empty sheds. He stops a few paces short of the doorway, gives his name, says Maela Thorn sent you for a sealed case of dye-salts, and asks if the man is the warden. He adds that the place is quiet for a working day and asks if something happened.

Sefa slows as the quarry opens up, then murmurs to you and Bram that the man in the apron looks like the warden, that he doesn't seem eager to hand anything over, and that no one is working. She tells you both to keep your hands easy and says she will speak first. Then she steps toward the house, hands open, dagger untouched, and stops well short of arm's reach. She says Maela Thorn sent you from Beregost with her mark for the sealed case, for the coach that leaves by sunset, and asks if his day is as strange as it looks.

You stop about twenty feet short of the door, a little apart from Bram, with a clear line back to the spoil heaps.

Reading the yard is a roof-runner's ordinary work, so it needs no roll. The dust holds a day's tracks, softened by wind but plain: a dozen or more pairs of boots heading down the cart track toward the Way, all together and unhurried, the prints evenly spaced. A mule's hoofprints run beside one man's boots, set a little apart from the rest. Nobody came up the track to meet them, and nothing was dragged. The cart traces weren't cut. Someone unbuckled them and looped them back over the shaft, the way a carter does when he expects to come back, or wants it to look that way. No doors are forced. The house window has no curtain, only shadow and the glow of a hearth, and nobody moves inside. One door stands ajar: a long low shed down by the lower cut, where the terraces drop into a darker, damper face.

The man in the apron hears Bram and Sefa out without unfolding his arms.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is low and dry with dust. "Yes. It's strange."

He looks past Bram at the cart, then back.

"Crew walked off. Noon bell yesterday. Three weeks, not a copper from the Gate." He says it flat, as if he has said it to himself all night. "They left the tools because the tools belong to the house. Let the house come pick them up."

You watch him while he talks and try to see what sits under the words. Your Insight read on him is not settled yet.

You watch him while he talks and try to see what sits under the words.

You read the anger easily. It sits in the set of his jaw and the way his fingers press white into his own sleeves. You can't get past it. He doesn't look like a man who fears whoever might be behind him, or like a man reciting a story someone gave him. If there's more under the anger, it stays out of your reach. His face is a closed door with nothing to pick.

"The case is inside," Osric says. He doesn't step aside. "It stays inside till somebody tells me where the money went. Your Thorn woman paid for that salt. Somebody took it. Wasn't me, and it wasn't my lads." His eyes go to Sefa, then to Bram, the two who did the talking. "Did she pay? Who'd she pay it to?"

Behind him the hearth ticks and settles. The iron keys on his belt shift as he breathes. The thin smoke from the chimney rises straight up into the bright, windless late-morning air, and down by the lower cut the shed door stands as it did, a hand's width open onto the dark.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: in the quarry yard, about twenty feet from the house door, apart from the others · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 2 — what does Pell Dunmore do?

Bram leaves the doorway clear and keeps his sword sheathed. He looks over the man's apron and hands, and past him into the house.

Sefa holds her ground and watches the warden. When he gives no answer, she keeps her voice level and doesn't press. She says you have no wish to make his trouble yours unless you must, that you are here for the case, and that if anything stands between you and it, you had best know now while the sun is still high enough to act. She glances once at the smoke, then back at him.

Osric does not answer straight away. His hands are a cutter's hands: broad, split at the knuckles, the nails worn to the quick, and no weapon anywhere near them. White dust is ground into the creases of his apron like flour. Near the pocket a faint smear of grit shows a different colour, pinkish, the shade of a rose gone pale, where something was wiped off once and not brushed away.

Past his shoulder you can see part of one room. A kettle hangs over the hearth coals, and a scrubbed table holds a fat book bound in stained canvas with a pen stuck through its strap. Beside it sits a small case of dark oak, banded in brass, about the size of a loaf, with a disc of red wax across the clasp. A coat hangs on a peg just inside the door, and a blackthorn stick leans under it.

"Something between you and the case," Osric says to Sefa. "Aye. The money."

He hears you out, and his jaw works at *same as your lads, near enough* as if he'd like to argue it and can't.

"House is Vandarren. In the Gate. Patriar house, or used to be." He says the name like a stone he's been carrying in his pocket. "Their man's Pryce. Factor. Salt goes out of here sealed, and the money for it goes to Pryce. Pryce sends the wages back by runner, first of the month and the fifteenth." A beat. "Didn't. Twice now."

He thinks about the letter longer than about anything else you said.

"Write it. Aye." He nods once, slowly. "Witnessed. That I'll do. You read it out to her, in front of her, not after." His eyes go to the sun, high over the white faces, and then to the coat on its peg. "I'm for the town at noon myself. Lads'll be drinking it out somewhere. Want them to hear it from me, not from a broadsheet."

When the shed comes up, his hand doesn't go to the keys at all. It stays pressed flat against his sleeve, and you can see why: the shed door hangs on warped boards and has no lock to need a key. He looks past you, not at the shed but below it, at the lower face where the terraces drop away into stone stained dark with damp.

"Lower cutting-shed. Nobody in it. Door's warped. Won't shut. Mule went with Hob, the carter. He was owed the most."

Then Osric unfolds his arms, turns into the house and sits heavily at the table, leaving the door open behind him. He slides the pen free of its strap, opens the canvas-bound book to a clean page at the back and starts to write, slowly, pressing hard, his lips moving over the words. The oak case sits at his elbow with its red wax catching the hearth light. The kettle starts to tick as it comes to the boil.

Where you are: yard outside Osric's house at the quarry · Time: Day 1 · morning

Round 3 — what does Pell Dunmore do?

You stepped up to the threshold, leaned on the frame with your hands in view, and asked Osric whose seal was on the wax and whether the stain on him was the salt. Then you told Bram and Sefa to stay with him while he wrote, and asked Sefa to read the letter back before it was sealed. You walked down toward the lower cut.
